text:
General Motors on Thursday reported a year-over-year sales decline of 5.5%, with 670,974 new vehicles sold during the third quarter.

GM's sales of all-electric vehicles are down across the board, as enthusiasm for EVs wanes. EV demand spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending up to $7,500 in federal incentives for consumers to purchase an electric vehicle. During the same period last year, GM reported record sales of its electric vehicles.

Against those comparisons, EVs this year saw dramatic drops, with the Equinox EV down 92.4% during the most recent quarter, at 1,905 vehicles sold. The Blazer EV was down 84.4% and Hummer EV sales fell 72.9%.

The report comes after Cox Automotive said last week that new vehicle sales have been stronger than expected this year and raised its 2026 forecast by roughly 2%, to 16.1 million units.

Hybrid vehicle sales are expected to capture a growing market share of car sales, as inflated gas prices pressure consumers.

Despite offering a broad EV lineup, the Detroit automaker only offers one hybrid vehicle, a Corvette. Experts expect GM's weakness in the sector to impact its overall sales.

Hybrids assisted other automakers in outperforming GM in third-quarter sales.

Toyota Motor reported that its EV and hybrid vehicles made up over 57% of the Japanese automaker's sales this quarter.

Toyota said sales were up 0.6% for the most recent quarter, with 633,223 vehicles sold. Sales of its electrified vehicles, which include hybrids, were up 28.5%, with 363,367 units sold.

That helped Toyota continue to narrow its gap with U.S. sales leader GM, which is now less than 136,000 units. That compares to a full-year gap of roughly 335,000 units last year.

Cox Automotive earlier this year said if such sales trends continue, Toyota could once again overtake GM to become the U.S. sales leader in the coming years.

Honda Motor, which also offers several hybrids and leads major automakers in fuel economy in the U.S., reported a 9.3% increase in U.S. third-quarter sales. Its hybrid sales were a record of more than 106,000 units during the quarter.

"We've got really high demand for hybrids," Lance Woelfer, head of American Honda Motor's U.S. sales, told CNBC. "We're finding more and more consumers are figuring out hybrids meet their needs."

High fuel prices, with an AAA national average of $4.41, were also expected to impact sales of big trucks and SUVs, sectors that GM relies on. GM's full-size pickups were relatively flat.

Each of the automaker's brands are down so far year-to-date, led by a 25% decline in Cadillac.

GM's lower-cost vehicles are a bright spot for the company as consumers face high inflation. The Chevrolet Trailblazer was up 51% for the third quarter, while sales of Buick Envista were up 18.4% and Chevrolet Trax up 16.3%.

Despite falling sales, President of GM North American Duncan Aldred remained optimistic.

"Our business is performing very well, the launch of our next-generation full-size pickup trucks is on track, and we are making investments in new vehicles, innovative technologies, and our U.S. manufacturing footprint to drive our next phase of growth," Aldred said in a statement.

text:
Attorney General Dan Rayfield today sued the Trump Administration for scrapping federal limits on greenhouse gas pollution from many of the country’s largest power plants. Earlier this month, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) repealed rules requiring coal- and gas-fired power plants to cut their emissions. That decision opens the door to more pollution, which means hotter summers, stronger storms, more flooding, and more wildfire smoke.

“Oregonians know what a changing climate looks like. We’ve lived through the heat dome and summers where the smoke was so thick our kids couldn’t play outside,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “Pollution doesn’t stop at state lines, and power plants are one of the biggest sources of it. The law requires EPA to do something about that. Instead, the Trump Administration is letting the biggest polluters off the hook and leaving families to pay the price.”

The lawsuit asks the court to throw out the repeal and put the protections back in place. Oregon is also putting EPA on notice that it intends to sue over the agency’s long-running failure to limit pollution from existing natural gas power plants.

The rules EPA repealed – adopted in 2024 – required many of the nation’s largest power plants to reduce the carbon pollution they release. Power plants produce about a quarter of the country’s carbon dioxide emissions. Rather than hold them accountable, the Trump Administration wiped out limits for most coal- and gas-fired plants and has proposed ending power plant emission rules altogether.

More carbon pollution means more frequent and more intense heat waves, which are especially dangerous for children, older adults, and outdoor workers. It also means stronger storms and heavier flooding that damage homes, businesses, and roads, and more wildfire smoke that makes the air unsafe to breathe. Pollution from these plants can also worsen asthma, heart disease, and other serious illnesses, and it hits low-income communities hardest. And when extreme weather strikes, state and local governments are left to cover billions of dollars in recovery costs.

The states argue EPA broke the law by throwing out these limits without seriously considering other options or accounting for the real health and climate costs of more pollution. Because EPA failed to properly calculate what the repeal will cost the public, the states say the decision was arbitrary and capricious under federal law.

Separately, the states today notified EPA that they intend to sue over its failure to limit greenhouse gas pollution from many existing gas-fired power plants. These include “peaker” plants, which fire up when electricity demand is high and are often located in low-income communities and communities of color that already carry more than their share of pollution. EPA set standards for new gas plants more than a decade ago but has never done the same for existing ones, as the Clean Air Act requires.

Attorney General Rayfield filed this lawsuit alongside the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, along with the Governor of Pennsylvania, the Mayors of New York City and Chicago, and the City and County of Denver.

Alex Plant, Chief Executive of Scottish Water and Co-President of the Congress, said: "It is a tremendous honour for Scotland to welcome the world's water community to Glasgow.

“Water underpins public health, thriving communities, environmental resilience and economic prosperity. Yet across the world we face growing pressures from climate change, population growth and increasing demand.

“This Congress is an opportunity not only to discuss those challenges but to accelerate practical solutions. By bringing together expertise from every continent, we can learn from one another and develop the partnerships needed to deliver lasting change.

“Scotland has a strong story to share, from long-term investment in water infrastructure and innovation to our work on nature-based solutions, digital technology and building resilient services for future generations."

Throughout the event from October 4-8, delegates will take part in technical sessions, site visits and international forums examining how water can support resilience and prosperity in communities around the world.

Scottish Water will also showcase projects and innovations from across Scotland, while welcoming visitors to facilities and locations that demonstrate the country's expertise and ambition in the water sector.

The Congress theme, "Water Action: The Path to Resilience and Prosperity", reflects the growing recognition that water is fundamental to economic growth, healthy communities and environmental sustainability.

Discussions at the Scottish Event Campus (SEC) in Glasgow are expected to help shape the international water agenda in the years ahead.

Mr Plant said the conversations at the Congress in Glasgow would go far beyond infrastructure and engineering and would focus on how water supports thriving economies, sustainable communities, and a healthier environment throughout the world.

He said: “And this most critical of conversations cannot be the water sector talking to itself. Water sits at the centre of energy, housing, health, agriculture, planning, transport, and economic growth.

“The Congress will therefore bring together governments, regulators, utilities, investors, and industry to think system-wide about climate, nature, and growth.

“The programme that the IWA Committee has put together will focus on moving beyond end-of-pipe solutions and towards upstream interventions, embedding whole-system thinking and planning, driving cross-sector collaboration and recognising the foundational nature of water and waste water.”

He added that Scotland’s policy and regulatory framework — based on long-term planning, public ownership through an arms’ length public corporation, and robust independent economic regulation — has enabled a steady and sustained approach to investment.

“From catchment-scale thinking and nature-based solutions to digital innovation, low-carbon treatment and blue-green infrastructure, Scottish Water is developing practical solutions that can help build more resilient services.

“For example, last year we completed our £235m investment to link the Glasgow and Ayrshire networks, improving security of supply for one million people. And right now, we are working with partners to develop Pioneer Catchments in areas like the Almond, Angus Glens and South Esk, and Dee. These innovative projects draw sectors together to develop upstream solutions to address the key challenges presented by a changing climate in ways that are much cheaper and effective than if we only deal with these problems downstream.

“Hosting the world in Glasgow allows us and colleagues across the UK to showcase that kind of innovation — not to say we have all the answers, but to share what we are learning and to learn just as much from others.”

text:
I’m bleary-eyed on a westbound jet, spewing carbon to campaign for House seats—if you can join Third Actors in Bakersfield over the weekend, please do (though be warned that there’s yet another huge heat wave building, and the forecast is for a toasty 102 degrees on Sunday). But I thought I might weigh in on yesterday’s news that a “permitting reform” deal of sorts has been struck between Senate negotiators, and that there will (maybe) be a bill (called BAAJA, for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, not the Mexican peninsula yesterday battered by Hurricane Polo) voted on in the lame-duck session following midterm elections.

For those who (lucky you) haven’t been tracking all this closely, permitting reform has become a grail of sorts over the years—a grand bargain that could allow the country to get on with the much-needed job of building out new energy infrastructure, especially transmission corridors, in the years ahead. The question’s not whether that would be a good idea—it’s one of the basic building blocks for converting more of our energy system to renewables. It’s how many pounds of flesh the fossil fuel industry would demand in return, and how close to vital organs that flesh would be located.

I’m going to try to lay out the competing arguments, and then offer some reflections.

Here’s Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island and one of the most stalwart climate champions in DC, who negotiated the deal with his Democratic colleague Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, and Republicans Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia. And here’s Jane Fleagal, analyst at the Searchlight Institute, which exists to “disrupt the dominant paradigm of smallness, purity, and fear.” Fleagal describes the new bill as “awesome,” in large part because it’s

“a real path to get connected to the grid means way cleaner and more reliable power. More renewables and nuclear in the mix, and the gas that gets built isn't wacky turbines pulled off the aerospace supply chain.

Transmission people tell me this is some of the best language we've ever seen, better than they expected. Interregional AND regional planning, and a backstop process that actually works, with clear, uniform rules on cost allocation.

but there’s more! 3 serious interconnection reforms, advanced conductors, VPPs, local transmission oversight, judicial review parity with pipelines, and ratepayer protections with teeth.

She cites new modeling predicting it could cut co2 emissions from the electric system 9% in 2035 (it will take a while for this new stuff to get built). Basically, it could open up vast federal lands in the West to produce solar and wind, and the transmission corridors to get that power to the coasts. “You really have to contort yourself to believe tech-neutral reforms that make it easier to build big stuff, especially on federal land, won't help clean energy more than anything else,” she writes.

Here, with five count’em five bylines, is Heatmap’s big explainer on the bill, which includes enumerating the pounds of flesh, and they are large. For instance,

Current federal law requires an environmental review under NEPA for “major federal actions,” a term that is defined broadly to mean any action subject to “substantial federal control and responsibility.”

BAAJA would narrow that definition so that NEPA review would not be required for federal loans, certain grant programs, and repairs of essential infrastructure, among other actions. Geothermal testing, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission permits for transmission projects, and gas pipeline projects within existing rights-of-way would also be excluded.

And

BAAJA would also codify several regulatory changes to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act that Trump’s EPA proposed earlier this year to limit state power. Under current law, a federal agency cannot issue a permit to a project that will discharge pollution into a body of water unless the relevant state or tribe issues a water quality certification or waives that right. The permitting bill would give states and Tribes a maximum of one year to review a project or otherwise waive their right to certify. Senators also proposed that if the state or Tribe waives certification, the matter is settled — the federal government cannot then conduct its own water quality review. If the state or Tribe decide to attach conditions to a certification, or to deny the project altogether, the bill would place a much higher burden of proof on them to back up their decision. States would only be allowed to reject a project based on water quality — they could not cite air pollution or climate impacts.

It’s provisions like these that set off an immediate reaction from many climate and environmental justice groups. Here, for instance, is Colin Rees, of Oil Change International, a reliable fighter against big energy projects

“This backdoor ‘dirty deal’ will worsen the climate crisis and put families at even greater risk of losing their homes and loved ones to extreme weather. The science is clear: There are no new fossil fuel projects compatible with a climate-safe future. Yet this ‘dirty deal’ would make it easier and faster for fossil fuel companies to steamroll community opposition to their polluting, climate-wrecking projects.

“This ‘dirty deal’ threatens to raise electricity prices for working families by accelerating the buildout of energy-guzzling AI data centers and liquefied natural gas export projects. Our recent research shows that the Trump administration’s support for reckless AI development and greater gas exports drives up energy costs for households.

“We all deserve a voice in the decisions that impact our lives. The ‘dirty deal’ shuts communities out of decisionmaking spaces, especially the Black, Brown, and Indigenous communities that are disproportionately harmed by polluting fossil fuel projects. We urge all senators to stand firm against this bill.”

And here’s Jeremy Symon, who plays a role perhaps analogous to Fleagal’s on the other side of the question, as a respected independent policy analyst. He wrote me this morning to say “this thing is awful.”

The scariest thing about this bill is that it hands Trumps unprecedented powers to lock in forever permits his buddies want so that congress, the courts, and the next president can’t undo his vision of fossil fuel dominance. The day after this bill passes, Trump will hang an even bigger “for sale” sign on the White House door for corporations that want forever permits for bad ideas. If his campaign donors want permits to drill for oil and gas along the Atlantic Coast, then the next president’s hands will be tied because of this bill. If the new congress wants to try to give communities more power to challenge data centers, it will be too late. Under this bill, they would have to pay Elon Musk and Trump’s other tech buddies compensation -- with taxpayer money -- to reverse whatever permits Trump hands them over the next two years.

In some sense I straddle these worlds. I’ve been to jail with Colin Rees in the fights against various pipelines, and I worked shoulder-to-shoulder with Symons to convince the Biden administration to pause development of new LNG terminals—perhaps the biggest win of the decade for the environmental movement, though one overturned by the Trump election. And I’ve also—as readers of this newsletter know perhaps too well—devoted myself to the rapid buildout of solar, wind, and batteries as the main scaleable way to drive down carbon emissions. So let me try to add some context on how to think about it.

The first thing to remember is, the real goal for people who care about the climate above all is not to build more renewables, it’s to drive down the amount of carbon flowing into the atmosphere. Building more renewables is a key way of doing that—but only if they displace fossil fuel.

And here is an important divergence: for many people working in the clean energy industry, victory looks like doubling or tripling their output, even if fossil fuel is growing fast at the same time. Even if they got into this fight for the right reasons, their commitment is—because, capitalism—to their bottom line. It’s important not to confuse the two motivations, because physics only cares about the carbon. If transmission corridors are matched by new gas pipelines, we haven’t made much progress.

And it’s easy enough to say: well, if sun and wind and batteries are cheaper and cleaner, they’ll win out once we’ve lowered the barriers for everyone here. But that ignores the context, which, regrettably, is the Trump administration. This regime has done literally everything possible to sabotage, hinder, and destroy the clean energy idea—they possess what I think can only be described as a pathological hatred of these new technologies, and have specialized in coming up with ever-more-inventive ways of derailing them. (New wind projects, even in the middle of the country, are currently on hold because of “national security,” which is the rough equivalent of asking if the turbines were at the Atlanta Hawks game). That means that climate writer Lissa Harris has a pretty good point when she asks

why do we presume any of these mfers will do anything but wipe their ass with this deal when Boss Baby decides he hates a wind project next year?

The answer is that so far we really don’t have an answer to that. Whitehouse said yesterday that there had been progress on guarantees from the White House (such a fun sentence to write) but that they were as yet “unresolved.” Remember, these people were insisting as late as last week that solar power can’t work because the sun goes down at night. I mean, Lee Zeldin, secretary of the Environmental Pollution Agency, was in New Hampshire yesterday arguing for ending all auto emissions tests

It’s hard, therefore, not to be suspicious that the support of the oil industry for this bill masks their confidence that they are best positioned to exploit it, and to use other powers of the federal government to block their rivals.

It is obvious that federal policy necessarily proceeds by compromise—the question is whether the compromise risks too much. This may be a place where being involved for too long in these fights is a handicap, making one risk-averse from prior experience. Here’s my nightmare:

In December 2015, when pretty much the entire environmental world was in Paris working on the climate accords, the Congress quickly and without much debate passed a law ending the ban on crude oil exports from America, in return for tax credits for the renewable industry. I wrote what I think was the only oped opposing that idea—I can remember tapping away at it in some Parisian cafe, and handing the result off to Mike Brune, then head of the Sierra Club, for review. We hastily published it at, I think, the Huffington Post, and on the Club website.

Behind closed doors in Washington, Republican leaders are trying once again to commandeer the federal budget to the benefit of their fossil fuel benefactors -- and they are getting an assist from some leading Democrats as well. They are apparently negotiating with the GOP to end the long-standing ban on crude oil exports, a move that would dramatically undercut America’s negotiation position, and demonstrate that the oil industry maintains a firm grip on both our political parties. A vote on lifting the ban could come as early as Friday -- the very day that the world is supposed to be reaching its final climate pact.

Ending the oil export ban is a poor idea on many grounds: Unions oppose it because it will cost refinery jobs, conservationists oppose it because it will lead to more drilling in sensitive areas and increased pollution in communities of color. It makes a mockery of the idea that we’re actually interested in “energy independence.” We’d get 4,500 more rail cars a day full of explosive oil. It’s such bad policy that 69 percent of Americans, across both parties, oppose lifting the ban.

And if it’s bad policy, it’s even worse timing. Right at the very moment when we desperately need to be reducing emissions and investing in clean energy solutions -- right when President Obama in his Paris speech and his Keystone XL rejection has called for leaving carbon underground -- lifting the crude oil export ban would do the exact opposite: add 3.3 million barrels of extra oil production per day between now and 2035. That’s more than 515 million metric tons of carbon pollution per year, the equivalent of the annual emissions from 108 million passenger vehicles or 135 coal-fired power plants.

Who wants this shift in policy? That’s easy. Kenneth Cohen, spokesman for ExxonMobil, told the New York Times in October “the sooner this happens, the better for us.”

As we lobbied via email, I exchanged opinions with a Senator deeply involved in that fight, and in this one. He assured me I was wrong—that the compromise would be “big, and net carbon reducing.” As it turns out, it’s possible that the disastrous bill may have been more important than the Paris climate accords. Over the course of a decade they turned America into the world’s largest hydrocarbon exporter, and rewrote the shape of global energy markets. They gave American oil interests the power to, among other things, help install Trump back in office. It was a well-meaning and utterly and profoundly disastrous compromise, one that the Serious People in DC and the press supported, as they will this one.

I’m not saying this is the same thing, or that it means it’s wrong to back this bill—this is far better thought out. But it has the weird coincidence of coming at another moment when we’re winning—then, the Paris accords; now, fingers crossed, the midterm elections. It’s going to be very odd to win those elections, in no small part on the strength of people’s revulsion with data centers and their effect on the air and water, and then immediately follow it (under yesterday’s agreement, this will be the first order of business back in DC) with a bill that makes it harder for states and tribes and anyone else to challenge water pollution.

And the data center stuff also makes the challenge harder than ever—a year ago it was just possible to imagine building enough clean energy to get ahead of the carbon curve in America. Now, as veteran climate warrior KC Golden put it to me yesterday,

It’s like we’ve been on a treadmill, trying to outrun capitalism with clean energy, and they suddenly tripled the speed

Although, of course, you could argue that that increased demand makes these kinds of reforms all the more important—because in the current climate we'll otherwise just build everything with gas, and so far we haven’t really been able to stop that.

It is a conundrum and it may get ugly—it’s possible that the wisest, if least satisfying, take yet came yesterday from the California congressman Jared Huffman, who offers a bit of something for everyone:

Passing a good permitting reform package will be one of my top priorities for the next Congress, so I'm very interested in these Senate negotiations.

From what I've seen, Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich have done some good work, but they've been negotiating from a position of weakness and the tentative deal unveiled today raises significant questions and concerns that would have to be resolved before most Democrats could support it.

I'm all for streamlining transmission and clean energy buildout, but the threshold requirement before making major policy concessions is to actually end Trump's war on renewables so that hundreds of bottled-up clean energy projects can bring that affordable power to the grid. Further, we can't throw states, tribes, impacted communities, and threatened and endangered wildlife under the bus. And as we streamline and cut red tape, we must make sure the American people — not just powerful corporate interests — have a say in government decisions about what happens to our air, water, and public lands. That's what serious, responsible permitting reform looks like.

There's a way to get there, and parts of this deal are helpful, but some of it concedes too much. Hollowing out the Endangered Species Act through the delegation of authority and problematic definitions, for example, is so extreme that a milder version of it spooked several House Republicans off of Bruce Westerman's ESA bill earlier this year, so you can imagine how it's going to land with the American people who overwhelmingly support protecting wildlife. And the provisions that seek to guarantee fair treatment for wind, solar, and battery storage are novel, untested, and don't really end the war on clean energy, but they will still trigger cries of "Green New Deal" and fierce opposition from the House Freedom Caucus, clouding any path to pass this deal through the House unless it gets much worse. And knowing the GOP players, that's exactly what will happen if this bill advances in the lame duck.

The bottom line for me, and I believe most Democrats, is that November 3rd is coming and we are likely to soon have a far better negotiating position. Folding our hand now or in the lame duck makes no sense when we can keep working on this and, in a few more months, have a much better deal that works for everyone.

Here’s how Symons makes the point, less politely

Trump’s war on clean energy is a temporary problem, but this bill is a permanent giveaway to the fossil fuel industry.

There’s a reason the top lobbyists for oil, gas, chemical, and tech companies are demanding fast action on this bill before Democrats gain power in congress. The next congress might demand more instead of waving the white flag to the oil and gas industry.

Ultimately, this may come down to power. A truly convincing win in the midterms might embolden Democrats; a narrower win would convince them this might be the best deal they’ll get; a Democratic loss and the Republicans/oil industry might walk away from it, convinced that they’ll get what they want regardless.

And if we win, maybe we can also keep some immigrants from getting deported too, and maybe end the damned war in Iran, so I’m back to knocking on doors. But I’ll do my best to keep you posted on all of this, so stay tuned.

Share

In other energy and climate news:

+Normally I’d be leading with this: A GIANT TRIUMPH in California where, with a few hours left to decide, Gavin Newsom signed the bill legalizing balcony solar in the state. As Sammy Roth reported,

California is playing catch-up here; nearly a dozen states had already passed similar legislation, starting with deep-red Utah. It would have been a shame if Newsom had vetoed it. But supporters were worried that he might, given opposition from Pacific Gas & Electric and San Diego Gas & Electric. (Southern California Edison didn’t take a position.)

The governor cut things close; as the clocked ticked down toward Wednesday’s midnight deadline to sign or veto legislation, SB 868’s supporters told me they didn’t know what Newsom would do. They bravely announced a Thursday morning press conference with the bill’s author, Senator Scott Wiener (D-San Francisco), basically crossing their fingers and praying the governor would come through.

Just after 5 p.m. Wednesday, he did. Bernadette Del Chiaro, senior vice president at the Environmental Working Group, was elated.

“Oh my God, we’ve doubled the market for balcony solar, just now, at 5:12 p.m.,” she told me. “The U.S. has just officially been opened for business for plug-in solar.”

As readers of this newsletter know, balcony has been a crusade of mine for a good long while—I think this is the first American outlet to write regularly about it. And I’m immensely grateful to my Third Act colleagues across the country who joined me in it. They, and others from places like Bright Saver and Solar United Neighbors, were crucial in passing the enabling laws in a dozen states, including New York and California. This kind of sweeping win is essentially unheard-of for a new policy in a single year—normally the reaction of state legislators to anything novel is, ‘come back next year.’

We have much work left to do—38 states to go, and regulations to be wangled from Underwriters Laboratory. But with California on board, a national market is now firmly established. By New Years I think you’ll be able to go into the big box hardware stores and price plug-in equipment. It’s a big win against strong currents.

And it wasn’t the only thing that Newsom signed. The folks at EarthJustice highlighted another win:

The Home Energy Choice Act (AB 2313), popular, commonsense legislation authored by Assemblymember Marc Berman (D-Menlo Park) which will offer California homeowners the choice and the support needed to electrify their homes. When a gas service line (the pipe connecting a home to the gas main line) is due for replacement, utilities will offer a voluntary incentive to electrify instead. This entirely optional program will enable more Californians to determine what energy powers their home appliances. Both owner-occupied and rental properties are eligible, and there will be additional support provided for families in disadvantaged communities.

There was also one sadness, as Roth reports:

Newsom vetoed AB 1813, which would have given a big boost to “community solar” projects — medium-sized solar farms that can reduce utility bills for nearby residents who sign up to buy the electricity. The Legislature actually voted to support community solar once before, tasking the Public Utilities Commission — whose members are appointed by Newsom — with designing an incentivize program. But the incentives were so atrociously low that Assemblymember Chris Ward (D-San Diego) said they were “wholly inconsistent with my bill.”

Lo and behold, California’s community solar market failed to take off — unlike in other states, where it’s thriving. So Ward tried again with AB 1813, which would have required the utilities commission to compensate community solar at higher rates. The bill passed overwhelming in the Assembly and Senate.

Newsom killed it anyway, suggesting in his veto message that forcing utilities to pay higher rates for community solar would “result in significant upward pressure on consumer energy bills.” It’s the same logic he’s used to undermine rooftop solar — that when certain utility customers go solar and save money on their bills, everyone else is ultimately forced to pay more to maintain the electric grid.

If you ask me, the “cost shift” argument might make sense for rooftop solar. But when we’re talking about a community solar market that barely exists, it’s just an excuse to avoid creating less competition for the utilities.

+Aaron Regunberg describes the effort in red states to limit suits against corporations for causing a public nuisance. He writes

Public nuisance was a primary basis for the litigation against Big Tobacco in the 1990s, and was the foundation of the opioid cases over the past decade. It’s played a prominent role in lawsuits on lead paint, predatory lending, water pollution, and “forever chemicals” like PFAS. It was the most important hook in recent successful cases against social media companies like Meta for designing their platforms to addict and endanger children. And most recently, it has been a key cause of action in litigation in several states against data centers for the air, water, and noise pollution they cause.

But not in Utah, Kansas, or Montana. Though it largely passed under the national radar, these states enacted laws this year or last that dismantle public nuisance as a cause of action—laws that, according to the Utah State Legislature’s own Office of Legislative Research and General Counsel, will make claims against data centers and other corporate wrongdoers “more difficult to pursue.” These states are not outliers, either—they’re forerunners. Their laws closely mirror a model bill published this summer by the American Legislative Exchange Council, the corporate oligarchy’s primary conduit for enacting right-wing laws at the state level. As I write this, ALEC’s Public Nuisance Reform Act is likely being distributed to Republican legislators in dozens of state houses around the country—and you can bet that Big Tech, eager to suppress a valuable tool of data center opponents, is lining up lobbyists to coax its passage.

Meanwhile, the crucial Supreme Court case on local efforts to hold Big Oil accountable for climate damage will be argued Monday, and Kate Yoder has an interesting account of the slightly scrambled support for the Boulder County Colorado’s efforts:

Much of the support for Boulder and the oil companies falls along familiar, partisan lines. Republican states and business associations tend to side with the oil companies; Democratic states and environmental advocates typically back Boulder. A watchdog organization found that 25 of the 38 briefs filed to the Supreme Court in support of Exxon and Suncor were written by groups with financial ties to the fossil fuel industry or foundations opposing climate science and regulation. But Colorado ranchers aren’t the only surprising source of support for Boulder’s case — some conservative thinkers are challenging oil companies’ arguments…

If someone has harmed you, you should be able to go to court and make the case that they harmed you and that they need to pay you for it,” Alejandro Camacho, a professor at UCLA School of Law, said. “It’s a centuries-old common law principle. And these companies are basically trying to say, ‘You shouldn’t be able make the case in court.’”

+Rooftop solar is now providing so much energy to New England that it’s making a major gas plant obsolete. As John Fitzgerald Weaver writes,

ISO-NE (Independent System Operator—New England, which oversees the regions grid) logged its 500th BTM (behind the meter) solar duck curve day on September 21, more than eight years after it observed the region’s first in April 2018. The grid operator has told federal regulators that behind the meter solar growth was a leading reason it no longer saw a reliability need for a new natural gas terminal.

Here’s what that “duck curve” looks like

Meanwhile, the BBC reports on my home state of Vermont, where the biggest source of electric supply is now…batteries in people’s homes.

The programme now provides some 110MW of power – about the same as a small-to-average-sized natural gas plant – and is the largest power source in the state.

Virtual power plants themselves don’t actually produce power, though the solar panels tapped into it do (around 50% of the houses in its programme with home batteries also have solar panels, GMP says). Instead, they use software to manage and conserve energy in more intelligent ways, making what we have already go further – especially at the times the grid needs it the most.

+”Catastrophic melt” reported on Swiss glaciers this summer, according to Irish radio

Switzerland’s glaciers, which are disproportionately impacted by climate change, have lost nearly 20% of their mass in five years, experts have said, with 2026 registering the second-biggest melt on record.

Swiss glaciers saw 5.5% of their volume melt away this year, the Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS) network found in a new study, published after a record hot summer preceded by a winter with little snowfall.

“The glaciers this year have lost enormous quantities of ice,” said GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss, describing 2026 as “a catastrophic year”.

Perched on the Scex Rouge glacier, at an altitude of nearly 3,000 metres, he gazed across the landscape in despair.

“This is a glacier that isn’t surviving,” he said.

+A disturbing account from the Financial Times of what’s happening in the oceans. Attracta Mooney and Steve Bernard describe quick accelerations in sea level rise, and changes in the chemistry of seawater

Heatwaves and melting ice were bringing “profound changes” to the world’s ocean as a result of climate change, more than 120 scientists concluded in a flagship report, including salty seas getting saltier and the ocean more acidic.

The ocean has absorbed some 90 per cent of the world’s excess heat trapped as a result of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions. In 2025 alone, it gained an estimated 23 zettajoules in heat — or about 40 times the energy the entire world consumed last year.

The dramatic effects included an accelerated sea level rise observed by the study since 2012, the EU marine service Mercator Ocean International said in the report drawing together the work of international scientists.

“Warming, rising seas and ecosystem degradation are interconnected signs of significant and long-term change,” said Pierre Bahurel, director-general of Mercator. “The ocean is changing rapidly.”

+And finally, from Faseeh Mangi and Lili Pike, a stirring account of the ongoing solar rush in Pakistan

About an hour’s drive east of Karachi, Pakistan’s coastal mega-city of more than 20 million people, a coal-fired power station hailed as a flagship project in China’s $1.5 trillion Belt and Road Initiative is being engulfed by a sea of solar.

Glinting arrays crown steel plants and manufacturing sites across a vast industrial zone of about 400 companies flanking the Arabian Sea at Port Qasim, part of a rapid — and largely unplanned — advance of renewable energy that’s added new risks to the nation’s already precarious energy economics.

“There are solar panels almost everywhere one sees,” says Zaheer Allana, owner of a packaging factory, where the rooftop is crowded with photovoltaic modules that generate about a fifth of the facility’s electricity needs. “We have utilized almost all available space,” he explains, as workers load burlap sacks onto delivery trucks. “If we had space, we would take it to 100%.”

name: Texas Environment
title: Texas PUC Greenlights Coal Plant Closure and Renewables Construction, Saving Millions ...
description:
“Texas doesn’t need coal anymore – even as it prepares for increased demand – and today’s decision clearly shows that.
According to Sierra Club’s new analysis Watts Wasting Texas Water, in 2024, Tolk used 1.2 billion gallons of groundwater.
As recently as 2015, the plant consumed 3.3 billion gallons of water in a single year.
The Tolk coal plant is in Sudan, about one hour northwest of Lubbock.
Earlier this summer, the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission permitted SPS to proceed with construction of the renewable energy and gas plants, while also ruling that it couldn’t receive an early exemption from New Mexico’s renewable energy requirements.
text:
AUSTIN, Texas – The Texas Public Utility Commission (PUC) ruled today that Southwestern Public Service Company (SPS) can proceed with closing its Tolk coal plant near Lubbock and constructing renewable energy and battery storage to provide reliable, clean electricity to Southwest Power Pool customers. While also approving two new gas peaker plants in Texas – with strict cost caps – the PUC’s decision paves the way for significant water savings and enough renewable energy to power about 375,000 homes in Texas and New Mexico, including 1,100 megawatts of wind, 322 MW of battery storage, and 189 MW of solar. (Note: Commissioners take up this item at 4:10 in the video, and discuss Chairman Gleason's cost cap recommendation.)

STATEMENTS FROM SIERRA CLUB

“Contrary to what the people in power want us to think, there is a common-sense path in Texas to transition away from expensive, dirty, thirsty coal,” said Josh Smith, a Sierra Club Environmental Law Program attorney who has worked on the Tolk plant for years. “Texas doesn’t need coal anymore – even as it prepares for increased demand – and today’s decision clearly shows that. When Tolk closes, it will save abundant water in a drought-prone region, millions of ratepayer dollars, and eliminate millions of tons of harmful pollution every year, making rural West Texas a healthier place to live.”

“These solar, wind, and battery storage projects are clearly the most cost-effective and efficient means of replacing the aging and increasingly expensive Tolk coal plant while also maintaining system reliability, saving scarce groundwater resources, utilizing existing transmission rights, and reducing harmful pollution,” said Cyrus Reed, the Legislative and Conservation Director of the Lone Star Chapter of Sierra Club.

BACKGROUND

SPS (owned by Xcel Energy) first said it would retire Tolk no later than 2032 due to a 2020 agreement with Sierra Club and agreed to study an even earlier retirement based on the plant’s costliness and declining levels of the Ogallala Aquifer, which the plant depends on to operate. SPS then proposed retiring the plant in December 2028, and this summer’s decisions from New Mexico and the Texas PUC confirm a retirement just a few months later, in early 2029. Retiring Tolk has long made sense considering how much water it withdraws from the rapidly depleting Ogallala Aquifer to cool its coal-burning boilers. According to Sierra Club’s new analysis Watts Wasting Texas Water, in 2024, Tolk used 1.2 billion gallons of groundwater. As recently as 2015, the plant consumed 3.3 billion gallons of water in a single year. Renewables use negligible water resources.

The Tolk coal plant is in Sudan, about one hour northwest of Lubbock. Tolk is regulated by both Texas and New Mexico's utility oversight agencies because it provides power to both states. Earlier this summer, the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission permitted SPS to proceed with construction of the renewable energy and gas plants, while also ruling that it couldn’t receive an early exemption from New Mexico’s renewable energy requirements. It also declined to rule on the company’s request to treat new gas-fired power plants as zero-carbon resources (SPS claimed it would be helping to electrify the oil and gas industry in the Permian) under the state’s Energy Transition Act. For their part, Texas regulators placed capital cost caps on the gas plants, and production expectations on the wind contract.

title: AI, robotics could make 'dark' auto factories a reality - News 8000
authors: Luke Ramseth, Ford Motor Co, Clarence Tabb Jr, The Detroit News, Breana NobleThe Detroit News
description:

text:
In parts of a Zeekr factory in northeastern China, hundreds of robots piece together luxury electric vehicles in the dark.

If there's no need for human workers, there's no need to keep the lights on.

Experts say no fully "lights-out" mass-vehicle plants exist yet, but that could change soon, exerting enormous pressure on legacy automakers from Detroit to Germany and Japan.

With fast-improving artificial intelligence and new, more agile robotics hitting the market, automakers and suppliers increasingly study how to eke out more efficiency inside their plants — even in notoriously complex stages of the process such as final assembly.

China is out front; some Chinese carmakers, such as Geely Group's Zeekr, BYD Co. Ltd. and Xiaomi Corp., already automated large swaths of their manufacturing processes.

"There are entire sections where lights aren’t on or you don’t see people,” said Tu Le, managing director of consulting firm Sino Auto Insights, of several Chinese plants. “Usually in final assembly, though, there’s people. But it’s much more automated than I think rank-and-file Westerners believe.”

Detroit knows it must keep pace on automation to compete with China's increasingly dominant auto industry.

A growing number of physical AI and similar automation firms from Silicon Valley and beyond are arriving to test their technology and hardware in Michigan's manufacturing-dense environment. The prospect of auto factories completely or largely run by robots powered by AI also raises uncomfortable — even existential — questions about employment levels and the need for widespread job retraining.

"We are in a fight for humanity," United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain said of AI during a Detroit conference over the summer, warning the technology could be a job-killer for the union's members just as the North American Free Trade Agreement was decades ago. He added, "the rainy day is now; it's here," and the union must respond quickly.

'Greatest labor issue'

The UAW is watching major auto plants it represents become increasingly automated. Ford Motor Co.'s $2 billion overhaul of its Louisville Assembly Plant to make the new Fathom electric pickup, for instance, will include a highly automated assembly process that will mean about 600 fewer employees at the plant. That overhaul comes as CEO Jim Farley marveled at the pace of innovation and manufacturing know-how in China, and plainly stated it threatens Ford's existence as a company.

General Motors Co., meanwhile, took heat from the union for recently adding dozens of collaborative robots, or cobots, to its Factory ZERO in Detroit even as more than 1,000 workers remained laid off. Stellantis NV touted new AI-powered robotics systems in areas including quality control and tracking parts inventory inside factories.

Lear Corp., a major auto seating and electronics supplier headquartered in Southfield, recently opened an “advanced manufacturing and integration center” in Rochester Hills where it demonstrates lights-out production and other advanced manufacturing methods it aims to integrate into more plants. On a recent earnings call, CEO Ray Scott also described how Lear successfully ran a fully lights-out shift using automated injection-molding machines at one of its plants in Germany.

AI-fueled automation became a key issue in UAW leadership elections set to conclude in October. One candidate for president, Greg Mooney, built much of his campaign message around how the union must both adapt and fight back against AI. He's advocated for writing strong AI-specific contractual language and setting up job retraining programs within the union to help workers transition to new, in-demand roles involving AI and robotics.

“We need to have a seat at the table on how it’s going to be implemented — AI’s not going away," Mooney said in an interview. "This is the greatest labor issue of our generation.”

Given AI's rapid advancement, UAW leadership should prioritize bringing back tough contractual language setting minimum employment levels — language that was watered down following the Chrysler and GM bankruptcies, said Tony Totty, president of UAW Local 14 in Toledo and a candidate for one of the union's vice president roles. Such a policy would require a certain number of jobs to be maintained, regardless of whether carmakers introduce new automation inside their plants.

“We’ve got to have jobs, because those robots aren’t going to buy these vehicles," said Totty, who represents members at a large GM transmission plant and made AI a central plank of his campaign. Automation inside auto plants steadily increased, especially when new production lines were installed. Now, he said, the pace and intensity are gaining speed.

Suppliers explore dark factories

In a “perfect world,” a dark factory might be the goal, Paul Thomas, president and CEO of Bosch in North America, told The Detroit News at an Automotive Press Association event on Sept. 22.

The current automation phase for the Germany-based auto supplier emphasizes people working alongside robots, as the company balances costs, quality and social responsibility. That means Bosch is adding more cobots and other purpose-built robots to its plants.

“We've been able to integrate automation while also increasing the knowledge of our workforce,” he said during the event. “So, the people that used to assemble parts are now controlling the (Programmable Logic Controllers) that run our automation. And for me, that's amazing."

Forvia SE of France, another major auto supplier with a large Michigan presence, is developing AI-powered tools that can automatically check weld quality or other potential flaws with products such as its seats, said Chad Durkee, the company's technology scouting director in North America. It's studying other robotics that could have the adaptability to pick and place seating materials, from metal and plastic, to foam and leather.

"AI is unlocking the potential for automation to scale much faster, because it gives it an intelligence level that we never had access to before," he told The News.

Forvia is studying the prospect of lights-out manufacturing in the long term. Durkee said even with rapid AI advancement, such a change would take time, and involve tweaking the designs of parts and sub-assemblies themselves to more easily be assembled by robots.

Auto companies invested more than $100 billion in AI across their operations in the past five years, and those investments are surging, said a recent report by consulting firm PwC. In addition to product-centered uses for AI, automakers and suppliers are pouring those investments into AI-powered quality inspection products and other areas where AI can help factories run more efficiently.

The next phase of investment: More AI-powered robots on the factory floor, said C.J. Finn, PwC U.S. automotive industry leader and one of the report's authors. Still, he noted that transition to smart robots won't happen overnight, nor will the emergence of fully dark auto factories.

'Can't compete' without automation

Many Chinese auto plants are built from the ground up, allowing them to be designed with automation in mind. Strong demand among Chinese consumers for electric vehicles that are less complex and have fewer parts also means assembly is easier and is more conducive to robotic work. China’s robot installations surged in recent years: In 2024, more than half of industrial robots worldwide were installed in the country.

Older existing U.S.-based plants, meanwhile, often aren't as optimized for automation. U.S consumers also haven't shown the same appetite for EVs.

Still, it's a safe bet that there will be a dark auto factory in the United States within 15 years, Le said: "We can't compete unless we automate our factories."

Some question the wisdom in pushing for fully lights-out operation, however. Jeff Burnstein, president of the Ann Arbor-based Association for Advancing Automation, is a prominent advocate for robotics and similar technology. But even he has concerns about the idea of a dark factory future where humans are completely sidelined from auto manufacturing and other industries.

"I mean, don't we still want the people?" he said. "I try to think of a world in which you take it to the extreme — there's no people doing anything. How are we going to survive? Who's going to buy your car? Is the government going to give you money to buy your car? And how much are we getting for this universal basic income? I just don't see it. I guess I can't imagine that world."

title: Attorney General James Challenges EPA Rollback of Power Plant Pollution Limits
description:
“Future generations are going to pay the price for our federal government’s callous disregard for Americans’ health and the environment,” said Attorney General James.
More climate pollution contributes to more frequent and more intense heat waves that put children, older adults, and workers at risk.
In addition, Attorney General James and the coalition today filed a notice of intent to sue EPA over the agency’s continued failure to regulate greenhouse gas pollution from many existing gas-fired power plants.
Despite issuing standards for new gas plants over a decade ago, EPA has never fulfilled its legal obligation to limit pollution from existing gas plants.
If finalized, that proposal could make it significantly harder for future administrations to limit climate pollution from power plants.
text:
NEW YORK – New York Attorney General Letitia James today led a coalition of 25 states, counties, and cities in suing the Trump administration for dismantling federal greenhouse gas pollution limits for many of the nation’s largest power plants, gutting one of the country’s most significant climate protections. In September, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) repealed safeguards that had required coal- and gas-fired power plants to reduce their emissions and curb the pollution fueling the climate crisis. The administration also proposed additional steps to prevent future administrations from introducing new regulations. Attorney General James and the coalition argue that by eliminating these guardrails, the administration is clearing the way for millions of additional tons of greenhouse gas emissions that will worsen extreme heat, deadly storms, flooding, and wildfires. The coalition is filing a petition for review to strike down the repeal and notifying EPA of its intent to sue over the agency’s continued failure to fully regulate pollution from existing natural gas power plants.

“Future generations are going to pay the price for our federal government’s callous disregard for Americans’ health and the environment,” said Attorney General James. “This administration’s insistence on giving the nation’s biggest polluters a free pass will set our country back decades in the fight against climate change. Dismantling these protections is a betrayal of American families, and the stakes are too high to allow this administration to once again put profits over people.”

Attorney General James and the coalition are challenging EPA’s repeal of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, which required many of the country's largest power plants to significantly reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. Power plants are among the largest drivers of the climate crisis, producing roughly one-quarter of the nation’s carbon dioxide emissions. Rather than hold those polluters accountable, the Trump administration elected to erase federal pollution limits for most gas- and coal-fired power plants and instead prop up outdated, unhealthy, and expensive fossil fuel plants, which will only increase electricity costs.

Eliminating limits on these emissions threatens communities across the country. More climate pollution contributes to more frequent and more intense heat waves that put children, older adults, and workers at risk. It also contributes to stronger storms and heavier flooding that damage homes, businesses, and transit systems, as well as more wildfire smoke that makes New York’s air dangerous to breathe. Increased pollution from fossil fuel power plants can worsen asthma, heart disease, and other serious respiratory illnesses, especially in low-income and other overburdened communities. These changes also increase the financial burden on local and state governments, which must spend billions of dollars recovering from increasingly extreme weather.

EPA unlawfully abandoned these pollution limits without properly considering reasonable alternatives or the enormous health and climate costs of allowing more pollution into the atmosphere. Moreover, the rescission was arbitrary and capricious because EPA did not sufficiently calculate the full cost of repealing the rule. With today's lawsuit, the coalition is asking the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to strike down this unlawful rollback.

In addition, Attorney General James and the coalition today filed a notice of intent to sue EPA over the agency’s continued failure to regulate greenhouse gas pollution from many existing gas-fired power plants. Those facilities, including “peaker” plants that often operate during periods of high electricity demand, are frequently located in low-income communities and communities of color that already bear a disproportionate share of pollution. Despite issuing standards for new gas plants over a decade ago, EPA has never fulfilled its legal obligation to limit pollution from existing gas plants. By delaying these protections for years, EPA has left many frontline communities without the safeguards required by the Clean Air Act. The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) will also testify at an EPA hearing later today, urging the administration to abandon its dangerous proposal to eliminate greenhouse gas standards for power plants altogether. If finalized, that proposal could make it significantly harder for future administrations to limit climate pollution from power plants.

Joining Attorney General James in one or more of these actions are the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the Governor of Pennsylvania, the Mayors of New York City and Chicago, and the City and County of Denver.
