text:
(CNN) — Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked a GOP-led bill taking a stand on rising energy costs driven by the data center boom, thwarting a last-ditch effort by Republicans to show they are taking voter concerns about affordability seriously.

Even though the bill only recommends states take action and does not mandate lower prices for consumers, the bill’s failure deprives Republicans of an opportunity to counter attacks that they haven’t done enough to tackle high prices ahead of the midterms. It deals a setback to one vulnerable Republican senator in particular: Ohio’s Jon Husted, who led the charge for passage of the bill after being hammered on the issue in his race, one of the most competitive Senate battlegrounds.

Now, senators are expected to soon leave Washington and not return until after the midterms as a number of Senate Republicans have expressed concern that their party has not done enough to address the high cost of living in the run-up to a critical election where control of Congress is at stake.

The vote also opens Democrats up to criticism for blocking the bill, which passed the House earlier this month with widespread bipartisan support.

The measure — known as the “Ratepayer Protection Act” — was blocked on a 57 to 43 vote with only four Democrats voting with Republicans.

Senate Democrats said ahead of the vote that they opposed the bill because it did not go far enough. The bill requires state regulators to “consider” adopting a proposed federal standard that would require data center companies to cover their costs to the energy grid, rather than passing it off to consumers. Democrats said the language was weak and lacked enforcement mechanisms.

“Here we need some real action on data centers and what does the Republican senator from Ohio come up with? Something that is optional,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said on the floor Tuesday, as Democrats vowed to seek passage of more robust measures.

The vote, in the Senate’s final days in Washington before the midterms, highlights the fight between both parties as they scramble to show voters they’re better equipped to tackle the high cost of living. It also comes as the expansion of data centers powered by AI has sparked concern among Americans.

Republicans criticized Democrats ahead of the vote for their opposition, saying this was the best chance to take action on the issue.

“This is the bill that gives us a chance to prove to the American people that we’re for lower electricity prices and holding data centers accountable. So the only way that this happen is if this bill passes,” Husted said. “This bill is the only game in town.”

But Democrats brushed off concerns the optics of their opposition could backfire.

“If ratepayers read this (bill) and see that it’s a name that says ratepayer protection and provides no relief in rates, they’ll rightly be angry. They can see something that’s not on the level,” said Sen. Peter Welch of Vermont. “You know, I think voters see this for what it is: as kind of a political maneuver at the 11th hour.”

Ohio Senate race takes center stage in key vote

Husted had taken on the mission of passing the bill amid a critical and highly competitive Senate race as Republicans fight to retain their Senate majority.

Data centers have become a flashpoint in his race against Democrat and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, as communities in the Buckeye state have experienced firsthand the rapid development of AI processing facilities. In his role as lieutenant governor and as a senator, Husted has applauded the economic boom that the centers can bring but has also pushed to approve the “Ratepayer Protection Act” as a way to attempt to neutralize potential backlash.

It was Husted who pushed party leaders to return to Washington this week to vote on the bill after leaders had weighed an early exit ahead of the midterms. Multiple sources told CNN that Husted implored his colleagues not to head home early without at least attempting the vote to send a message that Republicans were doing something on the issue of affordability.

Back in Ohio, Brown has cut several ads attacking Husted on the centers. And in August, Senate Republicans’ campaign committee, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, sent an internal memo warning “more than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

“This has become a sleeper issue for the entire cycle,” the NRSC wrote.

Husted’s campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce accused Democrats of playing politics by blocking the bill.

“The House overwhelmingly passed Sen. Husted’s bipartisan legislation requiring data center companies to pay for the power they use, but Senate Democrats blocked it. Sherrod Brown and his friends would rather play politics and stick Ohio families with higher electric bills than pass a commonsense solution,” she said.

In a statement, Lauren Chou, a Brown campaign spokesperson, said, “Jon Husted led the charge to bring data centers to Ohio, forcing Ohioans to pay thousands more in higher electric bills and giving giant out-of-state corporations billions of dollars in out-of-control tax breaks.”

“Ohioans should get to decide if data centers are built in their communities and should never be forced to subsidize the electricity costs of big corporations,” Chou said.

Some Senate Republicans say party could do more

Still, in the Senate’s last days of work, some Republicans have suggested that the party could be doing more to tackle affordability.

“My view is that people would love some relief in the price of their gas. They would love some relief in the price of their health care. They would love some rights vis a vis these data centers. If it were me, I’d make those thing priorities,” Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley said.

Sen. John Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, bemoaned that the party is facing economic headwinds amid the fight to keep the House and Senate in the midterms.

“I mean you don’t have to be a senior at Cal Tech to understand that people are angry about the cost of living, and they’re confused about Iran and the two are inextricably linked,” Kennedy said last week.

text:
The U.S. Senate energy permitting bill unveiled Wednesday could streamline the buildout of high-voltage power lines across the country, potentially delivering billions of dollars in electricity cost savings and dramatically improving the power system’s reliability over the coming decade — if Congress manages to pass it into law.

So say grid experts digging into the transmission grid policy directives contained in the text of the long-awaited bipartisan reform package. The bill would order the country’s regional grid operators and utilities to streamline how power lines are planned and permitted. It would require the use of advanced transmission technologies that can expand the capacity of new and existing grids.

It would give state and federal regulators tighter oversight over less efficient local transmission planning. And it would require grid operators and utilities to coordinate grid buildouts to enable more new power plants, solar and wind farms, batteries, and other resources to serve growing demand for electricity.

“If Congress wanted to expand and de-congest the nation’s transmission grid, these are the policy changes that can get that done,” said Rob Gramlich, president of consultancy Grid Strategies and a longtime proponent of transmission grid reform. ​“It is very likely that this bill, if passed, would reduce consumer utility bills over time as the transmission system expands and access to low-cost generation improves.”

That view is backed up by analysis commissioned by the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, a nonprofit research organization, which studied the impact of the bill’s reforms on four major grid regions — from the mid-Atlantic coast to the California border — that provide electricity to more than half the country.

The analysis found that by 2035, the reforms in the bill could enable a grid buildout that would reduce the cost of delivering electricity by roughly $7 billion, compared with a business-as-usual scenario — a net savings after accounting for $1.9 billion in new transmission investment. That, in turn, could reduce residential electricity bills by about $1.1 billion.

“Really simply, we need to build more energy infrastructure in this country,” Nathaniel Keohane, the group’s president, said in a Wednesday press conference. ​“We need to do that faster, and these reforms will help.”

Many of the transmission provisions in the new legislation were previously proposed under a 2024 bill, Keohane said. And other parts of the bill would essentially strengthen previously mandated grid interconnection and transmission planning reforms.

But the new bill also adds reforms that will ​“make it more predictable, easier for new energy generation to connect to the grid,” he said. ​“That’s really important.” Across the country, transmission bottlenecks are preventing hundreds of gigawatts of solar, wind, and battery projects from being connected to the grid.

Ashna Aggarwal, director of analysis at Greenline Insights, which conducted the study for C2ES, said the modeling her group used indicated the reforms in the bill could enable almost 100 gigawatts more wind, solar, and battery storage, as well as nearly 40 GW of increased interregional transmission capacity that can carry power to far-off regions suffering from extreme weather events.

It’s unclear how the Senate package will fare in the House of Representatives, which has been adjourned by House Speaker Mike Johnson (R) until after the November midterm elections. Republicans and Democrats have squabbled over proposed reforms to environmental regulations, with Republicans pushing for changes that favor the fossil fuel industry, and Democrats demanding the Trump administration halt its attacks on clean energy.

Some environmental groups oppose reforms that would limit the time and scope of challenges to energy projects under federal environmental regulations, saying that such streamlining will unleash a harmful expansion of fossil fuel infrastructure.

But clean energy groups including Advanced Energy United, the American Clean Power Association, and the Solar Energy Industries Association are backing the bill. The reforms, the groups say, are vital to unblocking bottlenecks that are preventing all but a fraction of the country’s potential clean energy from being built to serve fast-growing demand for power from data centers, electric vehicles, and broader economic growth.

“Across categories, this tries to rein in delays and uncertainties that add time and cost to building new infrastructure in this country,” Caitlin Marquis, Advanced Energy United’s managing director, said in a Wednesday interview.

To be clear, the reforms in the Senate bill will also ease permitting and interconnection for the massive amounts of new fossil gas power plants being proposed across the country. ​“This is not a world in which natural gas disappears completely,” Aggarwal said. ​“It does remain the largest source of electricity generation in 2035.”

The Electric Power Supply Association, a trade group representing power plant operators with a preponderance of fossil-gas power plants in their portfolios, expressed support for the Senate bill. ​“Demand for electricity is rising, and the energy infrastructure, including power plants, transmission lines, and natural gas pipelines, required to supply that demand needs a more efficient and predictable path for investment,” the association’s CEO Todd Snitchler said in a Wednesday statement.

But clean energy groups argue that solar, batteries, and wind power are cheaper and faster to build than fossil-fuel power plants, giving them an advantage if the grid can accommodate new additions.

Conversely, if the grid can’t grow quickly enough, data centers may press on with plans to build tens of gigawatts of ​“behind-the-meter” gas-fired power plants, despite the costs and the climate and environmental harms, Keohane said.

“We all see the enormous booming energy demand that’s happening right now. That demand is going to be met,” he said. ​“Whether it’s met with clean energy that can compete on the economics on a level playing field, or whether it’s met behind the meter with all sorts of other kinds of technologies that don’t serve the communities they’re in, that’s really what’s at issue.”

Mike Toffel: Nat and Jody, thanks so much for being on this special episode, jointly produced by Climate Rising and Clean Law, with my co-host Jody Freeman.

Jody Freeman: It's great to be with you, Mike. And Nat, thanks for being our guest.

Nat Keohane: Well, thanks for having me. Really excited to do this, and with both of you, so it's fun to have that combination of business and law.

Mike Toffel: Jody and I have been talking about this for a long time, trying to figure out opportunities to come together and have a pan-university conversation that spans the business and climate intersection that Climate Rising holds, and the environmental policy and law focus of Clean Law, and we really couldn't think of a better person than Nat, you, who studies law, policy with an economic lens, sitting in Washington and focusing on a topic of super importance to both law and business, which is the energy transition. So, we're delighted to have you join us for this conversation.

Mike Toffel: So, Nat, why don't we just begin, if we could, with a little bit about yourself, your background, and your organization?

Nat Keohane: Sure. Well, thanks so much for having me on. It's a real pleasure to be talking with you both, and I know you've got a great audience and a great mix of business and policy and law, so it’s, which is a great, great place for me to be.

So, I'm an economist by training. I got a PhD at Harvard, actually. I spent seven years teaching economics at the School of Management at Yale, so I was a kind of business school environmental strategy professor. And just when I got promoted, I decided to leave academia because I wanted to get more involved in the policy debates. I went to the Environmental Defense Fund. This was right in the midst of the climate legislation battles in the US Congress.

I built the economic and policy analysis shop at EDF. I then was brought into the Obama administration,I think, Jodi, you and I just missed each other. Right. Because I came in in January 2011, the second part of the first term to work in the National Economic Council.

I left after two years, went back to EDF, ended up running the climate program at EDF, and then, left five years ago almost exactly to run the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, or C2ES, which is where I'm the president now.

We're all about climate and energy solutions. We're very pragmatic and solutions-focused. We work quite closely with the private sector. We've got a business council of forty-plus Fortune 500 companies and a broader array of one hundred and fifty to two hundred companies we work with on technology and innovation, climate resilience, and regional clean economies.

So, one of the things that sets us apart is working with business, working with the private sector. We're very involved in a lot of the policy debates in Congress in Washington, DC. We work on federal policy. A lot of our work is on emissions reductions, new technology, technology innovation, building out an economy, a clean economy in the US. We are doing more and more work on resilience, and some other issues as well.

Jody Freeman: One of the reasons I really admire your organization, Nat, and your work, is that sort of insistence that you have to engage with everybody, and you have to engage with business. And, at the law school in my program, we have a similar philosophy that you can't be an advocacy organization and talk only to one side of this equation. So I, I think that it's terrific what you're doing there, and, and your leadership is, is inspiring.

Mike Toffel: So, one of the topics that you deal with at C2ES is the energy transition. I'm not an energy person myself, but my understanding of the energy transition essentially is we have a demand side and a supply side. On the demand side, there's a growing interest, for those who want to meet climate targets, in shifting from fossil fuels to electricity and battery or other types of storage, and that's anything from automobiles moving to electric vehicles to other types of transportation, trucking, for example.

And it's moving from heat using fossil fuel combustion to heat pumps, so that's for the building sector. Lots of different pressures to move from fossils, but then to rely more on electricity. And then, of course, there's the whole data center revolution, which is getting a lot of press right now, and all the additional electricity that will be required to heat and cool and power those buildings. And then on the other side, there's this question of, well, how do we actually deliver new generation and distribution of renewables and perhaps even nuclear, which is another low-carbon electricity production technology. And in the midst of all this is, I think, a general consensus that things are moving too slowly, that the demands are outstripping the ability for the system to increase supply of renewables, and so maybe we have to unleash new fossil fuel power and sort of might set us back against the climate targets that we were hoping to achieve. . Pushing, when we say pushing interregional planning, which means trying to get the utilities to work to agree that they're going to build lines across the states and decide who pays for it, we've been trying that a long time.

FERC has been trying to pro- prompt the organizations of utilities, the, the regional transmission organizations that they participate in, to do exactly that through transmission planning. And the only reason I say all this is what I think we all are looking for is: are we going to still be incrementalist about this in a new piece of legislation that does the same old things we've done, or are there some new ideas that are bigger leaps that change the system more profoundly? And, and I, I don't know if that's possible, but I think that's what some watchers are going to be looking for.

Nat Keohane: And I think that's a really fair point, and there are some big ideas about, like, how do you think about the fundamental structure of the electric utility industry, which was then, all the electric utility regulation was built in the 20th century. That, I think there definitely are people talking about that. You're absolutely right. that's, I don't think that's going to be in the mix, you know, this year. But y- it's a good caution because, as you say, we've been collectively beating our heads against the wall on this.

I think there's more movement for all the reasons we've talked about, and more impetus, but you're right, and it might be that even if we get this passed, we need to start. If it doesn't hold or it doesn't stick, we need to be starting to think about more transformative approaches.

Mike Toffel: So, I want to ask what's at risk? So, if speed is the goal, and it certainly- Yeah is an important goal, what might we give up in exchange for that speed? And sometimes it's nothing. It's like, oh, we used to do things in a sequential process, and now it turns out, why didn't we parallelize it and start the clock on five processes that actually don't rely on each other, their independent assessments.

Just start them all in the beginning. Don't wait and do them one at a time. In which case, you're not giving up really anything, for, for speed. Hm. But other times, I think about sort of the urban renewal movement in America- Hm or the highway impetus that, that didn't give much voice, and then you end up with a highway right through the middle of the Bronx that destroyed a bunch of neighborhoods, and the clearing of a lot of land that was built up in neighborhoods in Boston. Not giving voice dis- can result in quite a lot of, of community destruction. So there, taking out some voice, taking out some ability to challenge decisions that are made centrally, we can see what that looks like from our history.

So, what's your sense of what's at risk? Because certainly I think just about everyone wants speed. I'm going to come back to that in a minute. But let's suppose everyone wants speed. What are we willing to give up at that speed?

Nat Keohane: Yeah, I think that's a good question, Mike, and it's useful to think about some of those other examples. I guess there are a couple of quick thoughts and responses. One is, I think when you look at sort of the amount of time, I mentioned the interconnection queues, you have transmission projects that have been proposed, and 11, 12, 15 years later they're still not built. We're not talking about like, "Oh, it'd be nice to get this done in, you know, two months rather than 18," right?

We're talking about, like, can we get it done every And, and the delays, right, the costs mount, the economics of the projects make it much harder. If you delay a project, it might make sense in the beginning, but by the time, you know, you But, but the, the delay invariably ramps up costs because you have to pay f- the waiting costs and the inf- and you get inflation over time, and you get supply bottlenecks and so on.

And so, number one, there's I mean, I'm not disputing this, but there I just want to point out there's a real cost. It's not like, oh, we have to race to get everything on as fast as possible. It's that there's a real cost to not building, especially on the clean side, to not building clean. We are finally at the point where clean energy is cost competitive, and if we're not, if we're blocking the potential to build that, then we're slowing down the transition.

We're seeing that with offshore wind for sure. I just want to point one more thing out that hasn't really come up, I will just say the general-- that was a reminder of how fast, it's a reminder to somebody in the NGO world who's spent time in government, how fast the private sector moves and I will just say, like, the, the private sector is not waiting around, by which I mean data center developers, some of those hyperscale’s that just want the speed to power they're not waiting around to be like, "Well, let's see if everybody, you know, if the NGOs resolve their policy concerns and this"

They are building data centers now, and if they need to, they're building dirty power, which I mean like diesel generator sets and natural gas, like, literally reports of taking jet engines and stripping them from planes, bolting them to the ground and running them in reverse as electric turbines. Okay? So that is happening to some. Nobody knows exactly how much, but there are anecdotal stories of that happening and you go to a conference and you're just overwhelmed and so the reason I raise that, and I'll come back to the risk, but the reason I raise that is because the alternative to figuring out how to make it easier and faster to connect power to the grid is to build a lot to connect clean power to the grid, is to build a lot of dirty power that's not connected to the grid. It's, it-- There's not another alt- There's not that alternative where we just sit around, and we get it right, and we wait and then get it perfect. I think there are risks, but I will say, like, I think you can, you can, manage those if you design smart policies.

Let's go back to that permit thing I mentioned, right? One of the risks in speed is if you say, "Well, we're just going to sort of shorten all the timelines and make sure that we just go ahead with the permits and the environmental impact statements and so on," one of the big risks would be, well, are you shutting communities out of the process?

Are you short-circuiting community engagement where there's a legitimate interest in people saying, "Hey, wait a minute. We're concerned about the impact of this facility," and so on, especially frontline communities that have typically borne the brunt of, you know, lower-income comm- communities, often minority communities that have borne the brunt of facilities in the past.

So, then you say, "Okay, well, how do we design this that encourages early participation? Are there things like permits that increase transparency, so we make sure that folks have an insight into this? If we're going to say there's an 180-day clock or 120 or whatever it is, how do we make sure that there's outreach in the beginning?"

From what I've seen, and Jody, again, you'll probably know more, but there's a lot of evidence, a lot of the lawsuits that get brought against, at least, you know, generically, a lot of the stuff they get, they, they want to get built, ends up being, you know, pretty wealthy private landowners who are just kind of NIMBY, not in my backyard. And so, I think there are ways, I think there are ways to manage for that community engagement risk with good policy, but I think, Mike, to your question, that's probably the biggest risk.

Jody Freeman: This, this really gets to something important, which takes us back to what we've all mentioned abundance once or twice. The abundance argument talks about environmental rules as part of the problem, that we don't build. They didn't say, you know, they're the only reason, but, but I think the argument has been taken by some to mean, "Oh, it's the environmentalists who block everything."

And, you know, I just think that's just not sufficiently nuanced. I mean, the reason projects don't get built in this country has everything to do with, you know, everything from interest rates to the c- you know, supply bottlenecks to, um- Yes you know, labor costs-Hundred percent delays in getting financing together and so on. And so, I worry a little about the sort of singling out of environmental rules as, oh, the problem to everything. If for the people who do that, I would just say, you know, it's a more complicated picture. That said, there's no question. That these processes, you know, these systems that are good i- in their core, they're about looking before you leap.

They're about early consultation to avoid avoidable harm. Why wouldn't you want to do that? Why wouldn't you want to improve public health instead of making it worse? Why wouldn't you want to save the natural environment if you could by moving the project, a little bit to the left, a little bit to the right?

I mean, there's a really, good principle at the heart of these processes, these permitting systems. But of course, there are reasons why they take too long, and I like what you said there, Nat, about this isn't necessarily something you lay at the foot of the environmental or conservation movement or interests or communities.

It's partly what's going on here is just pure NIMBYism, just a pure local resistance to something in your community, and that's a different problem. They're using environmental laws for that, but that's not the same thing. So, I'm always careful about what we identify as the issue here because it affects the solution you choose. And I think the worst result would be to throw all of this well-principled set of guardrails and constraints right out the window rather than improve it in a way that makes sense - for everybody. And your suggestion that community engagement be earlier, well, that's in everybody's interest, you know?

Nat Keohane: Just on that point, every company we talk about, just on the community engagement, every company we talk to says, you know, early communication is the key to success, those that have tried find that it actually turns out to make everything else easier.

Mike Toffel: So, we're talking about this with a little bit of abstraction as in terms of who's opposed to this. So, if you would think the hyperscale’s are still dedicated to wanting quick power and, to the extent that they want to deliver on their net zero and other type targets, they're in favor.

If there's a bipartisan consensus of people who want green power and want more power, they're in favor. For utilities, it's an opportunity for them to generate and distribute more power. They should be in favor. And so far, we've only talked about, like, NIMBYism or people who don't want the visual of offshore wind or onshore wind or transmission line. Who would we point our fingers and say, "If only we can get them on board, we'd be able to move the needle"?

Nat Keohane: Well, so let me answer that in two different ways. I think one version of that question is like, well, goes back to Jodi's point, like why has this not happened before? What I think this may be, I, I hope this isn't a cop-out, I think just, like, inertia.

Yeah. I mean, I think this has sort of accumulated over time. There are a lot of different reasons. You've got these environmental statutes that were born in the 1970s, they're written in the 1970s, that are the core bedrock. I mean, I'm an environmentalist, right? They're the core bedrock of the environmental movement.

Some of the biggest, certainly the Clean Water Act, one of the, and to some degree NEPA, I think we could argue about that, but some of the biggest, gains in the environmental movement, but that have now become weaponized maybe by some folks who want to kind of prevent any, maybe this is overstating it, but, but folks who are concerned about this sort of NIMBYism and want to prevent anything.

So, I think there's one piece, just part of the reason why we haven't gotten this: you've got these avenues for f- folks to challenge things; you've got utility business models that they might be open to some of this, but they're not in- you know, they, their incentives; I mean, the, the incentives of utilities, of regulated utilities, are just to build more capital projects.

It's not to build inter-regional transmission. It's just to build more generation and expensive generation and get, I mean, that's not quite fair. Well, but it's to build more capital projects and to get the rate of return. So, the first answer, like why is this still there? It's, it's not, I don't think it's like there's an evil villain out there.

I think it's just that there's, the, there's a lot of inertia in the system and, you know, that didn't show up as much when we were in that period of flat electricity demand, right? Yeah. For 20 years. And so all of a sudden now you've got this push, like, we got all the, the economics of clean energy are much better. You've got this huge energy demand, and I think that's where it's coming together.

Jody Freeman: The utility business model, right? The problem is they're mostly monopolies, and they have service areas over which they have monopolies. They have no interest in having competition introduced into this system where there might be developers who want to build new generation and sell it to the data centers in a way that will compete with and eat into the profit margins of the utilities themselves.

So, all I'm saying is there are winners and losers in this sector. And it's a competition over market share, and they want to capture all the market share, and they're not really interested in what the system needs, which is a lot of competition to produce new generation quickly for speed; instead, they want to retain their incumbent, advantage. So, there's a lot of criticism that I think appropriately lands on utilities.

Then the other thing to say, not just, just so that we think of me as an equal o-equal opportunity, critic, you know, what I'll call the environmental conservation/sustainability movement and leadership organizations, which are have all done historically hugely important work, it is true that, and I think the leadership of these groups would, would say this in a, in a sophisticated conversation, they have become more used to saying no to blocking than to saying yes because what was on offer to say yes was projects that were harmful, right?

Now we have the possibility of clean energy projects that work in the direction of trying to address climate change by helping with decarbonization, and so there's more to say yes to. And I think that dynamic is really important. And the third thing that I think is significant here is the anger from the public that will come when it turns out, if it turns out as many predict, including my colleague Ari Peskoe at the law school has written a wonderful paper on this, if it turns out that it is regular old consumers, homeowners, rate payers who foot the bill for the build-out of AI data centers, there will be political hell to pay.

And I think politicians are starting to come to grips with this and realize they must do something to make sure the allocation of the cost for all of this new development on the grid and transmission will not fall upon regular people. So, to me, those things are all happening, moving us in the direction of yes and away from the direction of no. Do you think I'm missing something there?

Nat Keohane: I, I actually, I totally agree. I think you described it really well. I will just add a couple of quick nuances.

One is, I think my friends in the kind of traditional green groups, I think they really have seen, and for all the reasons you mentioned, now the projects that aren't getting built are, are clean projects, right? They're projects that are vital for climate change, for addressing climate change, and that have changed the calculus.

That doesn't mean you're going to see, you know, I've got good friends who run the environmental organizations on the left. You're not going to see all of them say, "Yeah, we're for this." And frankly, on the politics, that probably wouldn't be that helpful. But when you have private conversations with many of them, they'll say, "You know what? We get it. We get this is important for climate, and if done the right way, we're fine with this." And they're giving that permission structure to folks on the left. On the utilities, look, I'll just say two things. One is, I mean, I'm an economist, so I believe in incentives, right? So, you weren't quite doing this.

But I think there might be friends in the kind of abundance movement who are like, "Blame the utility." I mean, the utilities are responding to their incentives. So if we want to change the behavior, we should change their incentives, and you've seen examples at various points in the past.

And I'll say, in the electric power sector, there's a lot of diversity of views, especially regionally. We have companies that operate in the West that really want to see transmission reform, because they want to build new clean energy projects right and they need transmission, and you have folks in the Southeast who tend to feel like they've done what they need to do, and, and sort of they, they see, they, they're much more concerned about sort of federal overreach.

And so, these are the things we're going to have to navigate to get a deal. I'll just say quickly on affordability that, you know, and that's such a deep, such an important topic , and I'm not going to be the first or the last person to say that that's on everybody's minds politically.

Nat Keohane: I will say that the, it's complicated in the sense that there are ways to build more topic, generation, including in response to data centers, that reduce costs to consumers because of, because rates are a, they're a fraction, right?

They're cost divided by the base, and if you and the generation, and if you increase the amount of generation and you don't change the cost too much, you can actually lower rates. I know that PG&E has done that in California as an example. It depends on the circumstances. EPRI did a great piece on this that shows it's not cut and dried all the time, and so policy matters, right?

I mean, this is consistent, I think, with what you're saying. Policy matters. Pressure matters. I think we see, I mentioned Google. I think Google has done a great job of saying, "We will pick up the cost of this, of the new power." It's in their interest to do tariffs, to figure out rate tariffs where they take on the cost because they want the political license to do this, they need the data centers, and they have the money.

So, I think there are ways to solve that, but I agree that that is a political flashpoint, and if we don't solve it and we don't get that right on affordability,

Jody Freeman: So right now it's an uphill battle because while you're saying there might be some agreement in Congress, there really is no interest, it would seem, on the part of the administration that's pushing very much in the other direction, right? Trying to stymie wind, both offshore and onshore, trying to revive fossil energy, trying to make it so the coal plants retire later, not sooner.

You know, basically rescinding every important climate federal regulation, including the scientific underpinning, the endangerment finding. In view of all that, the retrenchment of the administration on climate, isn't it hard to see why the president signs this bill? I mean, is this a, a legislation that needs to wait until 2028 and beyond? What's your view of that?

Nat Keohane: Yeah. So, first of all, good reminder that it needs to pass Congress and get signed by the president. And look, it would be foolish to pretend that this administration, it's, it's easy to predict what this president will do. I think we see right now, I mean, as we're taping this, the president's holding up a housing bill that everybody in his party wants.

So, it's hard to predict. I will say, and Jodi, you know this from having served the administration, no administration is monolithic, so there are absolutely people in the White House who would like nothing better, I think, than to sabotage and undermine the possibility of a permitting deal.

But there are also people who see the need, all the arguments I made on the Republican side; they see the need for more electricity onto the grid. They see the value of a modernized grid. They worry about affordability. They see the value of getting some lasting permitting reforms. And so, I think there are some much more moderate and strong voices also inside the administration saying we should do this.

And I think the Republican leadership is behind this, at least this general push, in the Congress. So, I think there's a chance to do it. I guess when I sort of handicap things, I'm saying that there's a policy deal, like there is a deal on the table that I think could get bipartisan support in 60 and 218; that's not the same thing as saying it's definitely going to get passed.

Nobody ever lost money betting against Congress doing anything, you know, uh- maybe Congress getting anything done. And so, there are a whole host of obstacles. One of them is, will the president sign it? You know, does he throw a spanner into the works at the last minute? But I think for all the trends and the reasons we've said, the conversation's very different now than it was even two years ago. And, you know, I think, look, the midterms, who knows? I'm not smart enough to predict midterms. I do think that if they are on track with what polls say, and you have a Democratic House and, maybe a Democratic Senate or a closely contested Senate, I just don't think that, like, permitting a transmission reform is going to be the first thing that's on, you know, Speaker Jeffrey's mind.

I'm kind of joking a little bit, but I think the politics for this do not get I think they get worse in some respects, not better. So, I think this is the moment, hopefully this is the moment to do it, and we'll see whether that pans out.

Mike Toffel: You mentioned if we don't create the infrastructure to power these data centers, then they're going to do it themselves. That is one possibility. The other possibility is they're going to do it elsewhere, and then we're going to lose that potential competitive edge that we have now. Are we going to let the future of data centers go in the same direction as we let the future of EVs and the future of solar and the future of wind, which is to say other countries? So, I think that to me is the political angle about this.

Jody Freeman: There's a lot of money to be made here. And, a lot of, sometimes when there's a lot of money to be made, it inspires, cooperation to find a way, but there's also a lot of competition for a share of the pie, and, I, it, you know, it's hard problem because you don't, you don't just have interest groups that stand to win or lose, you have federal state division of authority that's been hardwired into our law. That's very, very hard to disrupt, and you have these historic commitments to what some people degrade and deride as process, but that we in the United States are really known for, which is a public-oriented, transparent, and deliberative process around, how we build things and site things in the communities that are going to be burdened by them and are going to pay for them that we ought to be proud of, and that we've exported around the world, you know?

So NEPA, this National Environmental Policy Act, says you do these environmental impact statements. You know that sounds very simple, but that was a revolutionary idea, in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and, and, you know, the idea that we would just jettison that I think would be a real loss.

So, there's a lot at stake in this debate and dialogue. What's so interesting to me is in the middle of a conversation that is about the demise of climate policy domestically and the retreat of climate policy internationally and the geopolitical, arrangement now that's shifted so drastically after the war in Ukraine and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz and the rising of fossil energy and the rest of it, and this narrative around climate as now having to be done secretly and quietly or, we are all now all in the age of climate realism and all this stuff, which is basically a story about climate's out.

We're done with that. In the middle of all that, you come, Nat, with a story of, hey, there's real progress here- that would help decarbonize our economy. That's a good news story, so I want to embrace your good news story.

Nat Keohane: And I will say, you know, there is obviously a lot more to talk about, but I think, you know, I think there's a lot more that could be done and will be done in the next few years.

We could talk a lot about all the topics you just raised, Jody, but I do think this has the potential to be an important positive step forward, even in this political climate.

Mike Toffel: So Nat, before we let you go, let me ask you the final question that I ask all of my guests on Climate Rising, which is, for those interested in this space, what resources do you recommend? Whether that be conferences or career activities or podcasts or newsletters, magazines. What resources should, should we point them to?

Nat Keohane: Well, that's a great question. I mean, o- obviously this podcast, both of your podcasts. I think there's a lot of good podcasts out there. You know, Rob Meyer has been doing some great reporting and heat. I mean, there's a huge number of newsletters coming out. Heatmap, I think a lot of folks look to that. He's put together a great team there. There's increasingly, you know, more take on sort of Substack. You, you can get the kind of controversial, moderate, you know, Dem view from people like Adam Jentleson and Matt Yglesias. I think there are some really good folks on the right of the center that are thinking about this ClearPath as an organization.

Obviously, there are a lot of resources at my organization, C2ES. You know, c2es.org. We have a lot of stuff online. I would just say, I think we've had a very rich conversation here, and we've even just scratched the surface. I, I, I think what you're hearing from me is I would encourage folks to read, to try to read a variety of perspectives.

My view, as somebody who's been working on this for twenty-five or thirty, now I guess longer, thirty years, we're-- if we're going to have dura, we need durable solutions for climate. We can't be swinging back and forth and pingback with every ping-ponging with every administration. And so, we're going to need to find solutions that attract a broader base and make arguments that appeal to a broader base of folks.

So, I would say, read folks on the left. You know, read some I mean, Heatmap doesn’t have a political, well, maybe a little bit bent to the left. Read folks like Jesse Jenkins. The Repeat Project at Princeton does some great work. If you want analysis, the Rhodium Group does some of the best analysis.

But also look at some of the folks who are a little bit either contrary voices, kind of the moderate Dems, or, or folks on the center right who view it from that Republican perspective, like ClearPath. And I think we're going to need to kind of bring all those perspectives together to make compelling arguments that can attract broad support for the kind of changes we need to, to address; I mean, we haven't touched on that. Normally, a climate podcast is all about, like, the terrible things that are happening. We just went through a massive heatwave on the East Coast. This remains as urgent as ever. So, I would just encourage folks to read as much as they can and then get involved.

Mike Toffel: Great. And we'll put links to all those materials in the show notes.

Nat Keohane: Awesome.

Mike Toffel: Great. Thanks so much

Nat Keohane: Thank you.

Jody Freeman: Great, great to be with both you guys. Fun.

text:
Washington, D.C.—The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC) today announced spring 2027 funding opportunities through the Energy I-Corps program. DOE National Laboratories, plants, and sites are invited to apply for funding and support designed to strengthen commercialization capabilities and accelerate the deployment of DOE-developed technologies.

Energy I-Corps helps equip DOE researchers with the skills and perspective needed to move promising technologies closer to the market. More than 850 researchers have participated in the program to date, and technologies supported through Energy I-Corps have gone on to attract over $234 million in follow-on funding. Participants also carry what they learn back to their labs, plants, and sites, helping broaden the use of customer discovery, market analysis, and other commercialization practices across the DOE lab ecosystem.

The lab call includes three topic areas focused on expanding commercialization knowledge and skills across the DOE enterprise, preparing researchers to better understand potential markets, and helping promising technologies move toward private-sector adoption. The following topic areas are open for applications:

Topic 1 — Pipeline Development: Topic 1 seeks proposals from DOE National Laboratories and DOE plants and sites for projects and programming that have the potential to directly increase participation in future Energy I-Corps Training Cohorts. Individual projects with a single DOE lab, plant, or site applicant will be considered up to a total of $100,000. Collaborative projects with at least three DOE labs, plants or sites applying together will be considered up to a total of $200,000.

Topic 2 — Cohort 23: This topic seeks team applications to participate in Cohort 23. Selected teams of researchers will participate in an intensive two-month, curriculum-based program during which they will learn commercialization skills, interview at least 75 stakeholders, and develop a business model for the market’s adoption readiness of their lab technology. Each selected team will receive $100,000 to support their participation in the training.

Topic 3 — Post Energy I-Corps: This topic provides an opportunity to build on and apply learnings gained through participation in Topic 2 to support continued technology advancement and progress toward commercialization. Each selected project will be funded at $100,000 for a one-year period of performance. The technology must 1) be from a DOE Laboratory, plant, or site AND 2) have gone through either an Energy I-Corps Training Cohort (Topic 2) or the U.S. National Science Foundation's Innovation Corps. Training Cohort graduates and non-graduates can apply to this topic. However, non-graduates are limited to individuals who are employed by or have a contractual relationship with a DOE National Lab, DOE plant or site (e.g. Technology Transfer Office personnel).

Additional details and the official solicitation are available on OTC Exchange. Submissions for all three topics are open through Friday, October 30, 2026, at 3:00 p.m. EDT. DOE National Laboratories, plants, and sites may submit questions to EnergyICorps@hq.doe.gov.

text:
Small modular reactors (SMRs) borrow steam turbine engineering from both coal-fired and nuclear plants, but the resulting “wet steam” problem, with exhaust moisture topping 15%, demands a fresh set of design countermeasures to keep blades from cracking.

With impressive breakthrough innovations in small modular reactor (SMR) technology, the quiet yet significant evolution of SMR steam turbines has been largely happening outside the limelight. Over on the turbine island there have been significant developments aimed at delivering a platform of efficient and reliable steam turbines that optimize fleet operations across the expected lifetime and contribute to lowering the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE).

As we stand on the cusp of a new generation of reactor technology, steam turbines for SMR applications were required to dig into the tried and tested engineering toolbox of both fossil and nuclear steam applications. This latest generation of steam turbines needs to provide compact solutions with a high level of factory-preassembly, capable of handling the thermal power range and longer-term design lifetime of SMR reactors.

The Best of Both Worlds

Steam turbines have evolved significantly over recent decades, enhancing efficiency and safety while reducing costs and lead time for power plants.

Most SMR steam turbines are designed for power-output levels typically associated with coal or gas-fired combined cycle plants or industrial applications. However, the inlet pressure, temperature, and steam conditions are currently often still similar to their large nuclear counterparts, especially when coupled with boiling water reactors (BWRs) or pressurized water reactors (PWRs).

Steam turbines designed for SMRs therefore need to leverage the full speed shaft line, architecture, and blading philosophies from fossil applications while conforming to design methodologies from large nuclear applications.

Dealing With ‘Wet Steam’

SMRs with conventional Gen III+ technologies often provide near-saturated steam at the turbine inlet, leading to high moisture of more than 15% at the exhaust of both high-pressure (HP) and low-pressure (LP) modules (Figure 1). In comparison, a comparable sized fossil turbine would typically see no moisture at HP and a much lower moisture content at LP module exhaust, of around 10%. Indeed, unlike fossil-fired turbines, moisture is present throughout most of the flow path in a nuclear turbine. Its detrimental effects intensify from stage to stage as fine droplets deposit on surfaces, coalesce into liquid films, and ultimately break up into larger, coarse water droplets.

Risks associated with wetter steam are well known and managed in nuclear steam turbines. Larger nuclear turbine islands, for example, in most cases include a moisture separator reheater (MSR), which takes the wet exhaust steam from the HP module and removes most liquid water before heating the now “dry saturated steam” ready for the LP modules.

Operating in a “wetter steam environment” demands additional design considerations for the turbine to prevent dangerous erosion and stress corrosion cracking (SCC) damage. SCC refers to the premature cracking and failure of metallic materials resulting from the simultaneous presence of sustained tensile stress and a corrosive medium. Material selection, heat treatment, and chemistry control are essential to prevent the cracking of rotors, blades, and attachments.

In addition, the long and most efficient last-stage blades need to cope with non-synchronous excitation with better damping features to reach the required reliability. Shot peening and strain hardening are widely used for LP module rear-stage blades to introduce beneficial compressive residual stresses and increase surface hardness. These techniques improve fatigue strength, resistance to SCC, and protection against wet-steam erosion, ultimately enhancing blade reliability and service life. Left unmanaged, these issues can seriously reduce the lifetime of the turbine, potentially causing drastic impacts on maintenance schedules or even significant damage.

Modifications of the turbine that can mitigate the water-droplet-driven erosion of blades include water extraction from the interim steam path by utilizing centrifugal forces to channel the damaging water droplets out of the flow path. Additionally, slitted guide vanes can be implemented to remove water films directly from the stationary blade surface upstream of last-stage blades.

Reducing the steam wetness is especially important for the last-stage blade, which is highly susceptible to suffering erosion damage. Mitigating stress corrosion cracking and water droplet erosion risks keeps the blades in operation for longer, thus reducing the cost associated with avoidable spare parts as well as the need for unplanned shutdowns. If not properly addressed, the steam turbine would require additional inspections, premature parts replacement, leading to potentially major repairs recurring multiple times across the plant’s whole operating life.

Designed for the Nuclear Lifetime

SMRs, like most nuclear power plants of the future, will be designed for an expected lifetime of up to 80 years, twice as long as the typical design life intended for fossil-fueled power plants. Consequently, any equipment, including on the turbine island, needs to be designed for the extended operational lifetime of the entire plant, enhancing reliability and reducing the need for major replacements or long modernization outages.

Equally important for a longer lifetime can be blading design improvements. In LP modules (Figure 2), the rotating blades of the last three or four stages, for example, may also be vulnerable to SCC due to the high stresses from the larger centrifugal pull generated in longer blades. Here a lighter blade airfoil and the implementation of an enhanced blade root design can mitigate the stress corrosion cracking risks and increase the overall reliability.

Nuclear Safety Considerations

In most cases, the turbine island is physically separated from the nuclear island; however, it still operates in relative proximity, especially on compact sites like SMRs. A rigorous probabilistic analysis conducted in accordance with stringent regulatory standards will ensure that the risk on essential systems remains acceptable, even for extremely low probability risks such as a part of the spinning turbine detaching and being projected out “like a missile.” Risks resulting from “off-design operation,” such as overspinning, can be further reduced by the turbine’s protection and control system architecture, incorporating robust redundancies as well as the ability to perform functional testing of valves and critical components without shutting down the unit. This enables a safe operation, high availability, and minimal impact on plant output during routine testing and maintenance activities.

Radiation protection can also come into play for some SMRs, like those relying on BWR technology, where the turbine also manages radioactive steam, carrying nuclear safety and radiation protection implications for operation and maintenance. With a culture of “safety first” across all nuclear power plants, operators frequently prefer modifications such as locating the turning gear toward the non-driven end of the generator. This reduces the risk of equipment damage from potential exposure and allows staff, if needed, to manually operate the turning gear while helping to minimize their radioactivity exposure risks.

Lowering the LCOE

Higher electricity production is achieved with improved turbine efficiency and output for a given application.

Features, such as highly efficient Controlled Flow blading, designed to reduce aerodynamic losses, or an optimum last-stage blade for the LP module, can further increase the plant efficiency. Meanwhile, an improved HP turbine module inlet configuration can enhance the accuracy of the turbine’s “swallowing capacity,” critical to ensure perfect matching between the turbine and reactor design mass flows and enabling an optimum plant efficiency. Even a fractional percentage of thermodynamic efficiency increase can, over the lifetime of the plant, be well worth the investment.

Indeed, the implementation of this high-efficiency blading, enhanced inlet configuration, and an improved swallowing capacity could, for example, add one or more megawatts of electrical output onto a 300-MW plant.

Additional features like the reduced-bearing shaft line design, with a single bearing separating each turbine module, can further enhance steam turbine reliability and efficiency by reducing mechanical losses, simplifying maintenance, while providing a more compact turbine train design.

Even these small improvements in optimization and reliability can, over time, have a significant impact on the SMR’s availability and help maximize the electricity production throughout the plant’s expected 80-year lifetime.

Supporting the Success of SMRs

For SMRs to fulfill their promise as a scalable, cost-competitive source of low-carbon electricity, the turbine island technology must play its part by delivering high efficiency and reliability within rigorous nuclear safety parameters. Bringing together the experience from full-speed fossil applications and large-scale nuclear design methodologies allows the SMR turbine island to reconcile the current high-moisture thermal realities of nuclear power plants with the compact, standardized, and factory-preassembled modules historically associated with fossil plants. The resulting standardized platform enhances reliability, reduces lifecycle costs and project risk, simplifies maintenance, and accelerates deployment.

The quiet evolution of SMR steam turbines can support the success of SMR solutions by enabling higher plant performance, longer service life, and improved operational availability, ultimately supporting a lower levelized cost of electricity throughout an 80-year plant lifetime.

—Cedric Couffignal is executive vice president for New Build at Arabelle Solutions, a turbine island leader, with its technology used in one-third of the global nuclear installed base, including the first SMR steam turbines in North America. The company is currently supporting more than 30 nuclear new-build units across Europe, North America, Asia, and Africa.

description:
The Albanese and Rockliff Governments are securing the future of Bell Bay Aluminium smelter, supporting the facility’s 550 workers, their families and the 1,000 workers indirectly employed across Northern Tasmania.
The Bell Bay smelter is a major contributor to Tasmania's industrial and manufacturing sectors and is vital to the Northern Tasmanian regional economy.
The Tasmanian Government’s Northern Economic Plan identifies Bell Bay as uniquely positioned to support the next phase of Northern Tasmania's economic development.
“We have delivered a globally competitive and lowest possible electricity price for Bell Bay Aluminium through Hydro Tas.
“With its deep-water port, advanced manufacturing capability and skilled workforce, the Bell Bay region has the foundations to remain a major industrial and economic powerhouse.”
text:
The Albanese and Rockliff Governments are securing the future of Bell Bay Aluminium smelter, supporting the facility’s 550 workers, their families and the 1,000 workers indirectly employed across Northern Tasmania.

We want to see Australia make more things here.

This investment will boost jobs in the region while strengthening our national sovereignty.

The Bell Bay smelter is a major contributor to Tasmania's industrial and manufacturing sectors and is vital to the Northern Tasmanian regional economy.

The $200 million investment over five years will help secure Australia's ongoing aluminium production capability and ensures all Australians share in the benefits – while a future regional industrial strategy is developed.

The Tasmanian Government’s Northern Economic Plan identifies Bell Bay as uniquely positioned to support the next phase of Northern Tasmania's economic development.

As the region's leading industrial and clean energy precinct, Bell Bay can attract the investment, infrastructure and skilled workforce needed to establish a new generation of high-value businesses that complement Northern Tasmania's traditional strengths in manufacturing, resources and export-focused industries.

BBA is Australia’s oldest and greenest aluminium smelter, owned and operated by Rio Tinto, and uses more than 25 per cent of Tasmania's electricity.

Quotes attributable to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese

“We want Australia to make more things here and support good well-paid jobs for Tasmania.

“That’s why we’re backing Bell Bay Aluminium – supporting hundreds of workers, their families and the region while boosting Australia’s national sovereignty.”

Quotes attributable to Premier of Tasmania, Jeremy Rockliff

“We have worked closely with the Federal Government and Rio to support hundreds of jobs at BBA, hundreds of associated supply chain jobs, support our economy and back Tasmanians.

“This investment also provides certainty for the supply chain, with many Tasmanian businesses having the confidence to invest, grow and do business.

“Our Northern Economic Plan highlights the central role the Bell Bay precinct will play in Northern Tasmania’s future growth, leveraging renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, export capability and strategic industrial land to attract investment and create jobs.”

Quotes attributable to Minister for Industry and Innovation and Minister for Science Tim Ayres

"The Albanese Government is backing Australian industry, Australian workers and Australian manufacturing by securing Bell Bay Aluminium smelter while a future plan for the Bell Bay region is worked through.

"This joint investment secures hundreds of local jobs in regional Tasmania and provides certainty for the workers, their families and the businesses that rely on its ongoing operations.

"The Bell Bay region has been facing difficult industrial circumstances, and the Commonwealth is backing in the Tasmanian Government and Rio Tinto as they work through the future of the facility and the region.”

Quotes attributable to Minister for Energy and Renewables, Nick Duigan

“This support package is in addition to the power deal, which has been locked in for the next five years.

“We have delivered a globally competitive and lowest possible electricity price for Bell Bay Aluminium through Hydro Tas. Together with this joint package, we have secured 550 direct jobs in the region and $5 billion of economic activity over the next five years.

“With its deep-water port, advanced manufacturing capability and skilled workforce, the Bell Bay region has the foundations to remain a major industrial and economic powerhouse.”

title: Meta Found a Way to Turn AI Data Centers Into a $3.9 Billion-Dollar Tax Break
description:
Research tax credits saved Meta roughly $700 million in 2023.
According to the Times, Meta began labeling portions of its AI data-center expansion as experimental “pilot models,” separating chips designated for AI training from those in conventional facilities.
Meta’s reported approach centers on the argument that designing and networking thousands of chips for large-scale AI data-center training involves genuine technical uncertainty.
The IRS has not formally rejected Meta’s AI data-center claims.
The $3.9 billion figure represents Meta’s total research-credit savings for 2025, not an amount confirmed as attributable solely to AI data centers.
text:
Research tax credits saved Meta roughly $700 million in 2023. By 2025, that figure had reportedly climbed to $3.9 billion, according to the New York Times, which would make Meta the largest publicly traded beneficiary of a credit Congress designed to encourage qualified research and experimentation.

The reported driver is a classification strategy. According to the Times, Meta began labeling portions of its AI data-center expansion as experimental “pilot models,” separating chips designated for AI training from those in conventional facilities. The company reportedly argued that server-rack layouts and networking configurations constitute qualified research under federal tax law.

A Credit Built for Lab Coats, Not Server Racks

Congress created this incentive to fund technical uncertainty, not large-scale commercial deployment.

The research and experimentation credit originated in the early 1980s, motivated by concerns that the United States was losing its technological edge to Japan. James Shannon, the former representative who sponsored the 1981 legislation, said the incentive was intended to support “people power, knowledge, information,” not simply “making things,” according to the Times.

The legal standard is specific. Companies must identify a technical uncertainty, evaluate alternatives, and conduct an experimental process aimed at resolving that uncertainty. A 2021 federal court decision involving an Indiana shipbuilder reinforced that standard, rejecting a credit claim because producing a new product alone was not sufficient to qualify.

Chips, Racks, and a Very Generous Definition of “Experiment”

Tax specialists question whether commercial hardware and large-scale infrastructure meet the credit’s narrow eligibility requirements.

Meta’s reported approach centers on the argument that designing and networking thousands of chips for large-scale AI data-center training involves genuine technical uncertainty. That argument applies even when the underlying hardware, primarily Nvidia GPUs, is a commercially available product.

Andre Shevchuk of BPM, a firm specializing in the research and experimentation credit, called the characterization of AI data centers as experimental “kind of wild and out there,” according to the Times. Other advisers, as reported by the Times, noted that commercially available equipment may qualify only when directly tied to resolving a documented technical uncertainty. That is a considerably narrower standard than Meta’s reported position.

Tax specialists note that commercially available hardware has rarely been accepted as experimental equipment under the legal standard the credit requires.

Meta spokesman Andy Stone defended the company’s approach, saying Meta invested $200 billion in research and development over five years, including $57 billion in the most recent year, according to the Times. Stone argued that the company is using incentives Congress created to encourage domestic investment and employment.

Uncertain Ground, Certain Reserves

Meta’s own financial disclosures acknowledge significant legal exposure tied to its research-credit positions.

Meta’s securities filings signal that exposure directly. The company reported $11.23 billion in net uncertain tax positions at year-end 2025. It also reported $16.45 billion in gross unrecognized tax benefits, predominantly linked to research-credit uncertainties and transfer pricing, according to its 2025 annual filing with the SEC.

The IRS has not formally rejected Meta’s AI data-center claims. Those figures represent accounting reserves for positions that could be challenged on audit or in litigation.

The research credit cost the federal government approximately $32.1 billion in 2025 across all claimants, according to the Joint Committee on Taxation as reported by the Times. Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft each reportedly claim more than $1 billion annually. Available reporting does not establish that any of those companies uses the same AI-infrastructure equipment strategy.

Meta also faces separate IRS disputes, including an effort to recover roughly $355 million tied to Zuckerberg stock options treated as research expenses and a larger matter involving profits allegedly shifted to the Cayman Islands, according to the Times.

The $3.9 billion figure represents Meta’s total research-credit savings for 2025, not an amount confirmed as attributable solely to AI data centers. The reporting links the sharp increase to the data-center strategy, but a precise allocation is not publicly established.

If the IRS accepts Meta’s position, other AI developers could seek comparable treatment for billions in GPU and infrastructure spending. If it rejects the approach, Meta faces additional taxes and interest, with penalties depending on the specific facts and procedural posture of each challenged position.

title: The US Senate Negotiates a Bipartisan Deal to Speed Up Energy Permitting
description:
A bipartisan group of US senators has unveiled a legislative compromise aimed at speeding up federal permitting procedures for energy projects.
For developers, the goal is to obtain more predictable administrative decisions for future power generation and transmission projects.
Negotiators from both parties The compromise brings together the chairs and ranking members of the Senate committees responsible for energy and environmental policy.
According to an explanatory fact sheet presented by Martin Heinrich, the text would strengthen the role of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the US federal energy regulator, in authorizing major interstate transmission lines, improve grid planning and speed up interconnections.
The text would set a filing deadline for certain challenges related to federal environmental review.
text:
A bipartisan group of US senators has unveiled a legislative compromise aimed at speeding up federal permitting procedures for energy projects. The bill, named the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, also seeks to strengthen the legal security of already-approved projects. For developers, the goal is to obtain more predictable administrative decisions for future power generation and transmission projects. The compromise remains, at this stage, a legislative proposal, whose actual effects will depend on its adoption by Congress and its implementation.

Negotiators from both parties

The compromise brings together the chairs and ranking members of the Senate committees responsible for energy and environmental policy. On the Republican side, Mike Lee, senator from Utah, chairs the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, while Shelley Moore Capito, senator from West Virginia, leads the Environment and Public Works Committee. On the Democratic side, Martin Heinrich, senator from New Mexico, serves as ranking member of the Energy Committee, alongside Sheldon Whitehouse, senator from Rhode Island, who holds the same role on the Environment Committee. The reform comes as several countries are also seeking to modernize their power transmission infrastructure, as illustrated by the United Kingdom, which launched the Great British Grid programme to speed up electricity connections, or by the €700 million mobilized by the European Investment Bank and BNP Paribas for power grids.

The text posted online by the committees still contains blank legislative fields, indicating it has not yet received an official bill number. Its public presentation and the availability of its draft text allow its content to be documented, but do not establish the full sequence of its legislative path. No vote date has so far been set in the official documents reviewed, with the midterm election serving as a separate reference point from the legislative calendar.

Company BNP Paribas: company profile BNP ↗

The offshore wind lease precedent

The emphasis placed on permit stability stems from a recent episode involving offshore wind. The Department of the Interior had suspended offshore wind project leases, citing national security risks based on classified reports. The federal agency's statement establishes the administrative decision and its stated rationale, without allowing independent verification of the risks invoked.

The negotiators behind the compromise now propose protecting already-granted permits from any further administrative suspension. This protection would apply except in extraordinary circumstances, proven violations of applicable law, or a contrary court ruling. The mechanism would aim to limit the risk that a later political decision could undo projects that have already been authorized.

FERC and electricity transmission at the heart of the reform

The reform is not limited to power generation permits. According to an explanatory fact sheet presented by Martin Heinrich, the text would strengthen the role of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the US federal energy regulator, in authorizing major interstate transmission lines, improve grid planning and speed up interconnections. The underlying mechanism would address generation and transmission needs jointly, rather than accelerating power plant construction without resolving grid access. This latter reading, however, constitutes an interpretation of the planning provisions reviewed.

Data centers represent another component of the compromise. According to the bill's sponsors' fact sheet, mandatory cost allocation for transmission costs tied to these facilities would be introduced. The text would also define a specific scope for computing loads eligible for tariff protection, with the stated goal of limiting cost shifting onto other customers. The savings announced for affected companies nonetheless remain a political promise, without independent quantitative assessment in the documents reviewed.

A contested framework for environmental legal challenges

Investment security comes paired with new constraints on environmental legal challenges. The text would set a filing deadline for certain challenges related to federal environmental review. The Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental advocacy organization, criticizes the proposed changes to water and species protections and to consultations with Indigenous peoples. This opposition reflects the position of one stakeholder, while the bill's sponsors defend the preservation of environmental safeguards, with the public record unable to adjudicate between these competing assessments.

title: Rising Energy Costs, Climate and Clean Air Among Top Concerns for Arizonans, New Poll Finds
description:
However, it’s not just energy costs that concern Arizona residents.
Across the Grand Canyon State, Arizonans rank climate change as their second biggest energy concern and air pollution as their third.
“Even as rising energy costs remain a top concern, climate change and air pollution are also important issues for Arizona residents,” said Nicole Hill, climate and energy program director for TNC Arizona.
“Energy efficiency programs are recognized as a proven and important tool to reduce costs, reduce energy waste and reduce air pollution.” Yet, despite strong support, awareness of available programs is limited.
The findings suggest that expanding awareness of existing energy efficiency programs may help Arizona households lower energy costs while addressing environmental and health concerns.
text:
As Arizonans face higher energy costs, a new statewide poll shows that energy affordability is now a leading concern for Arizona families, with residents expressing overwhelming support for programs that help lower their monthly utility bills.

According to the poll, nearly 80% of Arizonans say their electric bill has increased in the past two years. More than 60% say their summer utility bills are difficult to afford, and six in 10 report that they have raised their thermostat to an uncomfortable temperature to save money.

The poll was commissioned by The Nature Conservancy in Arizona (TNC) in partnership with Arizona PIRG Education Fund to better understand Arizonans’ energy needs and concerns, as electricity demand has surged to unprecedented levels across the state, due in part to economic growth and extreme heat.

The poll, conducted by Noble Predictive Insights, surveyed 1,020 Arizonans, including a combination of registered voters and a broader sample of Arizona adults.

The findings suggest that energy affordability is having a real and noticeable impact on daily life for many Arizona households. However, it’s not just energy costs that concern Arizona residents. Across the Grand Canyon State, Arizonans rank climate change as their second biggest energy concern and air pollution as their third.

Notably, only 13% of the respondents favored increasing fossil fuel production like coal and gas as a statewide energy policy, while 42% said expanding renewable energy should be the priority.

“Even as rising energy costs remain a top concern, climate change and air pollution are also important issues for Arizona residents,” said Nicole Hill, climate and energy program director for TNC Arizona. “That’s why it’s important to pursue solutions that can keep energy affordable while addressing environmental challenges.”

As a solution to these issues, the survey found overwhelming support for energy efficiency programs offered by utilities, with 88% of respondents showing their support. Additionally, 81% said they would financially support expanding rebates and incentives designed to lower monthly energy bills and reduce household costs.

“The data underscore that Republicans, Independents and Democrats; homeowners and renters; college-educated and non-college-educated individuals; and residents living in both rural and urban parts of our state are aligned on the need to address high electric bills,” said Diane E. Brown, executive director of Arizona PIRG Education Fund. “Energy efficiency programs are recognized as a proven and important tool to reduce costs, reduce energy waste and reduce air pollution.”

Yet, despite strong support, awareness of available programs is limited. The poll found that most Arizonans are unfamiliar with energy efficiency programs that could help reduce energy costs, and even fewer have taken advantage of available rebates and incentives.

The findings suggest that expanding awareness of existing energy efficiency programs may help Arizona households lower energy costs while addressing environmental and health concerns.
