text:
Washington, DC; September 30, 2026: Today, a bipartisan group of Senate committee chairs and ranking members released the text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, a bill to reform federal permitting processes. Pacific Legal Foundation applauds the bill’s focus on eliminating red tape and urges Congress to enact it quickly.

“Pacific Legal Foundation strongly supports the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026,” said John Nagle, federal policy manager at Pacific Legal Foundation. “Americans should not have to navigate years of costly and unpredictable government processes simply to build a home, develop new energy resources, or create the infrastructure our communities need. Reforming our permitting system is essential to removing unnecessary government barriers that delay projects, drive up costs, and discourage investment. We encourage Congress to move quickly to pass this bill to lower costs for Americans, protect property rights, and restore America’s ability to build.”

Introduced by Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) and Ranking Member Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), along with Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee (R-UT) and Ranking Member Martin Heinrich (D-NM), the bill will reduce regulatory barriers by streamlining permitting and environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Clean Water Act (CWA), and the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Reducing these barriers would lower costs, increase access to critical resources, and empower Americans to build more homes.

title: The Clean Energy Bottleneck Isn't Technology. It's Market Design.
description:
The transition to clean energy is underway, but major structural obstacles are slowing it down.
Wind and solar power accounted for a record 17% of electricity generated by U.S. utilities last year.
“It’s not a matter of technology or cost,” says Ömer Karaduman, an assistant professor of operations, information, and technology at Stanford Graduate School of Business.
It used to work because electricity consumption stayed flat for decades, despite economic growth, thanks to gains in energy efficiency.
“Assets are reallocated to firms with better management.” It’s reasonable to expect the same dynamic to apply as more electricity providers move to clean energy sources.
text:
The transition to clean energy is underway, but major structural obstacles are slowing it down. Wind and solar power accounted for a record 17% of electricity generated by U.S. utilities last year. However, fossil fuels still supply the lion’s share, and a huge number of new natural gas plants are in development to power data centers.

“It’s not a matter of technology or cost,” says Ömer Karaduman, an assistant professor of operations, information, and technology at Stanford Graduate School of Business. “The economics generally favor renewables.” The barriers to deployment, he says, stem from issues such as misaligned price incentives, red tape, and mismatched supply with demand.

Over the past few years, Karaduman, a fellow at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Researchopen in new window and the Precourt Institute for Energyopen in new window, has focused on identifying these roadblocks and proposing solutions. The central question in all of this work, Karaduman says, is “How can we redesign electricity markets so that clean technologies are able to scale quickly, while maintaining affordability and reliability?”

The Battery Paradox

One challenge is that solar and wind are intermittent power sources, which means that utilities can rely heavily on them only if they’re paired with grid-scale battery storage — typically sprawling facilities with hundreds of shipping-container-sized units, each packed with thousands of brick-like power cells.

In one paper, Karaduman modeled a wholesale electricity market in which storage operators buy electricity when it’s cheap and abundant, then resell it when demand exceeds supply and prices climb — for instance, buying solar power in the middle of the day and selling the excess at night. In this way, they smooth out supply fluctuations, drawn by the opportunity to arbitrage prices.

Yet Karaduman found that the private return on batteries falls short of the social benefit of emission reductions they enable. “The problem,” he says, “is that storage itself affects prices. By balancing supply and demand, it reduces price volatility — negating the source of profit.” In other words, if grid storage does its job and creates supply-side flexibility, it becomes less attractive financially.

It’s a result that earlier analyses missed because they assumed storage operators cannot set prices. By integrating storage decisions into a more complex dynamic model, Karaduman was able to capture second-order effects that are game-changers.

“In this case, relying on market forces to allocate capital leads to underinvestment,” he says. “So you need to realign incentives.” One idea is to change the business model so that storage operators get paid not per kilowatt-hour delivered but simply for maintaining a certain amount of power on standby. Such guaranteed “capacity payments” would also reduce investment risk.

Breaking Gridlock

An even bigger bottleneck is the engineering review that proposed electrical generation and storage facilities must undergo before construction begins. Here, renewable energy is a victim of its own success. There are currently so many proposals that what used to take a year or two can now take seven or eight, causing many developers to give up.

The review process is rigid and sclerotic, Karaduman says. It used to work because electricity consumption stayed flat for decades, despite economic growth, thanks to gains in energy efficiency. But with the explosion in demand from data centers and consumers opting for electric cars and heat pumps, more generating capacity is needed, and fast.

“The capacity of projects in the interconnection queue is twice the existing capacity in the U.S.,” Karaduman says. “It’s an operations issue, really. We need to increase throughput in the review stage.” That’s the focus of a recent paper, in which he and his Stanford GSB coauthors Yue Hu, an assistant professor of operations, information, and technology, and postdoctoral scholar Lin Zang evaluate ways of speeding up the process.

Quote

Humans are very adaptable when they have no choice. I think we're going to figure this out.

Author Name

— Ömer Karaduman

One such innovation is “cluster studies,” in which projects are evaluated in geographic groups rather than individually. Another approach focuses on screening out proposals that waste reviewers’ time and slow down more feasible projects. For example, requiring large up-front deposits and proof of site acquisition would weed out speculative or underfinanced proposals.

To measure the effect of these reforms, the researchers built a model based on PJM Interconnection, the largest grid operator in the U.S., which shut down its queue for new generation projects in 2022 to tackle its backlog.

Karaduman, Hu, and Zang showed how coordinating cluster studies and financial requirements could help grid operators process projects more efficiently. The measures need to work together: When a project withdraws, others in its cluster may need to be studied again. PJM incorporated these measures when it reopened its queue this year, adopting a “first-ready, first-served” review process. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution,” Karaduman notes. “What we provide is a framework that firms can adapt to their own circumstances to design better interconnection queues.”

Automating Demand

While storage allows some flexibility in power supply, it’s not enough to make wind and solar primary sources. “A grid based on renewables needs flexibility on the demand side too,” Karaduman says, “to better align consumer usage with generation patterns.” That’s the focus of a paper he wrote with his Stanford GSB colleagues Stefan Wager, an associate professor of operations, information, and technology, and postdoctoral scholar Mohammad Mehrabi.

Demand shifting has been tried using peak and off-peak pricing, with meager results. “People don’t want to be burdened with yet another complicated optimization problem,” Karaduman says. “I want to plug in my car when I get home and not have to remember to go back out at 10 p.m. to charge it.”

The key, he thinks, is automation. Using a home energy management system, consumers can specify outcomes — such as having the car charged by 8 a.m. or keeping their house cool — and let the system decide how to achieve them. On a hot summer day, for example, it might pre-cool a user’s house in the late afternoon, before they return from work, yet while solar plants are pumping out cheap electrons.

The researchers also developed an algorithm for utilities to determine optimal dynamic prices, based on total demand response. “A system like this allows demand to shift without reducing comfort or needing constant attention from consumers,” Karaduman says.

Transfer of Power

Finally, Karaduman says, innovations at the grid level can spread through industry restructuring. In a study of two decades of mergers and acquisitions involving more than 3,500 fossil-fuel power plants, Karaduman and Mert Demireropen in new window of MIT Sloan School of Management found that these ownership changes generally resulted in improvements.

When operational control of power plants changed hands, their efficiency increased by 5%, on average. (When only the ownership of a plant’s parent company changed, there was no improvement.) What’s more, capacity utilization increased, electricity output grew by 7.3%, outages declined by one-third, and carbon emissions per unit of electricity generated declined.

“It seems that acquisitions in this industry facilitate the transfer of organizational know-how,” Karaduman says. “Assets are reallocated to firms with better management.” It’s reasonable to expect the same dynamic to apply as more electricity providers move to clean energy sources.

Other problems are slowing the energy transition, Karaduman notes, such as outdated infrastructure. While fuel-burning power plants are located near cities, the best sites for solar and wind are often in remote deserts and plains, where there are no transmission lines to connect to.

Wind and solar have very low operating costs, but building a reliable electricity system still requires substantial investment. The challenge is designing markets that support that investment and reward flexibility as the generation mix changes. “You no longer have fuel expenses, and that means you can’t rely on pricing through marginal cost, the way markets usually work. At some point, our current pricing system will break down.”

Yet Karaduman is optimistic that these challenges can be solved and the switch to clean energy will accelerate. “It has to, right? Humans are very adaptable when they have no choice,” he says. “I think we’re going to figure this out.”

text:
EV Sync by S2G Energy Joins Hubject’s intercharge Ecosystem

Mexican energy tech company S2G Energy partners with Hubject to create a more connected, interoperable, and seamless EV charging experience across Mexico.

IRVINE, CA, UNITED STATES, September 30, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Hubject, the global provider of eMobility interoperability solutions, and S2G Energy, a Mexican energy technology company specializing in electromobility and digital energy solutions, today announced that EV Sync by S2G Energy is joining Hubject’s intercharge ecosystem, marking an important step toward a more connected, interoperable, and seamless EV charging experience in Mexico.

As the first phase of the integration, S2G Energy will begin making Point of Interest (POI) data from its EV Sync charging network available within Hubject’s ecosystem, increasing the visibility and discoverability of participating charging locations across connected eMobility services.

The integration establishes the technical foundation for a broader interoperability roadmap between the companies. Future phases are planned to expand into eRoaming and reciprocal network access, while S2G Energy will participate as an eMobility Service Provider (eMSP). Plug & Charge capabilities are part of the longer-term opportunity as the collaboration evolves.

For S2G Energy, the collaboration is part of a broader strategy to remove friction from the EV charging journey. EV Sync is designed around the real-world needs of EV drivers, creating a connected experience that can extend from finding and accessing a charger to starting and managing a charging session, completing payment, and receiving a fiscal invoice.

Rather than approaching charging only as an infrastructure challenge, S2G Energy combines technology, operations, and an understanding of how drivers actually interact with charging infrastructure across different environments. Whether charging at home, at work, at a destination, in public, or as part of a fleet operation, each charging journey presents different needs and expectations. EV Sync is designed to adapt the experience accordingly while keeping the interaction as simple and intuitive as possible.

EV Sync is S2G Energy’s cloud-based charging management platform and network, integrating chargers from multiple manufacturers while providing centralized visibility, operational control, energy management, user management, and monetization capabilities. Its technology supports residential, workplace, destination, public, and fleet charging applications, reflecting the range of charging use cases already addressed by S2G Energy.

“Partnering with S2G marks another important step in strengthening Mexico’s eMobility ecosystem,” said Trishan Peruma, CEO of Hubject North America. “Together, we look forward to accelerating interoperability and making EV charging simpler and more accessible for all drivers.”

“Our vision for EV Sync has always started with the driver experience. EV charging should feel simple, regardless of what technology, network, or infrastructure is operating behind it,” said Geronimo Martinez, CEO & Co-Founder, S2G Energy. “That means understanding what the driver needs in each charging journey and using technology to remove friction from the moment they look for a charger through the completion of the session, payment, and invoicing. Joining Hubject’s ecosystem is a natural next step for us because interoperability is fundamental to creating that experience at scale. Together, we are building the foundation for a more connected and seamless charging experience for EV drivers in Mexico.”

END OF TEXT

‍About S2G Energy

S2G Energy is a Mexico City–based energy technology company with more than 10 years of experience across two core areas: electromobility and digital energy solutions for commercial and industrial customers.

Through EV Sync, its Charging Station Management System and charging network, S2G Energy designs, deploys, operates, and monetizes EV charging infrastructure for multifamily residential, destination, public, workplace, and fleet applications. EV Sync integrates charging infrastructure from multiple manufacturers while providing centralized visibility, operational control, energy management, user management, and monetization capabilities.

At the center of EV Sync is a customer-experience-driven approach to EV charging. The platform is designed to make the charging journey as seamless as possible for EV drivers – from discovering and accessing a charger to starting the session, monitoring the charging process, completing payment, and receiving an invoice.

S2G Energy develops this experience by combining technology with a detailed understanding of the real-world context in which charging takes place. Residential, workplace, destination, public, and fleet charging each create different user needs, operational constraints, and expectations. EV Sync is designed to respond to those different charging journeys while minimizing complexity for the driver.

By continuously expanding connectivity and interoperability – including through its integration with Hubject – S2G Energy aims to make EV charging increasingly simple, connected, and frictionless, helping create the digital infrastructure required for electric mobility to scale in Mexico.

The EV Sync network currently includes 175 charging points and has supported more than 233,000 charging sessions for 2,313 registered users, delivering approximately 4.84 GWh of energy. For more information, please download EV Sync and follow us on LinkedIn.

About Hubject

Hubject simplifies the charging of electric vehicles. Through its eRoaming platform intercharge, the eMobility specialist connects CPOs and eMobility Service Providers (eMSPs) to provide standardised access to charging infrastructure. Hubject operates the world's largest cross-provider charging network, connecting over 1,100,000 charging points and more than 3,500 B2B partners across 75+ countries. Hubject is also a leader in Plug&Charge technology reaching 5,000,000 PnC ready EVs, using ISO 15118-2 and -20 standards to deliver secure, seamless EV charging experiences, and is the first EV-related company to offer financial services for EV companies based on its own payment license.

text:
At first, Chinese automakers were the butt of a joke by well-known Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Then Chinese autos became a real concern, and their rapid development and expansion became a hushed secret.

Now it's an industry consensus: Chinese automakers such as BYD (BYDDY +0.95%) are a serious threat to automakers globally, forcing the U.S. to quickly slap on massive tariffs to prevent, for now, their entry into the U.S. market. Similarly, many scoffed at BYD's bold claim that it would catch Toyota Motor in global sales volume by the end of 2030 -- an achievement that would require more than doubling its current global sales volume.

But this is no longer a joke, and more data just came out overseas that emphasizes just how rapidly markets are changing. So is it time for investors to scoop up shares of the Chinese auto giant?

Show me the numbers

The threat of Chinese automakers undercutting the competition and overwhelming the market with advanced, affordable electric vehicles (EVs) may not be as clear to U.S. investors as it is overseas, since tariffs currently "protect" us from that development. Europe, however, is an entirely different ballgame, as Chinese automakers are increasingly exporting their vehicles overseas to avoid the margin-eroding price war in China's domestic automotive market.

The speed at which BYD is making its presence known in Europe is impressive. Starting more broadly, though, Chinese autos more than doubled their sales in Europe in August, setting a record market share of 11.7%. Chinese brands' sales soared 111% in a European market that grew only 4.6% in August. Of course, one company helping to lead the charge was none other than BYD Co., which has seen its global sales volume soar, even surpassing Detroit legend Ford Motor Company last year.

King of the hill

Looking more specifically at BYD in Europe, its sales jumped an even more impressive 131% to finish August as the best-selling Chinese brand in Europe. It's also clear, looking at sales volume growth, that BYD is accelerating toward an even more lucrative future: BYD and Chery combined accounted for 60% of overall Chinese volume growth in August.

Skeptics might be saying to themselves that "it's probably just a high percentage from a low base number," but that would be disingenuous, incorrect, and more importantly, irrelevant. BYD checked in as the top-selling Chinese brand in Europe for May, July, and August. Zooming out just a little, BYD is also the top-selling Chinese brand in Europe through the first eight months of 2026, with sales volume up 144% to 232,600 units.

A catalyst and a hurdle

Some might be wondering why tariffs weren't slapped on Chinese EVs in Europe, as in the U.S., and the answer is that Europe attempted to do so, but it was ineffective. More specifically, the European Union has a maximum tariff of 35.3% on Chinese battery electric vehicles (BEVs), on top of the standard 10% duty.

But that left a plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) loophole. Chinese PHEVs aren't subject to additional import tariffs, only the standard 10% duty, and already European lawmakers are discussing changes to the policy while simultaneously asking China to voluntarily limit hybrid imports to avoid a potential trade war, according to the Financial Times.

Back to the original point: Chinese automakers have arrived globally; they're for real, and it's evident from sales data worldwide. When BYD states that it intends to surpass Toyota as the world's top-selling automaker (not just in EVs or hybrids) by 2030, it should be taken very seriously.

But one hurdle remains: the significant tariff barrier to entering the lucrative U.S. market. It's unclear how or when Chinese autos, such as BYD, could enter the U.S. market, but it's likely to happen in time. Whether BYD can surpass Toyota without the U.S. market is hard to say, though, of course, BYD believes it can. Either way, savvy investors should be doing extensive research on BYD because its growth in Europe is merely a hint of what it is doing globally.

SEOUL, South Korea, Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LG Energy Solution today announced that it has signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MoU) with U.S.-based commercial electric vehicle (EV) startup indiGOtech to explore battery supply and technological collaboration.

indiGOtech is headquartered in Woburn, Massachusetts, and specializes in electrifying commercial van platforms for the North American market. The company is developing an ecosystem that integrates vehicles, charging infrastructure, and digital services.

Under the MoU, the partners will work toward a final agreement for LG Energy Solution to supply 46-series NCM cylindrical battery cells from 2027 to 2030 for indiGOtech's upcoming Flow Ride and Flow Cargo EVs.

The partners will support joint business development through vehicle-battery integration and performance verification efforts. To maximize vehicle performance, both companies intend to review opportunities to extend driving range and reduce charging times.

"Urban ride hail and delivery must electrify and automate at scale, but today's electric vehicles are not designed for purpose, and are severely limited by the local charging infrastructure – that's why vast majority of rides and deliveries are still driven by gas vehicles." said Will Graylin, Chairman and CEO of indiGOtech. "Working toward a long-term relationship with LG Energy Solution brings together advanced battery technology for durable economic advantage for vehicles, drivers and fleet operators."

"Based on LG Energy Solution's 46-series NCM cylindrical battery technology that boasts high energy density and rapid charging capabilities, we will closely collaborate with indiGOtech, which is successfully building the Transportation-as-a-Service (TaaS) ecosystem in the U.S.," said Sunghwan Oh, Mobility & IT Battery Marketing Group Leader of LG Energy Solution. "Leveraging this partnership, we plan to enter the diverse commercial vehicle market in the U.S., including logistics, last-mile delivery, and ride-hailing."

LG Energy Solution is also strengthening its competitiveness by securing additional customers for its 46-series cylindrical batteries. The company reported that cylindrical battery shipments increased by 1.5 times year on year as of Q2, supported by stable mass production and expanded deliveries of its 46-series batteries.

Trump announced Wednesday that South Korea will invest about $200 billion in U.S. energy infrastructure, including $54 billion for the long-planned Alaska LNG project, eight large nuclear reactors, and a 6-gigawatt power-generation facility in Texas.
The investments are part of a broader trade agreement reached last year, under which South Korea committed $350 billion for U.S. projects, including $150 billion for shipbuilding and $200 billion in strategic investments, in exchange for a 15% tariff rate on South Korean goods.
"Part of that money is going into this project,” Trump said of the Alaska LNG development, calling it “one of the largest energy projects in American history."

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said South Korea would invest “just under $200 billion in America, in energy infrastructure, to strengthen American energy dominance.” Trump said the project would deliver nearly 4 billion cubic feet of liquefied natural gas per day and save Alaska households as much as $2,220 annually on energy costs.

text:
Statement of Nathaniel Keohane

President, Center for Climate and Energy Solutions

September 30, 2026

On introduction of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026

“With the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, Congress takes a critical step forward in modernizing our nation’s electric grid – and, by doing so, boosting economic growth and competitiveness, enhancing national security, reducing emissions, and helping provide clean, reliable, and affordable energy for everyone.

“We need to build new energy infrastructure in America, and build it fast, to meet the challenges and opportunities of the moment. These reforms will help make that possible.

“Thanks to bipartisan leadership in the U.S. Senate, Congress has an opportunity this year to pass durable, lasting legislation that will make it easier to build new transmission lines and connect power to the grid, getting more energy faster to businesses and consumers across America. Investors and developers of energy projects will be able to count on their permits once granted, and these projects will benefit from faster and better-coordinated environmental reviews that maintain meaningful environmental and community protections.

“C2ES looks forward to engaging in the debate, leveraging our expertise and trusted relationships to rally businesses, communities, and policymakers behind a deal that will finally bring our nation’s electric grid into the 21st century.”

Additional Background

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 would require neighboring regions to jointly identify and plan for transmission needs across regional boundaries – a vital reform that will unlock the full potential of existing resources and open the door to vast untapped clean energy across the country. Interregional planning coupled with targeted federal authority will help ensure that the transmission projects most likely to lower costs and increase reliability are built. At a time when electricity demand is rising for the first time in decades, this proposal will reduce wasted electricity, improve system efficiency, slash emissions, and ultimately lower costs for consumers.

The legislation also secures much needed certainty and confidence for companies building in America, offering a durable, technology-neutral framework that protects lawfully issued permits from political interference. Stronger protections will ensure American companies can earn a fair return from their clean energy investments.

Finally, the legislation includes common-sense reforms to the NEPA process., focused on the material effects of a proposed project. More predictable reviews and sensible reforms to litigation of projects can help clean energy infrastructure move forward more quickly while maintaining meaningful environmental and community protections.

Beyond these priorities, Congressional leaders have worked out a path forward on historically challenging and politically fraught topics, from the Clean Water Act to the National Historic Preservation Act and more. These good-faith negotiations have put us closer than ever before to fixing the current permitting system that has held the U.S. economy and clean energy back for far too long.

To speak with a C2ES expert, contact Tim Carroll at press@c2es.org.

About C2ES: The Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES) works to secure a safe and stable climate by accelerating the global transition to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions and a thriving, just, and resilient economy. Founded in 1998 as the Pew Center on Global Climate Change, C2ES advances practical, innovative, and durable climate and energy solutions through policy analysis, business engagement, and bipartisan collaboration.

text:
Electric terminal tractors are moving beyond pilot projects as more fleets report operating-cost savings and expand deployments, according to new research from the North American Council for Freight Efficiency (NACFE).

NACFE released its “Beyond the Pilot: Electric Terminal Tractor Adoption, Four Years Later” report as a follow-up to its 2022 research, “The Use Case for Terminal Tractors.” The new study looks at how fleet experiences and the market have changed over the past four years.

“NACFE gathered insights about fleet procurement behavior and preferences related to electric terminal tractors and found that today, terminal tractors are a proven option for a growing number of fleets,” said Bruce Stockton, NACFE senior fleet consultant and one of the report’s authors.

Economics Take a Larger Role in Adoption

NACFE pointed to three findings as evidence that electric terminal tractors are moving beyond the pilot stage.

Among fleet operators surveyed, 76% reported operating-cost savings compared with diesel. NACFE also found that direct economic benefit, rather than sustainability goals alone, is now the most commonly cited reason for adoption.

More fleets are also moving from testing to larger deployments. According to the report, 54% of fleet operators surveyed have progressed to partial deployment or full standardization.

Terminal tractors are also serving as an entry point to broader fleet electrification. NACFE found that 58% of fleet operators surveyed either adopted electric terminal tractors before another type of battery-electric vehicle or have electrified terminal tractors exclusively.

The yard can offer fleets a more controlled environment to gain experience with charging, vehicle performance, and electric-vehicle operations before considering on-road applications.

One Fleet Reports Significant Operating Savings

The report includes one fleet with nearly a decade of side-by-side operating data comparing electric and diesel terminal tractors.

That fleet reported roughly 50% lower maintenance costs per operating hour and 75% to 95% lower energy costs per operating hour for its electric units. NACFE said the fleet’s combined savings have exceeded $5 million.

The figures represent the experience of that individual fleet rather than the entire survey population, but they provide a longer-term look at the potential economics behind terminal tractor electrification.

The report includes seven case studies covering a range of outcomes, from fleets that have fully standardized on electric terminal tractors to organizations that ultimately decided not to adopt them.

Survey Covers Fleet Operators and Industry Partners

NACFE based the report on a survey of 62 respondents from its fleet and industry-partner network. That group included 44 fleet operators and 18 industry partners.

The organization supplemented those responses with seven in-depth interviews and additional independent research.

The report was produced in collaboration with electric terminal tractor manufacturer Orange EV. The company helped sponsor the research, facilitate interview participants, promote the online survey, and provide a manufacturer perspective.

NACFE said Orange EV did not write any part of the report or provide the data used in it.

“This research confirms trends we’ve seen for over a decade: the yard is where fleet electrification is proven to deliver outstanding financial and operational benefits,” said Zack Ruderman, vice president of sales and marketing at Orange EV.

“Fleet operators used to be skeptical about whether electric terminal tractors could actually do the job. Now they are asking about how quickly they could standardize around EVs.”

NACFE Adds Electrification Readiness Tool

Along with the report, NACFE developed an interactive Terminal Tractor Electrification Readiness Tool to help fleets assess whether the technology fits their operations.

The tool evaluates seven factors: daily duty cycle, capital access, external motivators such as regulation or internal decarbonization targets, incentive availability, power and charging infrastructure, prior EV experience, and site control.

Fleets receive a score that places them into one of five readiness tiers, ranging from “strong candidate” to “not yet a fit.”

text:
MANCHESTER, N.H. —

On a trip to New Hampshire on Wednesday, the head of the Environmental Protection Agency sat down with state lawmakers to discuss the state's efforts to remove itself from certain Clean Air Act requirements.

The request from New Hampshire to the EPA came after the state repealed its vehicle inspection program last year.

"New Hampshire knows its air better than any bureaucrat who's sitting in Washington, D.C.," said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.

The state is asking the EPA to take New Hampshire out of its Ozone Transport Region and to sign off on the elimination of emissions testing, now that annual state inspections are no longer mandated by law.

>> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go <<

"You roll in with a check engine light on, and you could spend several thousand dollars just trying to chase which electronic is malfunctioning somewhere," said state Rep. Henry Giasson, R-Goffstown.

In an interview with News 9, Zeldin spoke about the potential impact of approving those changes, as the EPA appears poised to do.

"This is not a decision as to whether or not to reduce air quality," he said. "This is a decision of whether or not to approve the state's request to remove a burden that was placed from the federal government on the state."

While the EPA is expediting New Hampshire's request, Zeldin said he wants his agency's final action to be "durable."

"We go through a process, and that's why we don't just wake up the next day after the ask and say, 'OK, it's granted,'" he said.

New Hampshire's inspections repeal is the subject of both great public interest and ongoing litigation.

"If we did not have a friendlier administration, this process would probably go really sideways really quick," said Majority Leader Jason Osborne.

Zeldin said it's a priority to wrap up the emissions testing issue for New Hampshire as quickly as possible.

"Before the end of the year," Zeldin said. "That was what we committed to out of the gate was to go through this process and complete it by the end of this year."

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senators from both parties said Wednesday they have reached a deal on legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for new energy and infrastructure projects that now face yearslong delays, as lawmakers seek to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy.

The bill, proponents argue, would cut down the arduous timeline for getting big energy projects off the ground at a time when demand is rising because of mushrooming data centers for artificial intelligence. The bill would ensure AI data centers are forced to pay for the increased electricity they use and would mark a significant change to a landmark environmental law that critics say slows the process of building energy projects.

Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee, called the bill “a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects” of all types while maintaining important environmental protections.

Vote on the bill won’t happen until after the midterms

“The American people sent us here to do big things. This is a big thing. It’s monumental and it’s legacy-setting,” Capito said at a news conference at the Capitol where she was joined by Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The four senators lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels.

Heinrich said the bill “will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require — not leave that bill to American families.”

A vote on the bill won’t happen until after the midterm elections — reflecting the fraught political reality as elections loom that could change partisan control of both chambers. But the bill represents a rare instance of bipartisanship over the country’s energy policy as lawmakers from both parties agree on the need to build new energy projects of all types.

Lee, who chairs the energy committee, said he is confident the bill will be approved in a lame-duck session in November, noting its bipartisan support and encouragement from business and environmental groups.

Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment panel, also was hopeful but said Democrats were still seeking clarity on how the bill will prevent President Donald Trump’s administration from blocking wind and solar projects.

He and Heinrich, the top energy Democrat, have decried what they call Trump’s “reckless and vindictive assault on wind energy” that includes repeated actions to block large-scale wind projects under construction off the East Coast. The administration suspended five offshore wind projects in December, citing unspecified national security concerns.

The projects later moved forward after federal judges intervened. A federal judge also struck down Trump’s executive order blocking wind energy projects early in his second term.

Brad Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, an environmental advocacy group, panned the deal, saying it “appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list.” He said the bill could roll back protections for clean water and endangered species, limit judicial review and curtail the power of the Environmental Protection Agency and states to consider impacts of energy projects.

Drew Maloney, president and CEO of the Edison Electric Institute, which represents for-profit utilities, said he was encouraged by provisions to streamline environmental permitting and “create project certainty.” The group is reviewing the transmission provisions to see how they affect efforts to deliver electricity to its 250 million customers, he said.

In a statement, the White House said the bill would “deliver transformative policies to lower Americans’ energy and housing costs, drive new construction and investment in American infrastructure, and create American jobs.”

Trump’s wind opposition played a role in delaying a deal

Trump’s opposition to wind power has been a consistent stumbling block to a deal on permitting reform, which Democrats say can only go forward if the administration agrees to allow previously approved projects to move forward.

Trump recently offered to ease his administration’s holdup on renewable energy projects, in part to entice Democrats to agree to a permitting deal. But it was unclear how long the offer would last and whether it would change after the election results are known.

Whitehouse called the administration’s proposal reasonable but said the overall issue remains “unresolved.”

Manish Bapna, president and CEO of the Natural Resources Defense Council, said his group was studying the bill’s details, but said: “Ensuring the agreement puts an end to the Trump administration’s war on clean energy — the cheapest and fastest sources of energy — will be a necessary element to any deal.”

Capito was confident such obstacles can be overcome.

Both parties recognize that for far too long, “America has had a permitting system filled with delays, expenses, red tape, uncertainty,’' she said. “Too long, too expensive. And we’ve seen projects that should be finished more quickly (take) decades” to complete.

The Senate bill would limit legal challenges under the National Environmental Policy Act, a bedrock environmental law that requires federal agencies to consider a project’s possible environmental impacts before it is approved. The law has increasingly been blamed for stalling projects of all types.

Challenges under the National Historic Preservation Act also would be restricted. The law protects Native American cultural treasures and other important artifacts.

The bill would ease siting of interstate transmission lines and strengthen the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s authority to review major projects at the same time as state reviews, helping needed projects move through the overall permitting process more quickly.

The bill also would require data centers to pay for all associated transmission costs, preventing costs from being passed on to families or businesses.

___

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, R.I.

text:
For years, automotive analysts have been predicting that electric vehicles would become cheaper than their gas-powered equivalents. They figured it would happen sometime in the latter half of the 2020s. BloombergNEF, for example, expected it to happen in 2026.

They weren’t far off.

EV prices have dropped significantly in the last few years, but it has been hard to compare prices with fossil fuel vehicles because not every EV has a like-for-like gas-powered model.

BMW has given us one. The 2027 BMW 3 Series comes in both gas and electric versions, and the EV is $4,400 cheaper.

The gas-powered M350 xDrive will set you back $65,900, while the electric i3 50 xDrive will cost $61,500; neither price includes destination charges. Both are similarly powerful, similarly styled, and aimed at similar pocketbooks. The difference is the EV is 6.7% cheaper.

Pedants will point out there’s a significantly cheaper gas-powered 3 Series trim, though it has no electric equivalent yet. The 2027 BMW 330 is priced at $49,900, and its upgraded xDrive trim costs $51,900.

The two comparable vehicles are built on different platforms, with the EV i3 benefiting from BMW’s newest chassis and technology. The gas-powered 3 Series makes do with an overhauled version of an existing platform.

For most people, the biggest difference will be the charging or refueling experience, but even there they’re more similar than some might expect.

The range of the new gas 3 Series is likely similar to previous models, or about 450 miles per tank in all-wheel-drive guise. The electric i3 will travel 468 miles on a full charge, and BMW says the vehicle’s fast charging is speedy enough to replenish 208 miles of range in 10 minutes. The difference might be noticeable to extreme road warriors, but for most drivers, it’ll be academic.

text:
FedEx has ordered 2,000 all-electric trucks from Harbinger in a deal valued at more than $300 million, the medium-duty manufacturer announced. Delivery is planned by the end of 2027, with the vehicles deployed across North America.

The order is among the largest single commitments to medium-duty electric trucks announced to date, and it comes from a fleet that has already run Harbinger vehicles in service. The order expands on a previously successful deployment of Harbinger vehicles within FedEx operations and follows FedEx’s co-lead investment in Harbinger’s $160 million Series C equity raise.

“FedEx is demonstrating that the business case for incorporating electric vehicles into real-world fleet operations at scale makes sense,” said John Harris, co-founder and CEO of Harbinger.

The OEM estimates the trucks will reduce fuel costs by an average of $20,000 per vehicle per year against conventional equivalents, roughly $40 million annually across the full fleet and approximately $800 million over a 20-year service life. It also projects the deployment will avoid an estimated 1.7 million tons of carbon dioxide emissions over the vehicles’ operating lives.

FedEx framed the order the same way, as an operational and financial decision that also advances an emissions target rather than one made in spite of cost.

“Expanding our deployment of Harbinger vehicles gives us an opportunity to continue making progress toward our fleet electrification goals while reducing fuel and operating costs,” said Paul Melander, senior vice president of safety and transportation at FedEx.

On the product side, Harbinger’s HC Series Cab carries a 26,000-pound gross vehicle weight rating and a 42-foot turning diameter, and the company lists up to 210 miles of range for its electric models. Harbinger engineers its vehicles for a 20-year service life, which is the assumption underneath both the $800 million fuel savings figure and the emissions estimate.

The turning diameter is not a throwaway specification in this application. Pickup and delivery routes put a medium-duty truck into residential streets, alleys and loading zones repeatedly through a shift, and maneuverability at that weight rating is closer to a daily productivity factor than a spec sheet line.

text:
MLB's special-event games, one of the most beloved parts of the league's operations, are hitting an unusual level of turbulence with a potential plan to play at Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming.

League sources said MLB has approached the Trump Administration about the viability of staging a game at a national park, with Grand Teton among the sites discussed. No final decisions have been made, nor have any permits been granted by the National Park Service, and several other unrelated ideas are also under consideration.

Advertisement

Before any formal steps are taken, though, the mere idea of building a temporary ballpark within a national park prompted pushback from a variety of political and business leaders and environmental groups.

"Americans want to see protections for our national parks and public lands strengthened. Bulldozing these lands for a baseball stadium does the opposite, destroying the magnificent landscapes that millions of people come to experience," said Sierra Club Wyoming chapter director Chris Kassar. "It is irresponsible and shortsighted. We can't pretend that a baseball stadium in Grand Teton is in the best interest of Wyomingites."

Seeking the Next Big Thing

MLB's exploration of playing in a national park marks an effort to find the next iteration of its domestic special-event games, which have become key tentpoles within the schedule each year.

Advertisement

Over the past decade, the league has staged three games at the Field of Dreams movie site in Iowa, with a fourth scheduled for 2027, and has also played at Bristol Motor Speedway in Tennessee, Rickwood Field in Alabama, and Fort Bragg in North Carolina. Since 2017, MLB has also played annually in Williamsport, Pennsylvania, in conjunction with the Little League World Series.

Those games have garnered widespread appeal among fans and players, and several milestones have been set, including an MLB single-game attendance record last year in Bristol. The biggest complaint, if any, is that MLB doesn't do more of these special-event games within its 2,430-game regular season.

"I definitely would like to have this be for three days instead of one day," said Phillies star Bryce Harper before this year's Field of Dreams game against the Twins. "I wish it was three days instead of coming in here so quick. It'd be nice to be able to settle down, get the family out there."

The national park consideration, however, has created a rather different vibe.

Advertisement

"Even temporary infrastructure can create lasting impacts through habitat fragmentation, noise and light disturbances, increased human presence in wildlife areas, and strain on park resources," read a joint letter to U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum from leaders of Jackson, Wyoming, the Teton County Commissioners, and the Jackson Hole Chamber of Commerce. "The proposal also risks setting a precedent that major commercial entertainment should occur within protected boundaries."

The White House, meanwhile, said the initial inquiries about the national parks were driven by the league and that it wasn't an "Administration priority."

As the 2027 MLB schedule is now set, any special-event decisions for 2028 and beyond will likely wait until after the league and MLB Players Association grapple with a difficult collective bargaining situation.

“We haven’t landed the plane on mass production of the UEV yet,” Farley said when referring to the platform at the recent Automotive News Congress event in Detroit. “It’s going to be a heck of an effort to launch this at scale, at cost, on time.”

Farley said that Ford is looking at multiple ways to save money on production of the electric truck, which is expected to start at around $30,000. Reaching that price target isn’t going to be easy, especially as the automaker tries to keep the Fathom affordable without making it feel too stripped down.

The Fathom is expected to play an important role in Ford’s push to offer more affordable electric vehicles. Although many electric pickups currently available are expensive and designed to compete with larger trucks (save the coming new $26,400 Slate truck), the Fathom is expected to focus more on value and practicality. That could make it appealing to buyers who want an EV but don’t need the size, power, or price tag of a full-size electric pickup. The vehicle is set to be built at Ford’s Louisville plant, which is currently undergoing a $2 billion retooling.

In a previous interview, Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, told GreenCars that the automaker was working with new suppliers it hadn’t used before. Ford also had to better understand what customers actually wanted in the vehicle, including which features should be included and which could be cut to help keep costs under control.

In short, it’s all easier said than done. Every feature adds cost, weight, and complexity, while removing too much equipment could make the Fathom less competitive against other affordable EVs. Ford will need to find the right balance if it wants to hit the $30,000 price target while still offering a useful and appealing truck.

Multiple Fathom prototypes have been spotted testing in different parts of the country, but Ford has remained tight-lipped about what the truck will offer. We do know that Apple Maps will power the built-in navigation system, as well as the EV route and charging planner. The base powertrain is expected to use a rear electric motor powered by a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack.

Farley didn’t say how far production could be pushed back. Ford had planned to open orders in early 2027 to roughly coincide with the start of production, but that timing could now be in question.

We’ll have to wait and see whether Ford announces an official delay in the next few months. Regardless, the Fathom remains one of the more interesting and intriguing electric vehicles we’re looking forward to seeing on the road, truck or otherwise. And we’ll find out soon enough if Ford can deliver on its $30,000 price target without cutting too many corners.

September 30, 2026 (Boston, MA) – Senate lawmakers on Thursday released the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. The proposal attempts to roll back many important protections for the environment and communities including safeguards under the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and other bedrock environmental laws. It also proposes to severely limit judicial review and lock in polluting fossil fuel projects advanced by the Trump administration.

Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) released the following statement in response:

“While Conservation Law Foundation has rallied for and secured sensible permitting reforms to expedite the deployment of clean energy infrastructure and other priority projects, the ‘Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026’ (as dubbed by its sponsors) emerged from a backroom negotiation among four Senators, two of them ardent supporters of President’s Trump’s obsessive obstruction of clean energy projects – projects that have demonstrably been the lynchpin to energy affordability in New England,” said CLF President Brad Campbell.

“The more than 400-page bill appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list, with passage slated before Christmas, sacrificing numerous protections for communities and the environment to achieve outcomes wholly dependent on President Trump’s highly qualified, pre-election assurances that his administration will act in good faith and allow clean energy projects to move forward. Given that Trump has consistently derided and unlawfully obstructed such projects since returning to office, any deal premised on a promise New Englanders know Trump will break has to be considered delusional.

“Striking this deal in the waning days of this Congress, in a pact and on a schedule that preclude public input or amendment, before midterm elections that can only improve the prospects for a more balanced approach, is indefensible.”

text:
State leaders are providing more insight into the possibility of Oklahoma becoming home to a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.

The campus would be a research park, an advanced manufacturing center and a technology campus.

"Huge potential, once in a generation potential for the state," said Jeff Starling, Oklahoma Secretary of Energy and Environment.

Earlier this year the U.S. Department of Energy opened a competition for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.

The department received 28 applications, and Oklahoma was named a finalist in late July.

"Right now the down select is it will happen by the end of this year for the states and then you know we'll have to work with them on what sites that we're putting forward in Oklahoma actually work with the solutions that they're wanting too. It may be more than one at the end of the day," Starling said.

The campus would consist of three nodes: reactor deployment and isotope production, enrichment through recycling and used nuclear fuel management.

Starling says communities in the state have come forward expressing interest in hosting the campus.

"We started by having the communities in Oklahoma City where we briefed them with Department of Energy officials, Senior Department of Energy officials about a month ago," he said. "We then got into the communities that have identified interest or self-selected. We're never telling them what to do. They've self-selected as wanting to host this campus."

Data center projects have sparked controversy across the state, but Starling says this project is different.

"Data centers are a completely different deal," Starling said. "Data centers come and they add maybe a handful of jobs. This is up to 25,000 jobs across the state. Huge economic input. And this isn't a drain on resources."

Starling said communities that live closest to nuclear are the ones that support it the most.

"We find as people learn more about this campus, the more comfortable they are with the aspects of it," Starling said. "And the economic opportunities that come not only for their kids and grandkids, but their great-grandkids and for future generations of Oklahoma students, our university research programs, the career techs and skilled tradesmen that are needed to operate these facilities."

Oklahoma is one of six states the U.S. Department of Energy is choosing from. The other finalists are West Virginia, Utah, Tennessee, Louisiana and Idaho.

Three states are anticipated to be selected by the end of the year.

text:
The U.S. Energy Department is awarding Entergy Corp. $13.7 million in federal funding to improve power delivery across the utility's service territory.

The funding will help deliver power and support economic growth across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi, according to a Wednesday news release.

The funding will go toward the utility deploying "advanced transmission technology" that will help strengthen grid performance and provide additional transmission capacity, the news release said.

John Hudson, chief external affairs officer for Entergy said in the news release that the technology is intended to help provide more reliable and affordable electricity to customers, by "reducing congestion, improving system readiness for large loads and potentially avoiding capital costs for other transmission upgrades."

He said with the federal funding, Entergy will be able to deploy advanced line rating technology across more than 1,000 miles of transmission lines across the three states, which will help boost the amount of power the utility can move through its existing infrastructure.

This is another example of Entergy doing all we can to modernize the electric grid while reducing the financial impacts of these large projects on our customers and communities," Hudson said.

Through the Energy Department's SPARK program, Entergy and its electric companies in Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi will implement "dynamic line rating technology, targeted geographic surveys, substation and terminal upgrades across 1,125 miles of existing transmission lines."

According to the news release, the upgrades will help the company more effectively manage energy infrastructure in areas experiencing load growth driven by new industrial development, manufacturing and data center expansion.

The four-year project also establishes a scalable, repeatable model for deploying advanced transmission technologies across multiple operating companies and as constraint shifts over time, Entergy will be able to redeploy dynamic line rating sensors to new corridors.

The project is designed to unlock at least 25% increase in transfer capability on selected transmission corridors, and early modeling has shown the potential for 29% to 61% increase in the project area.

"By expanding the capability of existing transmission corridors, Entergy will be better positioned to support new and expanding industries across the region, helping communities attract investment and sustain long-term economic growth," the news release said.

The Energy Department will spend almost $2 billion on the SPARK program to try and squeeze more electricity out of the nation's electric grid.

The money will go toward 31 projects across 26 states that are expected to produce more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity -- enough to power 16 million homes, The Associated Press reported. The projects will use new technologies such as sensors to measure real-time weather conditions to ensure safe transmission or direct power away from congested paths, the department said.

Mercedes-Benz has strengthened its decade-long partnership with ProLogium to gain priority access to its fourth-generation solid-state battery cells, marking a significant advancement in EV technology.

Solid-state batteries offer higher energy density, faster charging, and increased safety compared to traditional lithium-ion cells. Mercedes-Benz is partnering with ProLogium to test these Gen4 lithium ceramic batteries, aiming to integrate the technology into its next-generation electric vehicles within the coming year.

“At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility,” said Jörg Burzer, Board of Management member. “Our partnership with ProLogium helps us advance next-generation battery technology. Beyond its collaboration with ProLogium, Mercedes-Benz is actively diversifying its solid-state battery initiatives by testing lithium-metal battery cells from the American firm Factorial Energy.

In a notable development last year, a Mercedes-Benz EQS equipped with a Factorial solid-state battery pack successfully achieved a range of 748.8 miles (1,205 km) on a single charge. title: The Unlikely Solution to Climate Change: Nuclear Energy - The New Paltz Oracle
description:
That source is nuclear energy.
Many fear nuclear energy, repelled by concerns over toxic radioactive waste or world-ending meltdowns and explosions.
For context, nuclear energy is created in reactors within nuclear power plants through the process of nuclear fission; it uses atomic particles of the chemical element uranium, one of the heaviest naturally occurring elements on earth.
Returning to the paranoia people have surrounding nuclear energy as a whole, it certainly is understandable.

text:
Coming off of the latest brutally hot summer, a topic fresh in the minds of many, including myself, is climate change. The overall reaction to the approaching climate apocalypse from the public and powers at large has been shocking, as far as one would expect apocalypse reactions to go.

This is due to the fundamental challenge at the heart of responding to climate change — to lower emissions in our current oil- and gas-powered global economy, it would require very powerful people who have made a lot of money through the petroleum industry to independently give up their fortunes and levers of global control and work towards greener energy for the greater good. Something they clearly do not want to do in our increasingly data-center filled planet of today. It would also require world leaders to accept that less powerful energy sources should be made to phase out fossil fuels, which yield higher amounts of energy and power than options such as solar or wind power.

However, within the clean energy sector, there does exist a power source that provides vastly higher amounts of energy per unit than fossil fuels do all while keeping emissions just as low as other green alternatives. That source is nuclear energy. Many fear nuclear energy, repelled by concerns over toxic radioactive waste or world-ending meltdowns and explosions. However, these are threats that can be highly mitigated; given the real threat at hand, which is climate change, I think it is time to revisit solutions that some may deem too radical.

For context, nuclear energy is created in reactors within nuclear power plants through the process of nuclear fission; it uses atomic particles of the chemical element uranium, one of the heaviest naturally occurring elements on earth. These atoms are bombarded by extremely high-speed neutrons, which cause them to break down and split into new, smaller elements. (Similar to what occurs in a nuclear bomb, but without the massive explosion!) This releases a massive amount of energy, which is absorbed into a very large quantity of water, which rapidly heats and creates lots of steam. This chain reaction causes turbines within the powerplant to spin extremely quickly, this step being what actually generates electricity and energy. So when you look at a nuclear power plant and see massive plumes of white smoke, it is simply steam; not radioactive waste or polluting carbon. It’s clean; it’s just water!

In terms of energy creation, this process is actually superior in efficiency to fossil fuels. The reason that oil is a more powerful source of energy than green alternatives like wind or solar is that it has a much higher energy density. This means that burning, say, one kilogram of oil is equivalent to using a massive amount of something like solar energy, which is why it is so coveted by any and all institutions that want to build and create. However, by these same metrics, nuclear’s efficiency blows fossil fuels out of the water. To compare it to coal, utilizing just one gram of uranium within a nuclear reactor is equivalent to over 1.5 tons of coal. Clean energy sources like spring power and gas illustrate that the nuclear fission process creates millions times the energy of oil and gas per unit of mass. All of this gain would come at no environmental detriment; it would actually massively help the global emissions problem, with a vast majority of the energy created today coming from fossil fuels.

Returning to the paranoia people have surrounding nuclear energy as a whole, it certainly is understandable. Nuclear energy disasters like Chernobyl and Fukushima scare many away from accepting nuclear energy, viewing it as playing with fire. To that, I would say two things. Firstly, modern solutions to problems like these do exist. Modern-day radiation scientists have tested solutions to problems of the past, such as deep underground containers where nuclear waste can be stored, theoretically able to hold waste for thousands of years into the future without toxic leakage.

Secondly, I would consider the devastating effects that a fossil fuel-based global energy system has already wreaked on our planet. We are currently facing, potentially within our own lifetimes, the global catastrophic concerns that many fear nuclear energy might bring. Earth is currently facing drastic heatwaves, wildfires and ecosystem disruptions at an unprecedented rate. Climate refugees have already begun to flee these disasters en masse and it will only continue and intensify for years to come without drastic action. There’s a reason so many scientists think the world could be made uninhabitable and that we have very little time to fix it.

While for some this may border on conspiracy, many believe oil interests to be at the heart of international conflicts that have led to the devastation of millions of lives. Examples such as the 2003 Iraq War, America’s bombing of Libya in 2011 and Trump’s recent attack on Venezuela all share a common denominator of oil companies profiting and gaining access to higher supplies of petroleum. The owners of these oil companies, like Shell, ExxonMobil and Chevron, directly lobby our politicians and encourage more war and more death on behalf of fossil fuel acquisition. Who is to say the children who were killed in the U.S. invasion on Iraq are not equal victims of oil policy to someone killed due to droughts or floods?

Uranium, on the other hand, is much more globally common than oil and fossil fuels, being found underground in many, many regions of the world, where oil’s relative rarity makes it very valuable and powerful in the instances where it is discovered. This means that further global reliance on uranium and not fossil fuels could lead to more independence and self-sufficiency for many places in the world that are victims of the manipulative oil market and remain subservient to the U.S. dollar, which oil is globally priced in. This is especially true, since as mentioned prior, a mere handful of uranium could be enough to power huge growth and development. Not only could nuclear energy be used to drastically lower emissions in terms of climate change, but it could also level the playing field in a world that is so unequal in its current state. Unless you have a vested interest in the status quo, which those keeping oil as our primary energy source do, rethinking paranoia surrounding nuclear power before it’s too late would be very wise.

text:
Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin said the Trump administration is right on schedule to approve by year’s end changes needed to permanently eliminate mandatory safety and emission inspections for cars and trucks in New Hampshire.

At a roundtable at the New Hampshire Institute of Politics, Zeldin, a former four-term congressman, said he would not prejudge the agency's final rulemaking.

But Zeldin said he agreed with Republican legislative leaders that eliminating emissions inspections is broadly popular among New Hampshire residents.

“The commitment was to complete this before the end of this year. We are still on track to get this done,” Zeldin said, poking fun at Region 1 Administrator Mark Sanborn, a Laconia resident. “They might want to relocate you to Massachusetts if you don’t get this done.”

The comment period ended last Friday for the EPA staff’s recommendation to allow New Hampshire to leave the Ozone Transport Region (OTR) and to change its Clean Air Act compliance plan to permanently get rid of inspections.

Patrick Bird, deputy air division director with EPA Region 1, said his team is evaluating more than 400 pages of comments from individuals, environmental and business groups along with the vendor the state abruptly fired when it stopped the emissions program earlier this winter.

“We are working through these facts. Any response to the comments will be contained in the final action regarding this matter,” Bird said.

House Majority Leader Jason Osborne, R-Auburn, said there’s been no action the Republican-led Legislature has taken in the past debate that has been more popular.

“Inflation has escalated, we have to find those things that can be fixed,” Osborne began. “There is not a lot we can do in a tiny state with a global economy that can make a difference in peoples’ wallets and pocketbooks. This is one of those things.”

Year after year, interest groups defending these emissions hired lobbyists to kill changes to reduce the scope of these inspections, Osborne said.

“We decided this was the way to do it once and for all. I can’t thank you enough and our own DES (Department of Environmental Services) for working to get this done,” Osborne told Zeldin.

Clean Air Act led to mandatory emissions tests

The state adopted mandatory inspections after parts of the state’s air quality was found to have excessive levels of ozone. The state’s compliance with the federal Clean Air Act called for New Hampshire to join the OTR.

Environmental Services Commissioner Bob Scott said the EPA has always been a helpful partner to make the environmental mandates as cost effective for New Hampshire consumers as they could be.

“The Clean Air Act has an off ramp for a reason. This is a success story,” Scott said, pointing to improving air quality standards in recent years.

House Deputy Majority Leader Joe Sweeney, R-Salem, said federal environmental laws were adopted in the 1960s and 1970s with “good intentions,” but improving technology have rendered them less relevant and more onerous.

“We are constantly looking to make sure those regulations are not a barrier to economic growth in New Hampshire,” Sweeney said. “Our laws in this state were not in reality to the improving shape of the vehicles that were on the road.”

A representative with Gordon-Darby Holdings, the inspections vendor, said New Hampshire threatens to put citizens at risk by eliminating these tests permanently.

“New Hampshire may meet all federal air quality standards on a statewide level, but attainment data reflects regional averages rather than the specific street-level air quality an individual breathes every day,” Gordon-Darby said in its statement.

“In more densely populated areas, localized factors like heavy traffic, idling vehicles, and concentrated commercial activity can create micro-scale environments where pollution levels are higher than the regional average. For individuals like Marilyn (Jonas of Wilton), living with chronic respiratory conditions such as asthma, even subtle changes in air quality or the removal of localized control strategies can have a noticeable, real-world impact on their health.”

Environmental opponents to the changes pointed to the American Lung Association’s 27th annual “State of the Air” report.

"The Boston–Worcester–Providence, MA–RI–NH metro area (which includes five of the state’s ten counties, and 79% of the state’s population) continues to struggle with unhealthy air quality, earning failing grades for both ozone smog and short-term particle pollution, despite showing improvement in year-round particle pollution levels,” the report said.

Zeldin said the Clean Air Act was not adopted to impose restrictions to deal with climate change, and that would be a further act for Congress to make.

“My message to Congress is if you want us to regulate the heck out of greenhouse emission standards then change the law and we will follow that law,” Zeldin added.

text:
Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee, called the bill "a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects" of all types while maintaining important environmental protections.

Vote on the bill won't happen until after the midterms

"The American people sent us here to do big things. This is a big thing. It's monumental and it's legacy-setting," Capito said at a news conference at the Capitol where she was joined by Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The four senators lead the chamber's energy and environment panels.

Heinrich said the bill "will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require – not leave that bill to American families."

A vote on the bill won't happen until after the midterm elections — reflecting the fraught political reality as elections loom that could change partisan control of both chambers. But the bill represents a rare instance of bipartisanship over the country's energy policy as lawmakers from both parties agree on the need to build new energy projects of all types.

Lee, who chairs the energy committee, said he is confident the bill will be approved in a lame-duck session in November, noting its bipartisan support and encouragement from business and environmental groups.

READ MORE: Energy Department will spend nearly $2 billion to squeeze more electricity from the nation's aging power grid

Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment panel, also was hopeful but said Democrats were still seeking clarity on how the bill will prevent President Donald Trump's administration from blocking wind and solar projects.

He and Heinrich, the top energy Democrat, have decried what they call Trump's "reckless and vindictive assault on wind energy" that includes repeated actions to block large-scale wind projects under construction off the East Coast. The administration suspended five offshore wind projects in December, citing unspecified national security concerns.

The projects later moved forward after federal judges intervened. A federal judge also struck down Trump's executive order blocking wind energy projects early in his second term.

Brad Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, an environmental advocacy group, panned the deal, saying it "appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list." He said the bill could roll back clean water and endangered species protections, limit judicial review and curtail the power of the Environmental Protection Agency and states to consider impacts of energy projects.

"Striking this deal in the waning days of this Congress, in a pact and on a schedule that preclude public input or amendment, before midterm elections that can only improve the prospects for a more balanced approach, is indefensible," Campbell said in a statement.

In a statement, the White House said the bill would "deliver transformative policies to lower Americans' energy and housing costs, drive new construction and investment in American infrastructure, and create American jobs."

Trump's wind opposition played a role in delaying a deal

Trump's opposition to wind power has been a consistent stumbling block to a deal on permitting reform, which Democrats say can only go forward if the administration agrees to allow previously approved projects to move forward.

Trump recently offered to ease his administration's holdup on renewable energy projects, in part to entice Democrats to agree to a permitting deal.

Whitehouse called the proposal reasonable but said the overall issue remains "unresolved."

Capito was confident such obstacles can be overcome.

WATCH: Why the Trump administration is paying billions to abandon wind farms

Both parties recognize that for far too long, "America has had a permitting system filled with delays, expenses, red tape, uncertainty,'' she said. "Too long, too expensive. And we've seen projects that should be finished more quickly (take) decades" to complete.

The Senate bill would limit legal challenges under the National Environmental Policy Act, a bedrock environmental law that requires federal agencies to consider a project's possible environmental impacts before it is approved. The law has increasingly been blamed for stalling projects of all types.

Challenges under the National Historic Preservation Act also would be restricted. The law protects Native American cultural treasures and other important artifacts.

The bill would ease siting of interstate transmission lines and strengthen the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's authority to review major projects at the same time as state reviews, helping needed projects move through the overall permitting process more quickly.

The bill also would require data centers to pay for all associated transmission costs, preventing costs from being passed on to families or businesses.

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, R.I.

description:

Ionna is far from the largest DC fast charging network in the US.
