text:
A press release that the US Environmental Protection Agency published March 17 about debris and natural disasters seemed like just another minor announcement.

The agency was proposing two new actions, the release said, that would relax permitting rules for air curtain incinerators so communities could clean up faster after emergencies. Both actions seemed unimportant to the 30-year-old fight over air pollution rules for a type of chemical recycling called pyrolysis.

But there was something else in the EPA’s proposal. In section VI, more than midway through the document, was a third action not mentioned in the press release:

“The EPA is soliciting comment on revising the definition of ‘municipal waste combustion unit’ in the OSWI [other solid waste incinerator] NSPS [new source performance standards] and EG [emission guidelines] to remove the reference to ‘pyrolysis/combustion units.’ ”

Within this bureaucratic language lay a potential major development. If “pyrolysis/combustion units” were removed from this definition, they would no longer be classified as incinerators and no longer be subject to the strict hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emission limits in section 129 of the Clean Air Act (CAA).

Getting pyrolysis units out of section 129 is something the plastics industry has been trying to do for years, says Jessica Roff, plastics and petrochemicals program manager for the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives (GAIA), an environmental advocacy group. During President Donald J. Trump’s first term, the EPA proposed a change that was almost identical to the March proposal. But under the Joe Biden administration, the EPA withdrew the change.

“To have it just be this off-handed comment buried two-thirds of the way through a document that makes no reference to anything else about pyrolysis or gasification, other than in that one paragraph,” she says. “It’s bonkers, how much this was hidden.”

The window for comments closed on May 4, but not before eliciting over 55,000 responses. According to the EPA’s latest semiannual regulatory agenda, the final rule was expected in July 2026, but it hasn’t been announced yet.

Pyrolysis thermally breaks down plastics under low oxygen to make pyrolysis oil, or pyoil. This oil can be made into fuels or chemical building blocks for new materials. Pyrolysis can also create incomplete combustion products that are hazardous to human health, such as dioxins, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).

The plastics industry and industry groups such as the American Chemistry Council (ACC) say the CAA section 129 regulations are too strict and are getting in the way of chemical recycling innovation. The ACC has been lobbying states to pass laws saying that chemical recycling is manufacturing and that facilities shouldn’t be regulated as solid waste incinerators. The group has been successful most of the time.

Environmental and community advocates say pyrolysis facilities are too dangerous to take out of section 129. Air permits for manufacturing facilities might not require rigorous monitoring for some of the more toxic air pollutants from pyrolysis facilities, which would leave communities surrounding the facilities at risk, environmental and community advocates contend. They say the plastics industry is pushing chemical recycling as a solution to the plastic pollution problem, when it’s really an excuse for the industry to keep making plastic.

If the EPA does remove pyrolysis units from section 129, how will their air emissions be regulated? Supporters of the move say they’d fall under another part of the CAA. Opponents say there’s nothing in the proposal or current laws that says they would. Instead, regulation might be left up to the states, which have uneven rules about plastics pyrolysis facilities, or none at all.

Pyrolysis plants and the Clean Air Act: In theory

The EPA regulates a stationary source of air pollution if the source emits more than a certain amount of air toxics, says Jane Williams, executive director of the advocacy group California Communities Against Toxics.

Air toxics are dangerous chemicals that can cause acute harm to human health. The EPA regulates close to 200 such compounds, also called hazardous air pollutants (HAPs). The list includes carcinogens, compounds that cause reproductive and developmental effects, neurotoxic compounds, and more.

The EPA usually considers a facility that generates either 9.1 metric tons (t) (10 US tons) per year of any single HAP, or 22.7 t (25 US tons) of combined HAPs, as a major source. In general, facilities that generate less than this are minor sources. The EPA regulates HAPs emissions under CAA sections 112 and 129. There are some exceptions, but most stationary sources are listed and regulated under section 112. Specific emission requirements differ and depend on the source category.

Except incinerators. They fall under section 129. This is by design, Williams says.

When Congress was writing amendments to the CAA in the 1990s, the authors realized that incinerators wouldn’t be properly regulated, she says. “There's a special provision in the [Clean Air] Act for incinerators because their emissions are so uniquely toxic,” Williams says.

Also, incinerators might not emit enough of a combined or single HAP to be regulated by section 112. “So they decided, ‘We’re just going to write a special part of the act so it covers incinerators,’ and that’s what section 129 is,” she says.

This incinerator designation means that pyrolysis units must get a stringent type of air pollution permit called a Title V or major-source permit.

“You need a Title V major-source air permit if you combust solid waste,” says James Yskamp, senior attorney for the advocacy group Earthjustice. “So even for very small municipal waste combustion, whether it’s plastic, whether it’s any other type of waste, they still need a major-source permit,” he says.

Companies try to avoid Title V permits. “There are more limits, and more monitoring and reporting” requirements, Yskamp says.

Under section 129, some incinerators have other specific emission limits for HAPs and other compounds. But generally, the section lays out limits for nine substances: cadmium, carbon monoxide, dioxins and furans, hydrogen chloride, lead, mercury, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, and sulfur oxides.

Federal air regulations are complex, and it’s hard to know what would happen if the EPA removes pyrolysis/combustion units from section 129, Yskamp says. But if that removal does happen, it’s likely that the specific section 129 emission limits would no longer apply to pyrolysis facilities, he says.

The Clean Air Act in practice: It’s complicated

“The Clean Air Act is really tough to try to condense,” Yskamp says. Because of the way section 129 is designed, pyrolysis/combustion units are considered major sources even if they don’t emit enough pollution to get over the law’s major-source threshold. If the agency takes pyrolysis/combustion units out of section 129, they’ll probably be downgraded to minor sources. In general, the downgrade to minor source means they’re no longer in federal jurisdiction, Yskamp says.

“It’s one of these circumstances where it just falls through the cracks of federal regulations,” Yskamp says.

Supporters of removing pyrolysis facilities from section 129 say they’ll be covered by section 112 instead. But remember that the specific requirements of section 112 regulations depend on the stationary-source category, Yskamp says. “There is no category for these pyrolysis facilities,” he says.

To regulate pyrolysis facilities under section 112, the EPA could add pyrolysis/combustion units as a new source category. But this is unlikely, Williams says. The current list of source categories was set shortly after the 1990 CAA amendments, she says. “Those have not been added to since.”

Another way to regulate pyrolysis facilities under section 112 would be to roll them into an existing stationary-source category. But this action isn’t straightforward either.

“There isn’t one clear-cut provision that covers these facilities,” Matthew Kastner, senior director of media relations at the ACC, told C&EN in an email in April.

“It depends more on what is happening at the specific operational level,” he wrote. For example, Kastner said, some pyrolysis facilities could be classified as miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing facilities or as a chemical manufacturing area source. Carla Toth, vice president of sustainability and advocacy for Nexus Circular, which runs a pyrolysis facility in Atlanta, says her firm’s facility could be regulated as a stationary reciprocating internal combustion engine under section 112.

But in its March proposal, the EPA asked only for public comment on whether “pyrolysis/combustion unit” should be taken out of the definition of “municipal waste combustion unit.” The notice did not recommend what section of the CAA the units should fall under or suggest how they’d be regulated in the future.

So where does that leave the regulation of pyrolysis facilities? With the states, Yskamp says. “If [pyrolysis/combustion units are] not a municipalized combustion unit or a combustion unit, and EPA hasn’t developed a category for these, it’s really up to the state how to regulate them, as long as their emissions thresholds fall below the major-source thresholds,” he says.

Some states may have been preparing for this.

What do the states say?

As of Sept. 30, 29 states have laws that define chemical recycling, which includes pyrolysis facilities, or how to regulate it. Twenty-six of them have passed legislation defining chemical recycling in one of three ways: as manufacturing, as not solid waste processing, or as manufacturing and not solid waste processing.

Three states—Maine, New Mexico, and California—have passed laws saying that chemical recycling is defined as solid waste processing and should be regulated as such.

The ACC, which has been actively lobbying state legislatures in support of laws defining chemical recycling as manufacturing instead of solid waste processing, declined C&EN’s request for an interview on its efforts. “ACC will continue supporting policies that enable more mechanical and advanced recycling because we need every available tool to keep more plastic in productive use,” Ross Eisenberg, president of the group’s Plastics Division, says in an emailed statement.

So if the EPA removes pyrolysis/combustion units from section 129 of the CAA, and a state has already passed a law saying chemical recycling is manufacturing, or not solid waste processing, then any pyrolysis facility in the state probably wouldn’t have to comply with section 129, Yskamp says.

But how the shift in authority would play out is complicated, he says. “It depends on how the state regulates the activity,” Yskamp says. Some of the laws in the 26 states that regulate chemical recycling as manufacturing or not solid waste processing have similar text and wording, but some are very different.

In the states that have laws saying pyrolysis is solid waste processing, something similar to section 129 or more stringent probably would still apply. It depends on how the laws are worded, Yskamp says.

But 21 states don’t have specific laws regarding chemical recycling. What would the removal of pyrolysis units from section 129 mean in those states?

Again, it’s not clear, Yskamp says. If a state wants to regulate chemical recycling in a specific way, state lawmakers would have to scramble to get something passed, he says. Otherwise, pyrolysis units in that state would need some kind of minor-source permit. And his experience with other minor-source state air permits is that they usually have minimal monitoring and reporting requirements.

“It’d be very relaxed regulation, especially compared to anything else that would combust plastic,” he says.

If the EPA’s proposal does become a final rule, it’s hard to say if this federal decision will significantly change how states think about pyrolysis facilities and choose to classify them, says Veena Singla, an affiliate at the University of California, San Francisco, Program on Reproductive Health and the Environment. “Generally, what I see in [the air permitting] process is that states will often grant the facilities the designation they ask for in the permit application,” Singla says.

It’s important to note that as of right now, pyrolysis/combustion units are still in section 129 and still regulated as incinerators, she says. “That means that current laws and regulations remain in force, as they have been for years,” Singla says. Federal laws overrule state laws, so a state can’t legally regulate a pyrolysis facility as manufacturing while the federal government still regulates them as solid waste incinerators under section 129.

“A state can be more protective than the federal Clean Air Act, but it can’t be less protective,” Yskamp says.

On the other hand, if Congress passes a federal law defining chemical recycling as manufacturing or otherwise changing how pyrolysis/combustion units are regulated, that law would preempt any state laws. There have been many attempts to pass such a federal law, Williams says, but nothing’s gone through yet. “There’s not really been much appetite in Congress on this,” she says.

A bill currently in Congress, H.R. 7502, the Recycled Materials Attribution Act of 2026, mostly deals with using a calculation called mass balance to determine how companies present recycled-material claims on product packaging. But it also defines “non-mechanical recycling” as a process that “alters the chemical structure of the material and that produces an output used to manufacture products.”

This bill is interesting in that it defines recycling but doesn’t expressly tie it to the CAA, says Mark Duvall, a principal attorney at Beveridge & Diamond. It’s unclear if this bill would have a substantial impact on how pyrolysis units are regulated, he says. “It might be somewhat influential, but I don’t know that there’s a lot there because it’s really addressing a different issue.”

An older bill, H.R. 6566, the Recycling Technology Innovation Act, would redefine solid waste incineration units in CAA section 129 to exclude all types of chemical recycling, including pyrolysis. The bill was sponsored by Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-TX), but its future is unclear since in March, Crenshaw lost his primary campaign for reelection.

C&EN reached out to several lawyers who represent industry interests on chemical recycling and legal interpretation of the CAA. None agreed to be interviewed.

Why does it matter how pyrolysis facilities are regulated?

The plastics industry says chemical recycling is manufacturing and shouldn’t be regulated as solid waste processing. “ACC supports state and federal policies that appropriately regulate advanced recycling as manufacturing, including pyrolysis,” Eisenberg says in the ACC’s emailed statement to C&EN. “Pyrolysis facilities are like any other manufacturing facility that adds value to inputs by creating something new with them to sell as a product.”

But environmental advocates disagree. They say pyrolysis of plastics puts out too many toxic emissions and will harm people’s health if the facilities are regulated as manufacturing instead of incineration.

Singla points to pollution, transparency, and finances as the three main ways that regulating pyrolysis as incineration differs from regulating it as manufacturing.

“There are more limits around particular pollutants, and the requirements to measure and monitor particular pollutants, if it’s an incinerator versus if it’s manufacturing or recycling,” she says. In general, getting a Title V air permit for an incinerator means that the facilities must install ways to control emissions for compounds such as dioxins and certain heavy metals, Singla says.

Title V permits require that facilities regularly test their smokestacks for regulated compounds, Williams says. “Then they have to certify they’re in compliance with those emission limits,” she says. The facilities also must certify that they’re in compliance with the emission limits on a compliance certification document. “If they lie on it, they could go to federal prison,” Williams says.

The emission limits that pyrolysis/combustion units have under section 129, and requirements to control those emissions, aren’t necessarily going to be in air permits for manufacturing facilities, Singla says.

Toth from Nexus Circular says plastics pyrolysis is different from solid waste incineration, so different emission standards should apply. Section 112 would regulate pyrolysis plants “equally” to solid waste incinerators and “appropriately for the differences in our processes,” she says.

Incinerator permits also have public transparency requirements that manufacturing permits lack, Singla says. For instance, a Title V permit requires that draft air permits are released to the public and that a public hearing is held so the local community can comment and ask questions. “There’s not as much opportunity for the community to engage in the process and provide their input around that particular facility” when it’s regulated as manufacturing, she says.

The last way that manufacturing and incineration air permits differ is cost. “There’s more monitoring and reporting,” compared with a typical manufacturing facility permit, Yskamp says. Title V and section 129 regulations with strict requirements take more staff hours and more sophisticated technology to comply with, which can translate to higher costs.

Toth says many permitting requirements for solid waste facilities don’t make sense for pyrolysis facilities, such as requiring a 10-year plan to service and manage waste in a geographical area. This is an inappropriate investment of time, she says.

Costs are already a problem for pyrolysis facilities, some of which are shuttering because of bankruptcy, production issues, or other operational problems. In the past year, three newer pyrolysis plants in the US—Brightmark, Freepoint Eco-Systems, and Braven Environmental—have closed.

Is chemical recycling a solution to the plastic waste problem?

The ACC does not mention cost in its statements about regulations for pyrolysis or chemical recycling. The group says section 129 requirements stand in the way of innovation. “The input for pyrolysis is plastics that would otherwise be destined for disposal, which are converted into pyrolysis oil and then can be sold to make new products,” Eisenberg says in the ACC’s emailed statement to C&EN.

Recent reports by advocacy groups Beyond Plastics, International Pollutants Elimination Network (IPEN), and the Minderoo Foundation (PDF) say that very little pyrolysis oil is being made into new plastic. Of the marketable products the plants are making, most are oils that, after cleaning, are burned as fuel on-site or sold to third parties, the reports say.

“Ultimately, a barrel of pyrolysis oil (pyoil), regardless of its final fate, displaces a barrel of virgin crude extracted from the ground, and makes use of an untapped waste stream that would otherwise be landfilled, incinerated, or, at worst, become pollution,” Eisenberg says in an email to C&EN about the reports. What ultimately happens to the pyrolysis oil depends on what engineering assets the facility using the oil has, he says. “In several years we anticipate greater efficiencies as more research and innovation continue to optimize the process of converting pyoil into plastics,” he says.

There’s a narrative that pyrolysis and chemical recycling are the solution to the plastic pollution crisis, Singla says. “Turning plastics into fuel is not recycling. It doesn’t create new plastic. It removes materials from the production cycle by burning them,” she says. “When you do that, you have to extract more virgin resources to make new plastic.”

Yskamp argues that regulating pyrolysis as manufacturing instead of incineration is a way of rebranding so that people feel okay about continuing to buy plastic. Regulating pyrolysis plants as incinerators makes people think of burning plastic, he says. “Burning plastic doesn’t seem like a solution to the plastic problem, particularly for the communities around the facility,” Yskamp says.

Singla says the attention paid to how to regulate chemical recycling is taking away from what many advocates say is the real solution to the plastic pollution problem: stop making so much of it.

“Who wants a plastic knife, right? It can’t cut your steak,” she says. There are solutions on hand that are going to benefit the public and public health across the full life cycle of plastic, and the focus should be there, Singla says. “Recycling is an end-of-pipe solution. When we focus on recycling, we’re missing the opportunities to address this issue from the beginning to the end.”

text:
President Trump is expected to announce a major boost for a long-planned natural gas pipeline in Alaska in remarks on Wednesday.

South Korea will commit $54 billion toward the Alaska LNG project as part of a broader $200 billion investment in U.S. energy projects, according to a White House official.

The Alaska LNG project is an 807-mile pipeline that would carry natural gas from Alaska’s North Slope to the southern part of the state for export to Asian markets. The project has faced years of questions over its cost and commercial viability.

As part of a broader commitment from Seoul made during trade negotiations last year, the project will also include eight large-scale nuclear power plants and a 6-gigawatt power generation facility in Texas.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Energy Secretary Chris Wright are expected to join Trump, along with Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R), Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and Rep. Nick Begich (R-Alaska).

The event is scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. EDT.

title: Data Centers, Power Bills, and Your Ballot - Southern Alliance for Clean Energy (SACE)
description:
Across the Southeast, data centers are driving extraordinary growth in electricity demand, and monopoly utilities are using it to justify a wave of new fossil gas plants.
Duke Energy says data centers account for more than 85% of expected load growth.
That’s why SACE supports an 18-month moratorium on new large data centers in our region.
In Tennessee, where Knoxville and Knox County have already paused new large data centers, former Knoxville Vice-Mayor Andrew Roberto argues in his guest article, “No Blank Check for Data Centers,” that communities deserve to know who pays, who benefits, and what risks they’re taking on before projects are approved.
Our Where the Candidates Stand 2026 series shows where candidates in closely watched races stand on clean energy, data centers, and affordable utility bills.
text:
Note: This article was originally shared in SACE’s free newsletter, “Wired In,” which includes relevant articles, media clips, and actions to take. Join us to receive Wired In once a month in your inbox, and see September’s full newsletter here.

Across the Southeast, data centers are driving extraordinary growth in electricity demand, and monopoly utilities are using it to justify a wave of new fossil gas plants. Duke Energy says data centers account for more than 85% of expected load growth. Big Tech is racing to build, and our communities are left with higher power bills, strained water supplies, more pollution, and deals struck behind closed doors. But from rural counties to major cities across the Southeast, residents are pushing back, packing town halls and public hearings to demand answers and a real say in what gets built in their backyards.

That’s why SACE supports an 18-month moratorium on new large data centers in our region. It’s also why we launched our new Data Center Resource Hub, where you can learn what’s at stake, track proposals near you, and sign the moratorium petition for your state. We’ll keep adding resources, so check back often.

North Carolina shows what this looks like up close. Duke wants to build two massive methane gas plants and a first-of-its-kind “enhanced” LNG facility on the last serene stretch of the Yadkin River in Davidson and Davie counties, all to serve data centers. Our Q&A article explains how the complex would pollute nearby communities from 195-foot smokestacks, draw millions of gallons of river water, and light up the rural night sky. None of it is final. County commissioners and state regulators still have the power to say no.

In Tennessee, where Knoxville and Knox County have already paused new large data centers, former Knoxville Vice-Mayor Andrew Roberto argues in his guest article, “No Blank Check for Data Centers,” that communities deserve to know who pays, who benefits, and what risks they’re taking on before projects are approved. That matters even more in TVA territory, where the utility’s own board serves as its sole regulator.

Reining in this gold rush takes a whole-of-government approach. County commissions decide zoning and tax breaks. Utility regulators decide which power plants get built and who pays for them. Statehouses and Congress set the rules. No single level can fix this alone, and the people who hold or appoint every one of those seats answer to voters.

Those same decisions shape the Southeast’s clean energy economy. Our “Transportation Electrification in the Southeast” seventh annual report finds the region passed 1 million cumulative EV sales, with new passenger EV sales up 25%. At the same time, federal rollbacks and market consolidation pushed manufacturing investment and jobs down for the first time in seven years. Meanwhile, local solutions deliver real results. On Atlanta’s westside, community partners and Georgia Power built a workforce program that helped 16 of 20 graduates land jobs or enter continuing education within about a month.

Midterm elections are right around the corner. Make sure you’re registered, find out when early voting begins, and look up who’s on your ballot. Our Where the Candidates Stand 2026 series shows where candidates in closely watched races stand on clean energy, data centers, and affordable utility bills. Then keep going: sign your state’s moratorium petition and join the Clean Energy Generation to get timely ways to take action and keep the pressure on before and long after the polls close.

text:
LOWELL, Mass. – The National Governors Association (NGA) today convened energy officials from Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont at the University of Massachusetts Lowell Rist Institute for Sustainability and Energy for the 2026 New England Regional Nuclear Policy Summit. NGA partnered with the six New England states to hold the one-day summit to bring together state leaders, public and private sector experts, and regional stakeholders to examine the potential for advanced nuclear technologies and explore investment models and regional approaches for the deployment of advanced nuclear energy projects.

“Nuclear energy has long played an important role in New England’s energy system, and the governors leading these states continue to collaborate in thoughtful ways to explore the possible role advanced nuclear technologies could play in meeting future energy needs of their states and constituents,” said NGA Chief Executive Officer Brandon Tatum. “By bringing the New England states together, NGA is providing a forum for governors and their teams to learn from experts, hear directly from communities, and identify where working together can deliver reliable, affordable and secure energy. Governors are on the front lines of these decisions, and NGA is proud to support them in that work.”

The summit fulfills a directive issued by the six New England governors in a March 2026 joint statement to convene as a region to explore advanced nuclear energy policies and technologies. In the statement, the governors noted the regional meeting would help further their commitment to the continued safe, affordable and reliable operation of the region’s existing nuclear power plants while exploring ways to create a stronger and more resilient energy future for New England

“UMass Lowell and the Rist Institute for Sustainability and Energy have a proud history of working at the leading edge of energy research and technology,” said UMass Lowell Vice Chancellor for Research and Economic Development Anne Maglia. “We appreciate, and amplify, the value of working together with multiple stakeholders to engage in important conversations surrounding the future of energy and the needs of communities across New England. We are grateful to the National Governors Association for organizing this important meeting. UMass Lowell is thrilled to host along with so many great partners, and we look forward to continued implementation opportunities ahead.”

Over the course of the summit, state officials, energy experts, community representatives and industry leaders examined key questions surrounding the future of nuclear energy in New England, including:

New England’s electricity needs and future projects: How states, private-sector partners and the regional grid operator are preparing for the region’s future electricity needs and considering the potential role of new nuclear generation.

Safety, community engagement and public trust: How states and communities can approach potential new nuclear development while prioritizing safety, public engagement and durable benefits for communities.

Federal and international perspectives: Perspectives on the future of nuclear energy from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and international leaders.

State actions and a regional approach: An overview of initiatives underway in each of the six New England states and opportunities for continued regional collaboration on advanced nuclear exploration.

Advanced nuclear business models: A look at the range of advanced reactor technologies under development and potential approaches for integrating new nuclear generation into the New England power grid.

The summit featured opening remarks from University of Massachusetts Lowell Vice Chancellor Anne Maglia and Massachusetts Secretary of Energy and Environmental Affairs Rebecca Tepper, along with discussions with representatives from the six New England states, ISO New England, the nuclear industry, local government, environmental organizations, academia and international partners.

The program also featured a keynote presentation from Nuclear Regulatory Commission Commissioner David Wright on the Commission’s ongoing role to enable the safe and secure use of civilian nuclear technologies and the role state leaders may play in the future deployment of nuclear projects.

The summit builds on NGA’s ongoing work to support governors as they address growing electricity demand, energy affordability, grid reliability and the transition to emerging energy technologies. Through regional convenings and policy assistance, NGA works with governors’ offices to facilitate bipartisan collaboration among states and strengthen partnerships across the public and private sectors.

text:
Texas Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian is praising the Trump administration’s decision to lower federal fuel economy standards, arguing the changes will reduce regulatory burdens on automakers and expand consumer choice.

The U.S. Department of Transportation finalized the new standards under its “Freedom Means Affordable Cars” initiative. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates the new standards would achieve a fleetwide average fuel economy target of 34.9 miles per gallon by the 2031 model year, down from the Biden administration’s 50.4 mpg target.

According to the department, the revised standards are projected to reduce the average cost of a new vehicle by $1,300, save Americans $138 billion over five years, and prevent more than 300,000 serious injuries and 1,900 deaths by encouraging consumers to purchase newer vehicles.

“This isn’t just about fuel standards,” Christian said in a statement. “It’s about putting an end to the idea that Washington bureaucrats should be able to dictate what Americans drive, how manufacturers build their products or what energy sources our economy uses.”

Christian’s comments follow other recent efforts to reverse federal climate and energy policies.

The Trump administration repealed the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding in February 2026 and has also eliminated certain incentives for vehicle start-stop technology.

“Sound energy policy should be grounded in real-world conditions, not mandates built around unrealistic climate targets,” Christian said in his statement on the fuel economy standards. He added that he supports the administration’s efforts to reverse federal policies he believes have increased energy costs and harmed American manufacturing and energy production.

Christian has previously criticized government subsidies and regulations involving energy policy.

title: Study of Groundwater Near Fracking Sites Finds Low Radium Levels, but Raises Concerns ...
authors: Derek Harrison, Jon Hurdle, Lauren Nutall
description:
Researchers were looking for evidence that fracking has or has not increased concentrations of radium in drinking water.
Only six samples found shallow groundwater mixed with brine, and all traces of radium were below regulatory levels.
Even though the study suggests fracking may not be responsible for elevated radium levels around some drilling sites, there is not yet enough evidence to clearly answer the question, Warner said.
Dan Bain, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh, said produced water has shown elevated radium levels before.
In June 2022, produced water from a gas well in New Freeport, Greene County leaked into an adjacent abandoned conventional gas well, contaminating the town’s drinking water.
text:
Testing in a limited number of shallow aquifers near fracking sites in southwestern Pennsylvania found low levels of radium overall, but there aren’t yet enough samples to draw firm conclusions about the region as a whole, according to a new report from researchers at Penn State University.

Researchers were looking for evidence that fracking has or has not increased concentrations of radium in drinking water. Oil and gas wastewater can be toxic and radioactive. It is also generally extremely salty.

In 2024, the team took samples from 91 private water wells and springs mostly in Washington County, which is one of the most heavily fracked areas of Pennsylvania. Only six samples found shallow groundwater mixed with brine, and all traces of radium were below regulatory levels.

Radium concentrations were higher within three kilometers of oil and gas impoundments and spills, and there was a “weak correlation” between radium activities and the density of oil and gas wells at that distance, the study found. Nathaniel Warner, one of nine researchers who co-authored the paper, said it was difficult to reach conclusions about contamination closer to oil and gas sites because of a lack of samples available within 1 kilometer.

The results showing increased salinity in groundwater are attributable not only to fracking operations but also to road salting and septic tanks, Warner said. But he said that elevated salinity, regardless of the source, was concerning. More salt in water systems can corrode pipes, releasing metals like lead and copper, and it can have a similar effect in aquifers and wells, raising levels of lead, nickel, cobalt, chromium and radium. “It’s like a cascading effect,” Warner said.

Because so many Pennsylvanians rely on private wells for drinking water, and few of those wells are regularly tested, environmentalists have been concerned about contamination caused by oil and gas operations since the beginning of the fracking boom.

Critics of fracking have long accused the natural gas industry of causing water contamination near drilling sites. Wastewater associated with drilling may be contaminated with manmade chemicals, or with naturally occurring substances, some of them radioactive, that are brought to the surface when drill bores probe a mile or more underground.

In 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said fracking can sometimes hurt drinking water supplies as a result of surface spills or underground leaks of chemicals used in the process. Critics of the process often cite the contamination of groundwater at Dimock, in northeastern Pennsylvania, where a resident memorably set his kitchen tap water on fire because of its high concentration of methane, an event recorded in the 2010 movie “Gasland.”

Environmentalists worry that spills and leaks of contaminated water may find their way into aquifers that supply drinking water to people living near drilling sites.

Even though the study suggests fracking may not be responsible for elevated radium levels around some drilling sites, there is not yet enough evidence to clearly answer the question, Warner said.

“There’s not enough overall evidence to conclude that fracking does or does not cause elevated radium,” Warner said. “We have some limited evidence to say that overall, radium is higher. It would be nice to have a lot more samples.”

The researchers were looking for signs of higher radium near oil and gas operations, but they found little sign of it, Warner said.

“You would expect a certain signature of the radium isotopes and the strontium isotopes. We didn’t see that, so it didn’t look like any direct spills elevating radium in these areas,” he said.

The industry has contended for years that fracking does not threaten water quality because the chemicals used are pumped far deeper than water sources, and the water produced is recycled.

“Produced water can be managed safely, and questions about potential health impacts should continue to be evaluated using sound science and evidence,” said Stephanie Catarino Wissman, executive director of the American Petroleum Institute of Pennsylvania, in a statement.

Dan Bain, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh, said produced water has shown elevated radium levels before. Recent research from the University of Pittsburgh found much higher levels of radium in Pennsylvania’s oil and gas wastewater than studies conducted earlier in the fracking boom.

Bain said the study’s results highlighted the challenges of studying contamination in western Pennsylvania. “This is such a complicated waste stream. The oil and gas waste, particularly down in Washington and Greene Counties, is so extensive,” Bain said. “It’s hard to pin any set of waste on any one thing.”

“They were very careful to not be definitive,” he said. “It doesn’t look [like] this set of samples has a chemistry that’s consistent with an oil and gas release.” Still, that particular set of results “doesn’t necessarily mean that fracking is not responsible for elevated radium,” Bain said.

Spills of produced water are relatively rare, but they can damage water quality, so it’s important for scientists to understand the consequences, he said.

In June 2022, produced water from a gas well in New Freeport, Greene County leaked into an adjacent abandoned conventional gas well, contaminating the town’s drinking water.

In such cases, the public may be protected from drinking contaminated water simply by its smell, Bain said. “Truthfully, a lot of times that there is a big incident, the water is so foul tasting that people don’t necessarily keep drinking it,” he said.

David Hess, a former Pennsylvania environment secretary who now publishes an environmental newsletter, argued the new study was unlikely to find evidence linking fracking with radium contamination of water supplies simply because fracking takes place far below the level of aquifers used for drinking water. And he said the study lacked baseline samples taken before drilling began.

“At best, this sampling was an unorganized screening tool for that geographic area for finding results—a chemical fingerprint—that could indicate a well communication incident or spill,” he said.

text:
Ford Motor F CEO Jim Farley believes the U.S. still has time to defend its auto industry against fast-expanding Chinese rivals, even as Europe struggles to contain their growing market presence. His warning highlights a complicated challenge for Detroit automakers: competing against China's lower-cost electric vehicles while selectively tapping Chinese technology to improve their own competitiveness.

Ford, one of America's largest automakers, generates revenue primarily through vehicle sales, commercial fleet operations and financing. Its portfolio spans gasoline-powered vehicles, hybrids and EVs, with the company increasingly emphasizing affordable electrification alongside its profitable truck business.

Speaking at the Automotive News Congress in Detroit on Tuesday, Farley urged U.S. policymakers to consider Europe's experience before deciding how widely to open the American market.

I think it's just important for us to take our time to be considerate, Farley said, according to CNBC. I watch what's happening in Europe right now, where that was not the case, and it's really something that they have to deal with now, and it's too late.

The figures illustrate his concern. Chinese automakers' global market share increased nearly 70% between 2020 and 2025, according to GlobalData, while their European market share reached 12% in August, Dataforce reported.

Farley's strategy, however, is not to abandon Chinese partnerships entirely.

Ford and Geely announced plans in July to manufacture EVs at Ford's Spanish facility through a joint venture, with production targeted for early 2027.

Our answer is pretty simple. We're going to partner with the Chinese where we don't have [intellectual property], where we can be more capital efficient in places like Europe or Southeast Asia, Farley explained.

Investors Takeaway

Ford's answer at home is its Universal EV platform, beginning with the Fathom midsize electric pickup, advertised at a starting price of $28,350, with preorders planned for early 2027.

Investors should monitor whether Ford can achieve competitive production costs and sustainable margins at that price point.

Its Chinese partnerships also carry regulatory uncertainty. U.S. lawmakers are considering additional restrictions on Chinese automotive companies, potentially complicating cross-border investments and supply arrangements.

The central test is whether Ford can absorb Chinese manufacturing advantages abroad while building a sufficiently competitive, lower-cost EV business at home.

title: A Clean Energy Win for Darlington County South Carolina | Sierra Club
description:
Back in May, working closely with our Pee Dee Local Group, Sierra Club mobilized advocates in support of three 75 MW solar projects in rural Darlington County.
In early August, we learned that Darlington County leaders were considering a moratorium that would block any new solar and wind projects.
The clock was ticking to educate and mobilize supporters in the area before the County Council meeting.
Sierra Club South Carolina Chapter Chair, Rev.
When the issue came up for a vote, Darlington County Councilors decided 5-3 to reject the moratorium and allow new solar and wind projects to continue!
text:
When the Darlington County Council chamber filled with Sierra Club advocates on a Thursday night in September, the fight over a proposed 9-month moratorium on new solar and wind projects felt like it had already been won. Months of organizing were on the line: every call to a county leader, every packed public hearing, every testimony from a resident who wanted clean energy in their community. When the vote finally came, Councilors rejected the moratorium 5-3, a decisive win for clean energy in rural South Carolina and a reminder of what's possible when grassroots power shows up early and stays active.

Back in May, working closely with our Pee Dee Local Group, Sierra Club mobilized advocates in support of three 75 MW solar projects in rural Darlington County. We organized supporters to call their county leaders, show up in force at major decision points, and testify on the benefits of renewable energy for the region. Because of this strong public support, we were able to overcome targeted opposition from an entrenched anti-solar group and help these solar projects pass through county zoning.

But then we got some bad news. In early August, we learned that Darlington County leaders were considering a moratorium that would block any new solar and wind projects. The clock was ticking to educate and mobilize supporters in the area before the County Council meeting.

Sierra Club South Carolina Chapter Chair, Rev. Leo Woodberry – nationally known for his work elevating environmental injustices and supporting communities throughout the region in the aftermath of climate catastrophes – utilized his relationships and trusted reputation to voice opposition, rally supporters, and encourage quick and decisive action to keep these much-needed renewable energy projects moving.

Sierra Club members turned up to this month’s County Council meeting prepared to speak out and continue pushing for renewable energy growth in the region. Luckily, our advocacy had already made a big impact. When the issue came up for a vote, Darlington County Councilors decided 5-3 to reject the moratorium and allow new solar and wind projects to continue!

text:
NEW ORLEANS — The U.S. Energy Department has selected Entergy to receive $13.7 million in federal funding to improve power delivery across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi, the energy provider announced Wednesday.

The investment is meant to help Entergy provide more reliable and affordable electricity by deploying advanced transmission technology to strengthen grid performance and unlock additional transmission capacity.

Through the Department of Energy's SPARK program, Entergy says it will implement dynamic line rating technology, targeted geographic surveys, substation and terminal upgrades and hardware integration across 1,125 miles of existing transmission lines across the three states.

The provider claims these upgrades will help it more effectively manage its energy infrastructure in areas experiencing load growth driven by new industrial development, manufacturing and data center expansion.

The project is designed to rapidly unlock at least a 25-percent increase in transfer capability on selected transmission corridors by using real-time line ratings and operational enhancements. Early modeling has shown the potential for a 29 to 61-percent increase in available power capacity across the project area, Entergy says.

text:
The U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee is considering a $50 billion federal plan to create three nuclear innovation campuses, with Louisiana, Tennessee, Utah, Oklahoma, Idaho and West Virginia considered as potential host states, The Center Square reports.

The hubs will feature advanced reactors, nuclear fuel recycling and data centers, with heavy manufacturing industries expected to cluster around the hubs. They’re projected to generate up to $10 billion in long-term local tax revenue and 25,000 jobs. Supporters argue the program could expand reliable, affordable power, meet growing electricity demand from data centers and advanced manufacturing and turn the nation’s roughly 90,000-metric-ton stockpile of spent nuclear fuel into a domestic energy resource.

Lake Barrett of the American Nuclear Society said taxpayers and ratepayers face about $800 million in annual costs for temporary storage, while Energy Secretary Chris Wright and other advocates say regulatory changes are needed to accelerate next-generation nuclear development. The program would involve states agreeing to store nuclear waste, reviving long-standing debates over storage and federal responsibility following the stalled Yucca Mountain project.

Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, says his state’s participation remains exploratory until there is greater clarity on environmental oversight and the terms of a final agreement. Critics also question whether commercial nuclear fuel recycling can operate without government support, with nuclear expert Kathryn Huff noting that similar programs overseas rely on government subsidies.

text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Chairman of the EPW Committee, Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Ranking Member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee, and Mike Lee (R-UT), Chairman of the ENR Committee, introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 to reform the federal environmental review and permitting processes. This groundbreaking agreement will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act provides certainty that permitted energy and infrastructure projects will retain their permits absent extraordinary circumstances, violations of law, or court order, as well as targeted reforms for various energy projects. This legislation reflects input from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle and from a diverse group of stakeholders. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act also forces data centers to pay their fair share by requiring them to pay for all of their associated transmission costs.

“The American people want lower energy bills, and they want more clean energy. Our permitting reform plan gets us a long way toward both of those goals. If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share. Like all major pieces of bipartisan legislation, this bill is a compromise. We believe it is a compromise that will result in a brighter, cleaner, more affordable future,” said EPW Ranking Member Whitehouse.

“For far too long, our broken and outdated federal environmental review and permitting processes have stood in the way of energy reliability, secure jobs, modern infrastructure, and economic growth. The bipartisan reforms we secured in this deal will transform our nation’s ability to power our economy and fuel future growth, while continuing to protect the land, water, and wildlife we all cherish. I look forward to working with our colleagues in the Senate and the House, and President Trump to get this essential legislation signed into law so we can build the infrastructure America needs to grow and thrive,” said EPW Chairman Capito.

“America is entering a new era of energy demand. We have an enormous opportunity to build big things again to meet that moment – to build more generation, expand our grid, create more jobs, lower energy costs, and make sure we have the energy we need to compete. It should not take decades to build the infrastructure our country needs. Our Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help us get to ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on energy projects faster, while protecting important environmental safeguards and protecting the ability of Tribes to formally consult during these processes. It will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require – not leave that bill to American families. Our bill puts teeth behind that principle,” said ENR Ranking Member Heinrich.

“We once built projects like the Hoover Dam, the Golden Gate Bridge, and the Empire State Building in years, not decades. America still has the resources and the talent, but what too often stands in the way is a permitting system that takes too long and costs too much. After years of work in Congress and many months of negotiations, I’m proud we’ve reached a bipartisan agreement to fix this broken process and get America back to building,” said ENR Chairman Lee.

text:
Alliance combines CTLR’s network of senior clean energy executives with E2’s national reach, policy expertise, and advocacy platform.

WASHINGTON — E2, the nation’s most effective business organization for the environment, and Cleantech Leaders Roundtable (CTLR), the nation’s most influential group of cleantech leaders, today announced they are joining forces.

E2 is a nonpartisan organization of business leaders that, during its 26-year history, has helped pass some of the nation’s most important climate and clean energy policies. CTLR is the premier private network for senior leaders driving the transition to resilient infrastructure, energy independence, and sustainable economic growth.

Under the agreement, CTLR will retain its name and identity and will become a program of E2, backed by E2’s national and state policy, advocacy, and communications resources. CTLR CEO Ann Davlin and other CTLR staff will join the E2 team. The move comes as CTLR prepares to mark its 10th year in 2027.

The addition of CTLR’s cleantech executives to E2’s national network of more than 13,000 business leaders will significantly bolster E2’s reach, influence, and advocacy strength and expand its national footprint.

“This is a moment for business leaders to lead,” said E2 Executive Director Bob Keefe. “By bringing CTLR into E2, we’re creating a stronger, more influential voice to get our clean economy back on track in America.”

CTLR members will keep the strategic networking, investment opportunities, and dynamic events with the candid, off-the-record dialogue that has defined the network since its founding. As part of E2, CTLR members will now also have a powerful outlet to amplify their voices and help shape and pass policies to expand clean energy and improve our economy and our environment. They can also participate in E2’s national and regional events and access E2’s renowned data and research, which tracks the clean economy.

“This is about creating more value and more opportunity for our members,” said Ann Davlin, CEO of Cleantech Leaders Roundtable. “CTLR has built an extraordinary community of senior leaders who want to understand where the clean energy economy is going, learn from one another, and build the relationships that help move markets. By joining forces with E2, we can dramatically expand what we offer: more cities, more sectors, more resources and a direct connection between business leadership and the policy decisions shaping our industry.”

“We created E2 more than 25 years ago with the conviction that business leaders can change the paradigm on the economy and the environment,” said E2 Chair and Co-founder Nicole Lederer. “Clean energy right now is at the center of our nation’s economic and environmental future. By combining our organizations, we’re giving the business voice for smart policy more power and impact.”

“The energy industry has reached a point where dealmaking, capital, innovation, and smart policy can’t operate in separate lanes,” said Jigar Shah, co-founder of Cleantech Leaders Roundtable. “Bringing CTLR and E2 together creates that bridge — pairing one of the strongest networks of energy executives and investors with the policy infrastructure needed to cut red tape, unlock American manufacturing, and keep the U.S. competitive globally.”

“Jigar and I started Cleantech Leaders Roundtable to be the home for funded CleanTech founders and their ecosystems. We were convinced the leaders building clean economy growth companies needed a trusted place to come together and build meaningful relationships,” said Jacob Susman, co-founder of Cleantech Leaders Roundtable. “Joining forces with E2 lets us preserve what makes CTLR distinctive while expanding our reach and resources for members.”

###

E2 is a national, nonpartisan group of more than 13,000 business leaders across eight U.S. chapters who advocate for policies that are good for the economy and good for the environment. E2 members have founded or funded more than 2,500 companies, created more than 600,000 jobs and managed more than $100 billion in venture and private equity capital.

Over its 26-year history, E2 has helped pass the policies that built America’s clean energy economy: State and federal renewable energy standards that created the market for the cheapest, most abundant, fastest-to-deploy electricity available; clean vehicle standards that paved the way for hybrid and electric vehicle adoption; energy efficiency standards that save billions of dollars in energy costs every year; and federal and state policies supporting advanced biofuels and sustainable agriculture. Learn more at e2.org.

text:
Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed a bill last week to narrow an exemption to the California Environmental Quality Act for manufacturing facilities. But the long-running political struggle over the cornerstone law continues apace, with both sides now turning their full attention from the Capitol to the voters.

That’s because one of the 14 measures on this year’s ballot would speed up approval under the act for eight categories of building projects — housing and public health developments (such as hospitals); a wide range of clean energy projects; water infrastructure; schools including higher education facilities; public safety projects, including wildfire mitigation work like vegetation management; transportation; and broadband and digital access.

After Newsom’s veto of Senate Bill 954 — an attempt by concerned lawmakers to claw back environmental protections they said the Legislature gave away the year before — the ballot measure is now the primary front in a debate increasingly pitting CEQA’s defenders against both industry representatives and also more moderate Democrat politicians.

The long-simmering debate over CEQA “has become particularly acute and intense” said the bill’s author and Senate Environmental Quality Committee Chair Sen. Catherine Blakespear, D-Encinitas. Blakespear traced the growing fervor over environmental regulations to the 2025 publication of the book “Abundance,” written by Derek Thompson and Ezra Klein, who has long been considered a deep policy thinker by many moderate Democrats.

Newsom embraced the ideas in that book, as did other California Democrats. Now, Proposition 45 will put questions it raised to voters, testing whether they’re worried enough about California’s economy to change its bedrock environmental policy, at least for some projects. Measure opponents say environmental laws are being blamed for costs of living increases driven by broader economic forces.

“What’s happening is this bigger clash between a desire for the abundance movement to be successful, which is basically the understanding that we need to be delivering the things that people need for our society; housing and internet and transportation and clean energy,” Blakespear said last week, when she joined other lawmakers to speak against Prop. 45. “And then an effort to [scapegoat] environmental laws when the delays and the costs are not typically actually related to the environmental laws. It’s a whole range of reasons that things get delayed, and it’s easier to blame CEQA.”

But proponents point to what they say is mounting evidence of CEQA’s role in slowing the state’s growth, particularly in housing construction. Last week, the Yes on Prop 45 campaign highlighted a study published by the corporate law and lobbying firm Holland & Knight. The study examined 11 years of CEQA lawsuits and concluded that nearly two-thirds of them aimed to slow or block infill development with California towns and cities — where many state policymakers want to see more affordable housing built.

“California cannot solve its housing, infrastructure and affordability challenges if CEQA continues to delay the very projects the state urgently needs,” said the study’s lead author, Holland & Knight attorney Jennifer Hernandez, in a news release from the campaign.

Its backers and architects say Prop. 45 will streamline CEQA review for covered projects by imposing deadlines on agencies and courts to issue approvals or disapprovals. The proposition would put a 365 business-day clock on government agencies to approve or reject a project’s environmental impact report. And on the courts, it would impose a 270-day deadline to resolve any legal challenges brought by project opponents.

Tensions over CEQA have built for years as Californians grapple with housing scarcity, though experts disagree on its exact scale, and delays and cost overruns to infrastructure projects that the law’s critics say drive up the high cost of living.

In the Capitol, that tension drove legislation in 2025 to create a series of exemptions for housing and infrastructure development. Newsom put his foot down in that fight, refusing to sign the state budget unless lawmakers passed the exemptions. Blakespear and a large contingent of lawmakers had sought through SB 954 to narrow those exemptions for advanced manufacturing facilities. Seventy-eight Democrats in the Assembly and Senate backed the bill, while a handful of members of the supermajority party withheld their votes and Republicans voted en masse against it.

Opponents, which included a consortium of industrial and business interests including the Bay Area Council, an influential business advocacy group, accused Blakespear of seeking to repeal the exemption before it had a chance to spur development.

Newsom sided with those groups, writing in his veto message that the senator’s bill would have slowed “a long-overdue overhaul to get California building again.”

But Blakespear and her allies didn’t take long to bemoan the bill’s demise. A few days later, she and other lawmakers were speaking against Prop. 45, as a coalition of environmental groups and labor organizations ramps up the campaign against the measure.

The lawmakers said the measure, which runs 41 pages and would apply to eight fairly broad categories of building projects deemed essential, is CEQA’s opponents seeking to take a cudgel to an act that should at best be tweaked carefully in Sacramento. Blakespear pointed to four recent bills she said lawmakers passed to ease the approval of housing.

“We are actually working in the Legislature to promote what we want, and this just goes way too far,” she said.

Loading…

But some lawmakers do support the measure. Perhaps most notable was an endorsement in February from Assembly Appropriations Chair Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. The lawmaker has been a driver of bills to spur housing construction, and at one point in the legislative session, SB 954’s backers worried she’d use her powerful committee chairmanship to kill the bill. Wicks ultimately voted in favor of the bill after policy implications to housing construction were amended out.

“We have to build for the modern era, and I think we can do so in a way that still respects our environmental values,” Wicks said when backing Prop 45.

So far, the public polling on the measure’s popularity with voters hasn’t been definitive. In late June and early July, 73% of likely voters told pollsters for the Public Policy Institute of California they’d vote yes on a proposal to expedite CEQA reviews for housing, transportation, health, water and clean energy projects. But, those polling numbers changed earlier this month when PPIC again asked voters about the measure, this time using language closer to what will be on the ballot in November.

In that poll, only a slim majority, 49%, of likely voters said they’d vote yes, while 46% said no and 5% said they were undecided.

“It is clear that once voters learn exactly what this measure does — allowing developers to fast-track polluting projects like data centers in communities across California, lowering our state’s defenses to Trump’s attack on clean air and water and then sticking us with the bill — the more they sour on it,” said the No on Prop 45 campaign in a statement highlighting the sharply lower support.

The measures proponents have accused the No campaign of trying to scare voters away from what they describe as a limited set of rule changes designed to ease approvals for only projects in the public interest.

“The opponents have been shamelessly dishonest in stoking fears over the ballot measure’s impact on California’s natural resources and the health of our communities. They want to distract voters from the fact that Prop. 45 is a change in government process, not environmental protection,” said California Chamber of Commerce President Jennifer Barrera in a blog post.

The two sides have clashed vehemently over whether the measure would apply to data centers, which are extremely politically unpopular projects.

text:
BPR News | By Katie Myers

This coverage is made possible through a partnership between BPR and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.

The tourism industry is one of the top sources of employment in Buncombe County. So when Tropical Storm Helene caused everyone from nature guides to restaurant and hotel workers to lose months of work, not everyone returned when things calmed down. According to the N.C. Department of Commerce, about 16,000 people left the workforce in the 16 hardest-hit counties of Western North Carolina between April 2023 and April 2026.

Climate disasters are disruptive for every aspect of economic life, from housing and insurance markets to movement of goods to infrastructure to jobs. Helene was no different. The Governor’s Recovery Office for Western North Carolina last week released a plan for Western North Carolina’s economic recovery. One of the issues addressed in the plan is the instability of the region’s post-disaster workforce.

Sharon Decker is the senior adviser for long-term recovery at the Governor’s Recovery Office for Western North Carolina. She said the interruptions to hospitality and recreation, in particular, have caused long-term disruptions in employment for area workers.

“We’re actually losing workforce,” Decker said. “People are leaving because they don’t have jobs. The job they have or perhaps they need to find housing with family or they simply take this as an opportunity to relocate.”

Kris Smith is lead researcher at Headwaters Economics, a nonprofit community development research group. She told BPR that basic infrastructure, childcare access, workforce and government capacity are all basic scaffolding for a post-disaster economic recovery.

“Without them you can just have gaps and you get this kind of downward spiraling of economies because the foundation has been gutted by the disaster,” Smith said.

Smith said private investment is important, but investment in public social services that may be less profitable is also vital. That means providing services like childcare and eldercare, in addition to making investments like small business loans, she said.

In particular, Smith said, tourism-dependent rural economies, like those in much of Western North Carolina, often don’t have much else to fall back on when the economic lifeline is interrupted. As small businesses shut down and home rebuilding moves slowly, people can quickly find themselves in desperate straits.

Currently, the Economic Recovery Plan includes provisions for multiple types of investment in the region’s workforce. Some proposals involve incentives investments, like in affordable housing and small business grants. Other proposals in the plan hope to catalyze new growth in the textile industry. Still others point to education as a major pipeline for good jobs, which means providing support for community colleges and universities in growing sectors like healthcare, forestry and biotechnology, among other things.

According to Decker, the plan includes investment in affordable housing, education and childcare, and healthcare worker training.

“It’s not just one space that was impacted,” Decker said. “It’s massive. So, I think we have to think in a larger term and a bolder vision than maybe we historically had.”

text:
WASHINGTON — Today, Senators Mike Lee (R-UT), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Chairmen and Ranking Members of the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources and the Committee on Environment and Public Works, released the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. This legislation will strengthen American energy security by accelerating the permitting process for critical energy and mineral projects across the United States.

“We once built projects like the Hoover Dam, the Golden Gate Bridge, and the Empire State Building in years, not decades,” said Chairman Lee. “America still has the resources and the talent, but what too often stands in the way is a permitting system that takes too long and costs too much. After years of work in Congress and many months of negotiations, I’m proud we’ve reached a bipartisan agreement to fix this broken process and get America back to building.”

“For far too long, our broken and outdated federal environmental review and permitting processes have stood in the way of energy reliability, secure jobs, modern infrastructure, and economic growth,” said EPW Chairman Capito. “The bipartisan reforms we secured in this deal will transform our nation’s ability to power our economy and fuel future growth, while continuing to protect the land, water, and wildlife we all cherish. I look forward to working with our colleagues in the Senate and the House, and President Trump to get this essential legislation signed into law so we can build the infrastructure America needs to grow and thrive.”

“America is entering a new era of energy demand. We have an enormous opportunity to build big things again to meet that moment – to build more generation, expand our grid, create more jobs, lower energy costs, and make sure we have the energy we need to compete. It should not decades to build the infrastructure our country needs,” said ENR Ranking Member Heinrich. “Our Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help us get to ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on energy projects faster, while protecting important environmental safeguards and protecting the ability of Tribes to formally consult during these processes. It will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. Our bill puts teeth behind that principle.”

text:
Democratic and Republican senators on Wednesday announced a long-sought deal on permitting reform that they say will speed the construction of the nation’s energy and infrastructure projects while reining in costs from data centers.

After months of negotiations, Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) on Wednesday announced the agreement, which they expect to vote on in the lame-duck session after the election.

Heinrich told reporters during a Wednesday press conference that the text includes provisions that will force data centers to pay for the electricity costs they’re adding to the grid rather than passing those costs to consumers.

Capito said it would include “comprehensive reforms” to the nation’s environmental review and permitting processes under the National Environmental Policy Act. The law has come under significant scrutiny from various industries, with firms saying that its processes take too long and slow down infrastructure projects — though its supporters argue it is important for preventing harm to nearby communities and the environment.

Meanwhile, a major component of the negotiations has been the Trump administration’s efforts to hold up renewable energy projects.

Whitehouse said during the press conference that “the question of returning to regular order for wind and solar projects in the Trump administration” remains “unresolved.”

But, he said, lawmakers had received a “very reasonable opening proposal” from the Trump administration.

The administration expressed support for the legislation, with a White House official saying, “We support this deal, which will deliver transformative policies to lower Americans’ energy and housing costs, drive new construction and investment in American infrastructure, and create American jobs.”

“We look forward to seeing it pass quickly,” the official said.

The senators said they plan to take up the bill immediately upon their post-election return.

“Our goal is to have it be the first vote when we come back — at least to begin the process,” Capito said. “We struck that agreement … yesterday night and we all feel it’s a very good agreement.”

Previously, the timing appeared to be a sticking point in the negotiations, with the Trump administration pressing lawmakers to reach a deal quickly and indicating that it could rescind some concessions.

However, Whitehouse told The Hill Wednesday that the White House agreed to the vote schedule.

“It wouldn’t have happened without their support,” he said.

text:
Illinois EPA’s Office of Energy is offering funding to support the state’s Priority Climate Action Plan, made possible through Climate Pollution Reduction Grant Implementation Funds. The Residential Electrification Catalyst Grant Program expands efforts to make residential buildings cleaner, healthier, and more energy efficient.

Through this program, Local Action Agencies (LAAs) and Community Action Agencies (CAAs) engaged in home weatherization can broaden their residential services to fill remaining electrification gaps—such as installing heat pumps, heat pump water heaters, and other necessary upgrades. This support complements existing state and federal incentives available to low‑income households and is specifically designed to address funding gaps in municipal and cooperative utility service areas.

Only LAAs and CAAs offering services in these eligible service areas may apply. As program implementers, these agencies will distribute funding to each home using the following structure:

Total funding requested cannot exceed the award amount received through the Illinois Home Weatherization Assistance Program (IHWAP).

Up to $20,000 per home is available and must include at least one electrification measure. Whole‑home electrification is encouraged, but must demonstrate modeled cost savings.

Funds must be braided with IHWAP, with 50% allocated to IHWAP and 50% allocated to the Residential Electrification Catalyst Grant Program.

Client eligibility is limited to households approved through the IHWAP application review process.

The Residential Electrification Catalyst Grant Program plays a critical role in helping Illinois accelerate its transition to cleaner, more resilient homes—particularly for residents who face the highest energy burdens. Despite the availability of federal and state incentives, many low‑income households remain unable to take full advantage of electrification upgrades due to limited funding, high upfront costs, and gaps in utility service availability. These barriers routinely lead to “walk‑aways,” where projects that would meaningfully improve health, comfort, and long‑term affordability simply cannot proceed.

By strategically supplementing existing programs like IHWAP, this initiative ensures that essential electrification measures—such as heat pumps and heat pump water heaters—can be installed where they would otherwise be out of reach. The program not only reduces greenhouse gas emissions but also supports energy equity, enabling more Illinois residents to access modern, efficient technologies that lower utility bills and improve indoor air quality.

In addition, focusing on municipal and cooperative utility service areas closes a long‑standing funding gap that has limited the reach of electrification programs. The Catalyst Grant strengthens coordination across agencies, supports implementers already trusted within communities, and helps Illinois meet its statewide climate goals through practical, household‑level impact.

text:
Two local environmental groups are criticizing the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality for its tardiness in identifying and penalizing Clean Air Act violations in the Lake Charles area, Louisiana Illuminator reports.

The Environmental Integrity Project and Micah 6:8 Mission reviewed LDEQ’s handling of violations at 23 facilities from January 2021 through August 2026 and identified delays in enforcement, heavy reliance on companies to self-report violations and warning letters and a lack of required corrective actions. Meanwhile, the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality argues the assessment is too broad and does not account for the agency’s recent steps toward more timely enforcement.

The groups found that LDEQ took an average of 1.7 years to issue 45 warning letters after reported incidents or inspections, with one taking 10 years. They cite cases involving the Phillips 66 Lake Charles refinery and Indorama Ventures Olefins in Westlake as examples of how delays can limit the state’s ability to require fixes or collect penalties.

The review found LDEQ took formal enforcement action 28 times during the period, but none of those cases included required corrective measures or investigations to determine the root causes of violations. The groups recommended clearer standards for escalating warning letters to formal enforcement, enforceable corrective measures and follow-up inspections.

LDEQ officials point to a 365-day deadline implemented following recommendations from a 2021 Legislative Auditor report, as well as 3,456 enforcement actions, including 975 related to air quality, during the review period. LDEQ says most cases were identified, evaluated and processed without the extended delays highlighted by the environmental groups and argues that enforcement timelines vary based on workload and case complexity.
