title: Ratepayer Protection Act is a Start, But for Massachusetts, Clean Energy Can Help Keep ...
description:
By working to cancel or delay clean energy projects, the Administration has kept much-needed electricity from coming online.
Electricity demand is surging, and the Administration is preventing clean energy from rising to meet it.
To truly mitigate the impact of data centers on energy bills, the United States needs to massively deploy clean energy across the country.
To grow domestic energy generation and mitigate the impact of rising electricity demand, increasing clean energy deployment is a natural next step.
Just as importantly, Congress must pursue effective permitting reform legislation to allow clean energy deployment to proceed without undue bureaucracy.
text:
Electricity prices in Massachusetts have increased 46% since 2021 and will continue to climb through the end of the year. Energy costs have been increasing for some time, caused in large part by our aging electric grid and volatility in natural gas prices. But the recent growth in artificial intelligence has exacerbated existing problems, creating significant additional energy demand in the region. Data centers are putting upward pressure on energy prices and accelerating the need for investments to maintain and modernize the grid.

The Trump administration’s efforts to obstruct clean energy deployment haven’t helped. By working to cancel or delay clean energy projects, the Administration has kept much-needed electricity from coming online. Electricity demand is surging, and the Administration is preventing clean energy from rising to meet it.

To truly mitigate the impact of data centers on energy bills, the United States needs to massively deploy clean energy across the country. Anxiety is high, with one in six American households behind on utility bills. In Massachusetts, Governor Maura Healey moved to pause sales tax exemptions for new data centers and released a framework that calls for developers to bring in their own clean energy to mitigate their impact on the electric grid.

Congress is attempting to tackle the problem at the federal level by passing the Ratepayer Protection Act. But does the bill actually expand the supply of energy to mitigate data center-related price spikes?

What’s the Ratepayer Protection Act?

The growth of artificial intelligence means a growing need for energy-intensive data centers throughout the United States. While data centers don’t always raise energy costs, rising energy demand will increase customers’ utility bills in much of the country without preventive measures at the state and federal levels.

Policymakers of all stripes have offered solutions to growing energy demand from data center deployment—from temporary construction pauses at the state level to ‘pay your fair share’ proposals for tech companies to outright national moratoria on data center construction. Last week, the House of Representatives voted to pass one such proposal, the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act. Introduced by Congresswoman Kathy Castor (D-FL-14) and Congressman Gabe Evans (R-CO-8), the bill directs states to ensure large-load customers cover the full incremental costs their projects impose on the grid.

Congress can only do so much to blunt the impact of surging energy demand on consumers because our energy sector is jointly regulated, with jurisdiction divided between federal agencies and state governments. As a result, the Ratepayer Protection Act uses one of the few tools available to Congress: encouragement. Existing law gives the federal government the power to require states to consider taking steps like imposing a large-load tariff. It’s a small but sensible first step. On its own, however, the Ratepayer Protection Act won’t solve the problems posed by rapid expansion in energy demand.

What’s Missing from the Ratepayer Protection Act?

The federal government cannot force states to act. And many states, such as Michigan, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania, are already developing large-load tariffs to ensure data centers cover the full costs of connecting to the grid. These states are exempt from the Ratepayer Protection Act.

Massachusetts has not seen major data center development yet, but Governor Healey has already signed an executive order that sets guardrails for data center development. The order bars state permits for data centers above 25 MW until the developer meets the state framework and signs a community benefits agreement. The order gives agencies until the end of this year to set up a system where power users either use clean energy or pay a fee. It also tells the Department of Public Utilities (DPU) to finish the rate schedules it's been working on for large energy users.

The Ratepayer Protection Act would provide guidance encouraging every state to do the same, which is no bad thing. But the bill may do little more than spark conversation within states: those that have adopted large-load tariffs will simply need to determine whether they have met all the bill's suggested parameters, and those without existing tariffs will simply have to consider whether changes are needed in their state.

The Ratepayer Protection Act’s proposed large-load tariffs help divide up the cost of energy investments fairly. If implemented, these tariffs are intended to capture the direct costs that individual data center projects impose on the grid. But the bill does not do anything to address the rising indirect costs the industry may be contributing, let alone how high those costs are to begin with.

Protecting ratepayers from soaring power bills means not only requiring large-load users to cover the full cost of their own projects but also reducing energy costs in the first place. Doing so means deploying as much electricity generation as possible.

Amid tremendous instability in global fossil fuel markets and an ongoing need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to mitigate climate change, there is both an economic and an environmental case for ensuring that most of the energy brought onto the grid to serve data centers is clean. But that is, in itself, no easy feat.

States will need to figure out not only who will build and pay for this additional energy, but also how to remove the permitting and siting delays that are blocking clean energy deployment.

In short, a durable and effective solution to the challenge of growing energy demand from data centers also requires state and federal intervention to rapidly grow clean energy deployment across the United States.

The Reality of Price Increases in Massachusetts

Eversource and National Grid customers have experienced tremendous volatility in power prices over the past few years. This summer was no exception.

Last year, National Grid customers spent about $750 on electricity from June to September. We won’t know the reality of summer utility bills until later this fall, but early-summer forecast analyses of data from Heatmap and MIT suggest they may have spent more than $1,000 this summer. Eversource customers who spent about $740 on electricity last summer may see total costs top $950 by the end of the summer.

What’s Next for Massachusetts?

Rising energy costs are a compounding problem, and delayed action only makes the problem at hand more daunting. Federal, state, and local governments should be working together to expand generation and improve our aging grid. Instead, the Trump administration has made it significantly harder to meet rising energy demand.

To grow domestic energy generation and mitigate the impact of rising electricity demand, increasing clean energy deployment is a natural next step. Clean energy sources like wind, solar, and batteries take less time to build and aren’t subject to the same kind of supply chain shortages and price fluctuations that plague natural gas. But the Trump Administration has stymied clean energy deployment by undermining financing for clean energy, imposing administrative roadblocks that delay project reviews, and formally deprioritizing low-cost resources like solar and wind in federal directives.

What Comes Next at the Federal Level?

To expand upon the Ratepayer Protection Act, Congress, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and regional grid operators should quickly establish a federal transmission-tariff standard for large-loads, ensure the indirect costs being driven by the industry are effectively captured and reinvested in the energy system, and require greater transparency from data centers, including where they plan to build, when projects will come online, and how much electricity they expect to use.

Just as importantly, Congress must pursue effective permitting reform legislation to allow clean energy deployment to proceed without undue bureaucracy.

text:
Grid improvement projects strengthen reliability, boost resilience and lower costs for customers

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The U.S. Energy Department has selected Entergy to receive $13.7 million in federal funding to improve the power delivery to Entergy's customers and communities and support economic growth across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi. The investment will help the company provide customers with more reliable, affordable electricity by deploying advanced transmission technology to strengthen grid performance and unlock additional transmission capacity.

"Installing this new technology is intended to help us deliver more reliable, affordable electricity to customers by reducing congestion, improving system readiness for large loads, and potentially avoiding capital costs for other transmission upgrades," said John Hudson, chief external affairs officer for Entergy. "With this federal funding, we'll be able to deploy advanced dynamic line rating technology across more than 1,000 miles of transmission lines across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi, boosting the amount of power we can safely move using the infrastructure we already have. We appreciate the Department of Energy's partnership and its commitment to strengthening energy resilience in our region. This is another example of Entergy doing all we can to modernize the electric grid while reducing the financial impacts of these large projects on our customers and communities."

Through the DOE's SPARK program, Entergy and its electric companies in Mississippi, Arkansas and Louisiana will implement dynamic line rating technology, targeted geographic surveys, substation and terminal upgrades and hardware integration across 1,125 miles of existing transmission lines. These upgrades will help the company more effectively manage its energy infrastructure in areas experiencing load growth driven by new industrial development, manufacturing and data center expansion.

The project is designed to rapidly unlock at least a 25% increase in transfer capability on selected transmission corridors by using real-time line ratings and operational enhancements. Early modeling has shown the potential for 29% to 61% increase in available power capacity across the project area, demonstrating significant opportunities to reduce congestion and use existing assets more efficiently.

By expanding the capability of existing transmission corridors, Entergy will be better positioned to support new and expanding industries across the region, helping communities attract investment and sustain long-term economic growth. By improving visibility into grid conditions, Entergy can better manage congestion, defer capital investments and reduce costs — benefits that can ultimately translate into savings for customers.

The four-year project also establishes a scalable, repeatable model for deploying advanced transmission technologies across multiple operating companies. As constraints shift over time, Entergy will be able to redeploy dynamic line rating sensors to new corridors, extending the value of the investment and accelerating future modernization efforts.

We're focused on keeping costs for our customers as low as possible while providing reliable energy that our communities count on. We're also investing in growth for the future with a more resilient, cleaner energy system that includes modern natural gas, nuclear and renewable energy generation. As a nationally recognized leader in sustainability and corporate citizenship, we deliver more than $100 million in economic benefits each year to the communities we serve through philanthropy, volunteerism and advocacy. Overall, U.S. light-duty electric vehicle electricity use has more than doubled since 1H23, totaling nearly 14 billion kilowatthours in 1H26.
Both battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles can consume electricity from the grid and are included in our electric vehicle electricity consumption estimates.
Internal combustion, hybrid electric, and fuel cell electric vehicles consume other fuels, do not connect to the grid, and are not included in our electric vehicle electricity use data.
In 2024, the most recent year of available data, electric vehicles accounted for 2% of all registered light-duty vehicles in the United States.
text:
We estimate light-duty electric vehicles in the United States consumed 8% more electricity during the first six months of 2026 than in the last half of 2025 (2H25) in our Monthly Energy Review, down from the 13–24% growth seen in six-month periods in recent years. The slowing electric vehicle electricity consumption growth followed a decline in sales after U.S. federal tax credits expired in September 2025. Overall, U.S. light-duty electric vehicle electricity use has more than doubled since 1H23, totaling nearly 14 billion kilowatthours in 1H26.

Americans drive many different vehicle types. Both battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles can consume electricity from the grid and are included in our electric vehicle electricity consumption estimates. Internal combustion, hybrid electric, and fuel cell electric vehicles consume other fuels, do not connect to the grid, and are not included in our electric vehicle electricity use data.

The New Clean Vehicle Credit and Qualified Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit, which reduced the cost to buy and lease new electric vehicles, ended on September 30, 2025. In 1H26, new electric vehicle sales were down 19% compared with 2H25. New electric vehicle sales are relatively small compared with the total number of vehicles on the road. In 2024, the most recent year of available data, electric vehicles accounted for 2% of all registered light-duty vehicles in the United States.

Our electric vehicle electricity consumption data are estimates for on-road, light-duty vehicles that weigh less than or equal to 8,500 pounds. We do not collect these data on our traditional surveys. Instead, we estimate electric vehicle electricity use with a recently finalized model based on external data sources. Going forward we will continue to estimate these data series in our Monthly Energy Review and State Energy Data System.

title: A startup wants to build a massive nuclear-powered data center on public land in Utah - NPR
description:
Valar Atomics is planning what it calls "Project Beehive" on over 9,000 acres of land held under the Bureau of Land Management near Price, Utah.
Valar has also sought the use of around 650 acres of state land as part of the same project, according to state records.
The Salt Lake Tribune first reported on the project's use of state land last week, but not the much larger proposed use of federal lands.
In a written statement, the Bureau of Land Management's Utah office confirmed it had received an application from the company.
Valar's 25-megawatt electric units could be installed one at a time, allowing Project Beehive to be built in phases over a number of years.
text:
A startup whose founder has vowed to "make nuclear great again" is planning to place hundreds of reactors on federal land in Utah, according to documents reviewed exclusively by NPR.

Valar Atomics is planning what it calls "Project Beehive" on over 9,000 acres of land held under the Bureau of Land Management near Price, Utah. The facility would include data centers and some 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and others for storing nuclear waste, according to a proposal from the company to federal regulators.

In aggregate, the reactors would produce around 9.6 gigawatts of power for the data centers and even more thermal heat for other industrial applications. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces only around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average (though its peak capacity in summer can reach around 10 gigawatts).

The project's timeline calls for nonnuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028.

Valar has also sought the use of around 650 acres of state land as part of the same project, according to state records. The Salt Lake Tribune first reported on the project's use of state land last week, but not the much larger proposed use of federal lands.

The project has raised alarm among local activists, who are already facing a slew of data center proposals in the state.

"It's concerning to see that the Trump administration, with the support of the state of Utah, is pushing this forward on significant acreage of public lands," said Neal Clark, wildlands director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, a Utah-based nonprofit that seeks to protect public lands.

"The coalition of people who are concerned about these things completely transcends political lines," added Lexi Tuddenham, the executive director of the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah, which has tracked nuclear-related industries in the state. Tuddenham said that at the moment her primary goal is to raise awareness. "The biggest thing we can do right now is to let people know about it."

In a written statement, the Bureau of Land Management's Utah office confirmed it had received an application from the company.

"We are currently reviewing the application for completeness," it told NPR in an email. As the application moves through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, "we will make sure the public has meaningful opportunities to provide input," it added.

Valar did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment. In an interview with NPR in July, Valar CEO Isaiah Taylor said his company was committed to safety and community engagement. "We're doing it responsibly and accountably to this community," he said of a smaller test reactor that the company was operating in a neighboring county.

Small reactors, big plan

Project Beehive reveals the scale of the ambitions held by a new generation of companies planning a comeback for nuclear power. The companies are backed by the Trump administration, which has enacted a slew of regulatory reforms over the past year and a half to make their "small modular reactors" easier to test and build.

Valar has been both closely involved with those reforms and a beneficiary of them. Taylor was in the room when President Trump signed a series of executive orders last year designed to accelerate the development of nuclear power, and his company was accepted into the Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program in August 2025. This past February, the U.S. military flew Valar's test reactor from California to Utah aboard a C-17 transport aircraft.

The reactor, known as Ward 250, received rapid approval this year after the Department of Energy conducted a quiet overhaul of its internal safety and security regulations for nuclear reactors. It achieved criticality by reaching a self-sustaining nuclear reaction in June, in a tentlike structure in the Utah desert about 30 miles from the site of Project Beehive.

At a press event on July 1, the company marked another milestone when it used Ward 250 to produce electricity. Taylor powered up the test reactor and used a simple thermoelectric system to run a single Nvidia microchip.

"Ladies and gentlemen, Valar Atomics just became the first startup in history to make nuclear electricity right here," he told the crowd.

The scale of Project Beehive vastly outstrips that July demonstration. Since the turn of the century, the U.S. has switched on just three new nuclear power plants, producing a total of around 3.4 gigawatts of electricity. Those reactors are far larger than the small modular reactors that Valar plans to use, and each costs many billions of dollars to build.

Valar and other companies are hoping to upend the nuclear business model because small reactors can be mass-produced and placed in series, like a set of nuclear batteries. Valar's 25-megawatt electric units could be installed one at a time, allowing Project Beehive to be built in phases over a number of years. That in turn would reduce the cost and allow the site to enter operation relatively quickly. According to a document reviewed by NPR, the full site could be completed by 2032.

Tuddenham said she thinks the use of federal lands for such a project is unprecedented. "In this case, I think it's bigger than the local community," she said. "If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers, that's going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used."

name: North Carolina Environment
title: NC regulators just told Duke Energy 'no.' What's next? - Charlotte Observer
description:
The North Carolina Utilities Commission just did a good thing for customers: it said “no” to Duke Energy, protecting North Carolina families from paying for a gas expansion Duke doesn’t need.
Duke asked for permission to expand a gas plant in Richmond County, claiming the extra capacity was essential to feed a massive data center.
Building a new gas plant is essentially taking out a 30-year mortgage on our utility bills.
North Carolina can choose a far better path forward, often called the “Bring Your Own Clean” framework.
We can welcome economic development to North Carolina without sacrificing our health, our climate goals or handing everyday ratepayers “Big Tech’s” energy bill.
text:
The author is NC Policy Director, Environmental Defense Fund.

The North Carolina Utilities Commission just did a good thing for customers: it said “no” to Duke Energy, protecting North Carolina families from paying for a gas expansion Duke doesn’t need. This order earlier this month represents precisely the kind of cost scrutiny ratepayers need from their Utilities Commission, especially in the context of Duke’s rate hike proposals they’re currently reviewing.

Duke asked for permission to expand a gas plant in Richmond County, claiming the extra capacity was essential to feed a massive data center. But regulators saw the gamble for what it was. In unusually blunt language, the commission called out Duke for overestimating how much power these data centers will actually demand, warning that regular families could end up paying for a project we don’t need.

The commission hit the nail on the head. Duke’s rush to invest in a new generation of costly fossil fuel infrastructure to satisfy speculative tech growth is simply too rapid and too expensive. Building a new gas plant is essentially taking out a 30-year mortgage on our utility bills. If tech demand shifts or cleaner options take over down the road, everyday customers are left paying off the enormous cost of an expensive, polluting power plant — one that it turns out we never needed — for decades.

At the same time, we can’t let utility pushback lead to even worse compromises. Look at what just happened near Richmond County, where that same facility was permitted to run on an enormous fleet of nearly 600 heavy diesel generators. At a time when cheap, clean energy and storage solutions have never been more plentiful, replacing a polluting gas plant with dirty diesel engines is a terrible outcome for local air quality — it spikes climate pollution and burdens nearby neighborhoods with noise and health-harming air pollution.

North Carolina can choose a far better path forward, often called the “Bring Your Own Clean” framework.

Instead of forcing working families to bankroll the power needs of multi-billion-dollar tech giants, we should require data center operators to supply their own power using a custom mix of affordable solar, wind, and battery storage solutions. Google has already proven this model works in Minnesota, where a new data center will be powered by a mix of clean technologies, paid for by Google, on a similar timeline to building a new gas plant.

Under a setup like this, tech companies cover the cost of their own energy footprint, local communities are spared smoke and noise, and ratepayers are protected from footing the bill for bad investments.

The NC Utilities Commission has a clear opportunity to protect household budgets and our health by making this standard practice. Over the next two months, as regulators finalize new rules requiring big power users like data centers to pay their own way, they have the chance to order Duke and other parties to build this “Bring Your Own Clean” model directly into state policy and open the door for big data centers to choose affordable, rapidly deployable, clean power options.

If the commission misses this opportunity, Gov. Josh Stein and the General Assembly will need to step in and take action. We can welcome economic development to North Carolina without sacrificing our health, our climate goals or handing everyday ratepayers “Big Tech’s” energy bill. It’s time to make sure big data centers bring their own cheap, clean, reliable power to the table.

text:
The global energy transition is creating strong demand for technologies that can connect renewable electricity with low-carbon fuels. At the center of this transformation is the Electrolyzers Market, as electrolyzers enable hydrogen production by using electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. When renewable electricity from sources such as solar and wind powers the process, the resulting hydrogen can be produced with very low operational carbon emissions.

According to MarketsandMarkets, the global Electrolyzers Market Size is projected to grow from USD 2.08 billion in 2025 to USD 14.48 billion by 2031, growing at a CAGR of 38.2% from 2025 to 2031. Increasing adoption of green hydrogen, renewable energy integration, supportive hydrogen policies, expanding electrolyzer manufacturing capacity, and industrial decarbonization are among the major factors supporting market growth.

This rapid expansion is positioning the Electrolyzer Industry as an important part of the emerging hydrogen economy. From green steel and ammonia production to hydrogen mobility, energy storage, and grid balancing, electrolyzer systems are becoming increasingly important across the clean-energy value chain.

Why the Electrolyzers Market Matters for the Green Hydrogen Economy

Green hydrogen is produced through water electrolysis powered by renewable electricity. An electrolyzer acts as the core conversion system, transforming electrical energy into hydrogen that can subsequently be stored, transported, or consumed in industrial and energy applications.

The growing deployment of solar and wind power creates an opportunity for electrolyzers to absorb renewable electricity when supply is abundant. Hydrogen can then function as an energy carrier, providing another pathway for managing renewable intermittency.

This is particularly important for sectors that are difficult to decarbonize through direct electrification. Industries such as steel, chemicals, refining, and fertilizers already use hydrogen or hydrogen-derived products and can increasingly explore low-carbon alternatives.

The integration of renewable energy and electrolysis for decarbonization and energy balancing is a major opportunity for the market.

Hydrogen Electrolyzers Market Growth Accelerates

The Hydrogen Electrolyzers Market is expanding alongside investments in green hydrogen projects, renewable energy infrastructure, hydrogen hubs, and industrial decarbonization.

Several factors are contributing to this growth:

Increasing adoption of green hydrogen

Expansion of renewable energy capacity

Government initiatives supporting hydrogen development

Growth in electrolyzer manufacturing capacity

Industrial decarbonization targets

Increasing demand for low-carbon hydrogen

Development of hydrogen mobility infrastructure

Integration of hydrogen production with energy storage and grid systems

The scale-up of manufacturing is particularly significant. The global electrolyzer manufacturing capacity reached nearly 38 GW per year in 2024, based on nominal factory capacities announced by companies, with China being a major contributor.

As manufacturing volumes increase, technology developers and Electrolyzer Companies are focusing on improving stack efficiency, system modularity, durability, automation, and cost performance.

Electrolyzer Technology: ALK, PEM, SOEC, and AEM

The Electrolyzer Industry includes several technology pathways, each with different characteristics and potential applications.

Alkaline Electrolyzers

Alkaline electrolysis is a mature technology and currently represents an important part of the market. It can provide cost-effective hydrogen production for large-scale applications and benefits from established industrial experience.

The alkaline technology holds the largest market share because of its maturity, lower capital expenditure, and suitability for industrial-scale hydrogen production.

Proton Exchange Membrane Electrolyzers

PEM electrolyzers are gaining traction because of their rapid response capabilities and compatibility with variable renewable electricity.

Their ability to respond quickly to changes in electricity availability makes PEM systems suitable for applications where electrolyzers operate alongside intermittent solar and wind generation.

Solid Oxide Electrolyzers

Solid oxide electrolyzer technology operates at high temperatures and can provide opportunities for integrating waste heat into hydrogen production processes.

This technology is particularly relevant for industrial environments where high-temperature heat is already available.

Anion Exchange Membrane Electrolyzers

AEM technology is an emerging pathway within the Hydrogen Electrolyzers Market. The AEM segment to register the highest CAGR of 50.6% during 2025–2031.

Its development is attracting attention because it has the potential to combine characteristics associated with alkaline and PEM systems while reducing dependence on certain expensive critical materials.

Renewable Energy and Electrolyzers: A Powerful Combination

The future growth of the Electrolyzers Market is closely connected with the expansion of renewable electricity.

Solar and wind resources are variable. Electricity generation can sometimes exceed immediate demand, creating periods of surplus renewable power. Electrolyzers can potentially use this electricity to produce hydrogen rather than allowing renewable energy to remain unused.

The hydrogen can subsequently be:

Stored for later use

Used as an industrial feedstock

Converted into ammonia or other hydrogen-derived products

Supplied to mobility applications

Injected into appropriate gas or energy systems

Used for power generation through re-electrification

Renewable-electrolysis integration as an opportunity for both decarbonization and energy balancing.

Industrial Applications Driving the Electrolyzer Industry

Industrial applications are a major demand center for electrolyzers. Hydrogen is already used in several industrial processes, creating opportunities to replace conventional hydrogen production pathways with lower-carbon alternatives.

Green Ammonia

Ammonia production requires hydrogen as a feedstock. Green hydrogen can be produced using renewable electricity and electrolyzers, creating a pathway toward lower-carbon ammonia.

Refining

Hydrogen is widely used in refining operations. Electrolyzers can potentially supply low-carbon hydrogen for selected refinery processes as industries work to reduce emissions.

Chemicals

Hydrogen is an important input for several chemical processes. Green hydrogen can therefore become part of broader strategies for reducing the carbon intensity of chemical production.

Mobility

Hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles, particularly heavy-duty transportation applications, can create additional demand for hydrogen production infrastructure. The mobility application segment records the highest CAGR during the forecast period.

Electrolyzers for Energy Storage and Grid Balancing

One of the most important emerging roles for electrolyzers is their connection with renewable energy and energy-system flexibility.

Electrolyzers can operate flexibly by adjusting hydrogen production according to electricity availability. During periods of abundant renewable generation, additional electricity can be directed toward hydrogen production.

The flexible electrolyzer operation, including load shifting, ramping, and dynamic modulation, can help optimize power consumption and align hydrogen production with periods of abundant renewable energy.

Electrolyzers Market by Power Rating

The market is segmented into:

Less than 500 kW

500 kW–2,000 kW

Above 2,000 kW

Smaller electrolyzers can support pilot projects, research facilities, distributed hydrogen systems, and smaller applications.

The 500 kW–2,000 kW range can support commercial hydrogen production and refueling applications requiring moderate hydrogen volumes.

Large systems above 2,000 kW are increasingly relevant for utility-scale green hydrogen plants, industrial decarbonization projects, renewable energy integration, and power-to-X applications.

Key Electrolyzer Companies Shaping the Market

The competitive landscape includes established industrial companies, hydrogen technology specialists, and emerging technology developers.

Some of the major Electrolyzer Companies include:

thyssenkrupp nucera

Siemens Energy

John Cockerill

Nel

Cummins Inc.

Asahi Kasei

SUNGROW

Next Hydrogen

Thyssenkrupp nucera, Siemens Energy, John Cockerill, Nel, and Cummins Inc. are among the Star players in its current competitive landscape.

The competitive environment is increasingly influenced by manufacturing scale, electrolyzer efficiency, stack technology, system integration capabilities, geographic reach, partnerships, and the ability to support large-scale hydrogen projects.

Asia Pacific Leads the Electrolyzers Market

Regional investment is another important component of market development.

Asia Pacific accounted for 40.5% of the global electrolyzers market in 2024.

The region benefits from expanding renewable energy capacity, industrial hydrogen demand, manufacturing capabilities, and government initiatives supporting clean-energy technologies.

China is also an important contributor to global electrolyzer manufacturing capacity, supporting the development of large-scale production capabilities and competitive supply chains.

Europe is another important market, supported by investments in renewable hydrogen, industrial decarbonization, hydrogen infrastructure, and clean-energy policies.

Key Trends Transforming the Electrolyzer Industry

1. Expansion of Electrolyzer Manufacturing

Manufacturers are increasing production capacity as hydrogen projects move from demonstration stages toward larger commercial deployments.

2. Larger-Scale Green Hydrogen Projects

The industry is moving toward increasingly large electrolyzer installations designed to supply industrial users and integrate directly with renewable power projects.

3. Digitalization of Electrolyzer Systems

Digital monitoring, automation, predictive maintenance, and energy management can improve system visibility and operational efficiency.

4. Modular Electrolyzer Designs

Modular systems can support flexible project development and potentially simplify capacity expansion.

5. Renewable-Energy Integration

The integration of electrolyzers with solar, wind, and other renewable sources is becoming a central strategy for green hydrogen development.

6. Development of Advanced Electrolyzer Technologies

AEM, PEM, and SOEC technologies continue to receive attention as manufacturers seek higher efficiency, improved durability, lower costs, and reduced reliance on critical materials.

Future of the Electrolyzers Market:

The next phase of the Electrolyzers Market will increasingly be defined by the transition from pilot-scale projects toward commercial and industrial deployment.

The development of green hydrogen infrastructure will also create opportunities across the broader hydrogen value chain, including hydrogen storage, transportation, compression, refueling, fuel cells, and hydrogen-derived fuels.

The Electrolyzers Market is emerging as a critical technology market within the global clean-energy transition. As renewable electricity capacity expands and industries search for lower-carbon alternatives, electrolyzers can provide the bridge between renewable power and hydrogen production.

MarketsandMarkets projects the global electrolyzers market to reach USD 14.48 billion by 2031, growing at a 38.2% CAGR from 2025 to 2031. Increasing green hydrogen adoption, renewable energy integration, industrial decarbonization, government support, and expanding manufacturing capacity are expected to remain important market growth factors.

For the Electrolyzer Industry, the opportunity extends beyond hydrogen production. Electrolyzers can become an important component of future industrial energy systems, renewable energy balancing, green fuels, mobility, and low-carbon manufacturing.

text:
Ørsted’s Barrow Offshore Wind Farm is celebrating 20 years of generating renewable, home-grown electricity for the UK, marking two decades of operation that have helped demonstrate the long-term potential of offshore wind.

The milestone also marks the 20th anniversary of Ørsted generating power in the UK. In that time, Ørsted wind farms have produced more than 180 TWh of affordable, renewable, home-grown electricity – enough to power the entire London Underground network for almost 150 years.

Located 7 km south-west of Walney Island in the East Irish Sea, Barrow was one of the UK’s first commercial offshore wind farms. Its 30 wind turbines have a combined generating capacity of 90 MW and began commercial operation in 2006.

Twenty years later, the offshore wind industry has transformed beyond recognition. What was once an emerging technology has become a major part of the UK’s electricity system, with offshore wind generating 18 % of the UK’s electricity in 2025.

Barrow has been at the heart of that transformation. It was the first UK offshore wind project for what was then DONG Energy – now Ørsted – and helped establish the company's presence in the UK and its long-term commitment to offshore wind.

The project has also played an important role in the development of the offshore wind industry in Cumbria. Ørsted's West Coast hub in Barrow-in-Furness has developed into a centre of excellence for offshore wind operations, with a workforce predominantly drawn from the local area and colleagues from across Ørsted’s global portfolio coming to Barrow to develop and share expertise.

The anniversary is therefore not only a celebration of the wind farm itself, but of the people, skills, and local expertise that have kept it generating electricity safely and reliably for two decades.

Godson Njoku, Chief Generation Officer at Ørsted, said:

“Twenty years ago, Barrow was part of a pioneering generation of offshore wind projects that showed what could be achieved by taking turbines out to sea and harnessing the UK's abundant wind resource.

“Today, offshore wind is a fundamental part of the UK's energy system, but Barrow remains special to us. It was Ørsted's first UK project and has been the foundation for two decades of learning, innovation, and operational excellence.

“Most importantly, this anniversary is about the people. Generating electricity for 20 years in an offshore environment takes highly skilled teams, a relentless focus on safety, and an enormous amount of dedication. Many of the skills and expertise developed here in Barrow have gone on to support offshore wind projects in the UK and around the world.

“We’re incredibly proud of what Barrow has achieved over the past 20 years and of the role it’s played in the growth of the industry. As the UK looks towards the next generation of offshore wind, the experience we’ve gained from operating projects like Barrow will be more valuable than ever.”

Richard Bodal Hanson, UK Country Manager at Ørsted, said:

“Barrow's story has always been one of innovation, engineering, and people with the skills to make big things happen. Offshore wind has become an important new chapter in that story.

“Twenty years of Barrow Offshore Wind Farm generating renewable electricity is a remarkable milestone. It’s helped put Barrow on the map as a centre for offshore wind and has created opportunities for local people to develop careers in an industry that now reaches around the world.

“The legacy of Barrow is about much more than the 30 turbines offshore. It’s about the knowledge, skills, and confidence that have been built here over two decades. That’s something the whole community can be proud of.

“As the UK continues to invest in renewable energy, we have an opportunity to build on that legacy and ensure communities such as Barrow remain at the heart of the UK's energy future.”

Barrow is a foundational project for an industry which employs more than 40,000 people in the UK and has attracted tens of billions of pounds in cumulative private and public investment.

For Ørsted, Barrow represents the beginning of a UK offshore wind journey that now encompasses a portfolio of 12 offshore wind farms around the country's coastline with a capacity of 5.7 GW, including Hornsea 2, the world’s largest offshore wind farm.

As Barrow enters its third decade of operation, the wind farm continues to provide renewable electricity while the expertise developed around it helps support the UK's next generation of offshore wind.

About Barrow Offshore Wind Farm

Barrow Offshore Wind Farm is located in the East Irish Sea, 7 km south-west of Walney Island near Barrow-in-Furness.

The wind farm comprises 30 wind turbines.

It has a total installed capacity of 90 MW.

The wind turbines each have a capacity of 3 MW.

The wind farm became commercially operational in 2006.

Ørsted has 100 % ownership of the project today.

Barrow was originally developed as a joint venture between Centrica and DONG Energy. DONG Energy acquired Centrica's remaining 50 % stake in 2014, becoming sole owner of the project.

Barrow was Ørsted's first UK offshore wind project.

text:
Ameren Missouri wants to significantly ramp up power plant construction to meet data center electricity needs, according to a 20-year plan released this week.

The new plan significantly increases the company’s reliance on natural gas plants while scaling back the percentage of energy produced by renewable sources like wind and solar. And in a change from previous plans, the company is no longer discussing a goal to reach net-zero carbon emissions.

Monopoly utilities publish these plans, called Integrated Resource Plans, every three years as required by Missouri law. This plan is now a case before the Missouri Public Service Commission, which will include pushback from outside parties and public comment submitted to regulators before being finalized.

Data center growth

There are currently 40 potential large data centers that could be built within Ameren Missouri’s footprint, according to the document, including multiple projects that have signed binding agreements with the company.

New data centers represent the majority of the company’s projected growth over the next 20 years, said Ajay Arora, executive vice president, chief growth officer and chief generation development officer for Ameren Missouri.

He said those projects could benefit regular consumers.

“Economic development is vital to the state,” Arora said. “It helps us modernize our electric grid to ensure reliability for everybody and have that fixed cost be spread over new customers.”

To meet that new demand, Ameren is planning to build power plants and renewable energy projects that would generate almost double the amount of electricity it was projecting to build in its 2023 projection.

Shifting climate goals

In 2020 and 2023, Ameren focused its planning on renewable energy, discussing goals to reach net-zero carbon emissions. Ameren removed that language in the 2026 Integrated Resource Plan, discussing how its plan will decrease carbon emissions, but saying technology like carbon capture would have to advance to achieve net-zero emissions.

“We are not changing our net-zero targets right now,” Arora said. “However, we do outline in the plan that new technology would need to mature in order for us to achieve our net-zero goals.”

Much of the new power would come from natural gas — in 2023, the Integrated Resource Plan called for two such plants. In 2026, the new plan lists nine plants to be built over the next two decades.

Environmental advocates took issue with that new focus on natural gas, including Jenn DeRose, the Sierra Club’s campaign organizing strategist for Beyond Coal in Missouri.

“Their own research shows that solar and wind are the cheapest forms of energy to build, and they're still choosing gas,” DeRose said. “I find that very interesting. I also find it very interesting that they cite extreme weather as a reason for building gas. Do you know what causes extreme weather? Climate change. Do you know what contributes to catastrophic climate change? Coal and gas.”

Ameren Vice President of Regulatory and Legislative Affairs Rob Dixon said a reliable energy system needs a diversity of energy sources.

“It's really important to remember that no single technology type can meet every customer need in every hour under every condition,” Dixon said.

Increasing renewables and keeping coal

The 2026 Integrated Resource Plan also increases the company’s renewable energy buildout, with new solar plants and battery storage.

“They are adding solar, they are adding batteries, and I think that's good,” said James Owen, executive director of Renew Missouri. “I think that makes sense for long-term considerations. But I think the continued reliance on fossil fuels is going to end up costing customers more money than Ameren is currently anticipating.”

For the IRP, Ameren calculated the lifetime costs of each source of new energy it is considering building. The company found wind, solar and the kinds of natural gas plants that run consistently were the least expensive per kWh, while nuclear plants and the kind of gas plants that can turn on and off, potentially to supplement renewables, were the most expensive.

The new plan also extends the lives of two coal plants. The Sioux Coal plant would close three years later than planned in 2023, while the Labadie plant would keep all four units operational until 2042, when two were originally set to retire in 2035.

Arora said that decision was made to save money.

“Labadie remains one of the most affordable plants in the country and recognizing the economic conditions for all our customers and how important reliability and affordability is, that's really factored into delaying the retirement of a few of the Labadie units by a few years,” he said.

Environmental advocates said there are other costs that come with coal.

“Do you know why that plant is so affordable?” DeRose said. “It’s because it doesn't have any modern pollution controls. So it's only affordable for the company. Those health externalities, those are what we have to pay for.”

Paying for new plants

To actually build power plants or to set new electricity rates, Ameren still has to take each request to the Public Service Commission as a case.

While this plan does not change people’s bills, Owen said the cost of the new power plants will trickle down to customers eventually.

“Any time they build more generation, it's going to increase rates,” Owen said. “I don't know how they can say that, ‘Oh, this is [only costing] data centers,’ when that's the main thing driving energy consumption right now. It's not that we're having this huge influx of people moving into Missouri. It is not this huge influx of other manufacturing jobs. It's data centers.”

Ameren’s representatives said a Missouri utility law known as Senate Bill 4 requires data centers to pay for the infrastructure to serve them and said the companies do not receive discounted electric rates.

“The safeguards in Senate Bill 4 are meaningful,” Dixon said. “That's exactly what ensures that other customers are not bearing the costs caused by data centers. And in fact, we've done some projections, and we expect that our customers are going to see projected savings of $21 million over the next two years driven by the data center customers that we've already committed.”

The Sierra Club’s DeRose wants more people to get involved in the utility planning process and is organizing a protest against Ameren on Oct. 10.

“They need to hear your voice, the average customer's voice, if we're going to see the company change its ways and change its addiction to fossil fuels into something that is more sustainable for our future,” DeRose said.

text:
By Todd C. FrankelTHE WASHINGTON POST

The Trump administration unveiled new rules Monday rolling back the nation’s fuel economy standards, touting the move as a money-saving measure for American auto buyers struggling with affordability.

The regulations, first proposed in December, also further signal the end of federal support for nudging drivers to switch from gasoline to electric cars and trucks.

The rules still require fuel efficiency improvements but at a slower pace. Automakers now will need a car-and-truck fleetwide average of 34.9 mpg by the 2031 model year, instead of the stricter, projected 49.3 mpg under the Biden-era rule. Average fuel economy was 27.2 mpg in the 2024 model year, according to a government analysis.

The Trump administration has pitched these new rules as a way for people to save money – one potential solution to the affordability debate that has roiled the country in recent years amid high inflation and rising costs – though analysts have expressed skepticism about whether any savings would reach consumers.

The average new vehicle price in 2031 should be reduced by $1,289 due to the weaker fuel economy standards, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which drafted the regulation.

But that’s only if those savings are passed on to consumers, NHTSA cautioned.

“Freedom means affordable cars” was the headline on the administration’s event Monday announcing the finalized regulations.

And President Donald Trump touted the new standard in a social media post Saturday, writing: “That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car.”

Analysts were doubtful that car shoppers should expect $1,300 price cuts from the new regulations – and any savings would be hard to notice, with average new vehicle prices currently hovering around $50,000.

“You’re not going to see a vehicle that’s $1,300 less expensive,” said Stephanie Brinley, principal automotive analyst with Mobility Global. “That’s not quite how it works.”

Brinley said NHTSA’s assumptions about how automakers might save under the new regulations don’t necessarily translate into savings for consumers. Car companies will face less regulatory pressure to sell electric vehicles. But it’s possible consumers will still demand more EVs or hybrids – especially if gas prices remain elevated.

Automakers already are struggling under Trump’s tariffs, which increase costs, said Jessica Caldwell, head of insights at Edmunds. So any savings from weaker fuel economy standards would probably go to offset tariffs first, Caldwell said.

“I don’t see the direct savings being passed along,” she said. “It’s just not how vehicles are priced.”

The $1,300 cost savings come mainly through lower regulatory technology costs, according to NHTSA. It’s simply less expensive to comply with the watered-down fuel economy standards.

But the agency admits that in “some model years” the added fuel costs would outweigh the $1,300 drop in vehicle price.

NHTSA also noted that it projects the overall benefits to outweigh the costs.

Caldwell said she didn’t expect automakers to abandon EVs and focus just on gas-powered vehicles. Car companies know that the rules can flip with a new administration. And they need to plan years ahead for new models.

The larger problem for U.S. automakers is that the rest of the world is rapidly moving toward EVs, Caldwell said. American firms need to keep their foothold in global markets to remain competitive.

Still, Trump has been shifting the U.S. market away from EVs.

His tax and spending overhaul last year – known as the One Big Beautiful Bill – ended the $7,500 EV purchase credit program. The bill also eliminated financial penalties for automakers that failed to meet corporate average fuel economy standards, known as CAFE.

Now those standards are being relaxed.

title: US policy landscape has driven domestic manufacturing, but requires a more 'holistic' approach
description:
For India, Indonesia and Laos in particular, the targets of the most recent AD/CVD investigations, their contribution to US module imports has risen and fallen spectacularly.
This all comes as the total value of solar imports to the US has fallen over the last two years.
The survey’s respondents said that a “holistic” approach, combining both types of policy, would be to the benefit of the industry as a whole.
“A holistic carrot-and-stick approach works where neither instrument succeeds alone, and sequencing matters as much as the mix,” reads the Crux report.
Read more of our coverage of the US policy landscape in our monthly editor’s blog series; the most recent edition looked at the Indian AD/CVD investigations and bans on power equipment produced overseas.
text:
The report also notes that advances in US solar manufacturing, and foreign policies such as the anti-dumping and countervailing duties (AD/CVDs), have helped reduce reliance on the import of solar components from several countries. Crux notes that in the first half of 2024, four Southeast Asian countries were responsible for 86% of US crystalline silicon (c-Si) imports, but that this figure fell to just 2% in the first half of this year, with the Department of Commerce (DOC) conducting several AD/CVD investigations in this part of the world.

For India, Indonesia and Laos in particular, the targets of the most recent AD/CVD investigations, their contribution to US module imports has risen and fallen spectacularly. These countries accounted for 9% of US c-Si modules in the first half of 2024, before jumping to 72% as AD/CVD investigations advanced in other countries, before coming back down to 19% by the first half of 2026 as the investigations began to target these countries.

This all comes as the total value of solar imports to the US has fallen over the last two years. As shown in the graph below, taken from the Crux report, import value fell from a peak of over US$6 billion in 2024 to less than US$4 billion in the second quarter of this year.

There is also a notable disparity in the value of different parts of the solar supply chain that the US is currently importing, which reflects how the domestic manufacturing picture has changed. In the first half of 2024, modules accounted for 73% of the value of all solar imports; by the first half of 2026, this fell to 35%. This translates to a fall in value from US$7.6 billion to US$1.7 billion, and reflects how the US has been able to build new module manufacturing capacity more successfully than other parts of the solar supply chain.

The US has also made efforts to address this balance through investments made into other parts of the supply chain. The Crux report shows that, as of the second quarter of this year, companies have announced US$7.3 billion in new US module facilities, a smaller figure than the leading US$8.9 billion announced in new cell investments.

Gaps remain in the domestic supply chain

While the billions of dollars of new manufacturing capacity investment is a positive step, the Crux report notes that the US is not in a position of complete supply chain independence. Even the announced investment figures “overstate the footprint,” according to the report; US$2.1 billion has been announced in new ingot and wafer facilities, but all of this is tied up in the work of a single company, Corning, so US production of ingots and wafers is by no means expansive.

Even in modules, where the US has had some success in building enough new manufacturing capacity to meet current demand, it has not necessarily done enough to meet future demand growth. As a result, even for modules, the US remains reliant on overseas imports, and the plethora of AD/CVD investigations means that, rather than eliminating imports of modules entirely, US buyers are now forced to look elsewhere.

The graph below shows how different countries accounted for the US’ module imports in the first half of 2024 and the first half of 2026. While the most influential countries in 2024—Vietnam and Thailand, which collectively accounted for over two-thirds of US module imports—saw their influence reduced to a negligible amount in 2026, US buyers have instead shifted their attention to countries like the Philippines and Ethiopia.

Considering the DOC has started an AD/CVD investigation into Ethiopian cell production, there is a risk that any new source of overseas modules will eventually be subject to AD/CVD investigations, affecting supply at a time when US manufacturers cannot yet plug the gap.

While Ethiopia is a new participant in US cell imports—its contribution to US cell purchases jumped from nothing in 2024 to 13.5% in 2026—there is more stability in the US’ primary cell provider, South Korea. South Korean cells accounted for 39.1% of US imports in the first half of 2024 and 35.9% in the first half of 2026, and earlier this year Crux head of policy Hasan Nazar told PV Tech Premium that countries such as South Korea could be an essential part of ‘friend-shoring’, an initiative to source key components not yet produced in the US from allied nations.

The Crux report also included a survey component, asking 75 organisations involved in development, supply or manufacturing of key components in the US for their opinions on the current supply chain landscape. The survey reported that “firms are absorbing tariff costs” rather than switching suppliers, due to a lack of domestic supply and concerns over the long-term viability of sourcing components from overseas manufacturers, showing how the combination of tariffs and AD/CVD investigations are creating challenging economic conditions for US project developers.

Indeed, 89% of survey respondents said that at least some of their tariff-exposed inputs “have no domestic substitute that is available at a competitive price,” and 47% said that an absence of a domestic producer at sufficient scale is the “single biggest barrier” to robust domestic supply.

Crux calls for ‘holistic’ policy approach

Most of the new US manufacturing capacity can be tied to the strength of incentivising policies like the 45X tax credit, while there are certainly some benefits to foreign policies like the AD/CVD investigations that dissuade reliance on foreign products. The survey’s respondents said that a “holistic” approach, combining both types of policy, would be to the benefit of the industry as a whole.

“A holistic carrot-and-stick approach works where neither instrument succeeds alone, and sequencing matters as much as the mix,” reads the Crux report. “Cutting off Chinese supply before sufficient domestic or allied alternatives are available can put project financeability at risk.”

When asked about the most important parts of the supply chain that could be covered by these policies, the survey respondents, perhaps unsurprisingly, pointed to areas where the US lacks robust domestic supply. A total of 29% of respondents said that wafers and ingots would be the “highest priority” for inclusion in 45X coverage, followed by 16% who said polysilicon.

Transcript SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: When Hurricane Helene hit western North Carolina two years ago, it killed 108 people.
The install is a part of a $5 million state-funded initiative to get 26 such solar microgrids into libraries, fire stations and community centers - places people can come to after disasters.
Beacon of Hope is one of the first gathering places to get one of the planned solar microgrids.

text:
Transcript

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

When Hurricane Helene hit western North Carolina two years ago, it killed 108 people. It also left millions without power, some of them for months. Now, to try to become more resilient to future disasters, microgrids are popping up in public spaces where people often gather after storms. Katie Myers of Grist and Blue Ridge Public Radio reports.

(SOUNDBITE OF TOOLS CLINKING)

KATIE MYERS, BYLINE: Ryan Callahan is drilling a few screws into a panel in a back room of the Beacon of Hope Food Pantry in Marshall, North Carolina.

RYAN CALLAHAN: At this point, we've got everything plugged in, and we're about to put on the final covers - so kind of buttoning everything up.

MYERS: Callahan and another electrician, Steve Porvaznik, are putting the final touches on a solar install. It's a microgrid.

STEVE PORVAZNIK: We have three batteries plus two booster packs. So, in case of an outage, we were able to back up the whole store, essentially.

MYERS: The batteries store power from 74 solar panels on the roof of the organization's big warehouse-style building. The install is a part of a $5 million state-funded initiative to get 26 such solar microgrids into libraries, fire stations and community centers - places people can come to after disasters.

JESSI KOONTZ: These five - this row - coolers and freezers. And then this is our shopping space.

MYERS: Beacon of Hope director Jessi Koontz walks past an array of appliances. The group now helps 1,600 families each week with food. After closing the door to her office, Koontz says the last few years have been tough.

KOONTZ: Everything's been kind of compounded since the pandemic, and I feel like we were just kind of getting back on track when Helene hit.

MYERS: And since the storm, she says, hunger has increased in her community by about 50%. The center's power bills are now $1,200 per month, so she hopes the new solar install could save them some much needed money to feed people.

KOONTZ: People already come here, and so how can we, like, maximize the resources that are available when they come here?

MYERS: If the power goes out from disaster or other reasons, she says, more people can come here, get their phones charged, get on the internet and get food. Beacon of Hope is one of the first gathering places to get one of the planned solar microgrids. Sarah Nichols helps to find the best candidates for the solar installations. She's with a local economic development group. These microgrids will go up over the next few years in places where they'll be most effective, she says, and safe from flooding or mudslides, which caused most of the deaths from Helene.

SARAH NICHOLS: Should we put it in, say, a more rural area or in a community that might not traditionally get access to government services?

MYERS: As the region continues to take lessons from Helene, local leaders hope these solar microgrids can give people in distress a safe place to land. North Carolina officials say, along with the solar grids, other post-Helene and climate change preparedness projects can take shape - things like resilient internet and cell service.

For NPR News, I'm Katie Myers in Marshall, North Carolina.

"It has never been more important in the U.S. that we are creating a pipeline of new engineers who will be able to walk in on a factory floor and participate in new factories," said NC State Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost Jim Pfaendtner.

Though the makerspace is housed at NC State, university leaders said it is also intended to support industry partners. Among them is Toyota, which operates a nearly 7 million-square-foot battery manufacturing facility in Randolph County and plans to use the space for training and research.

Bridges said the partnership opportunities could be just as valuable as the technology itself.

"It allows for a lot of unique connections to be made with different companies around the area as well as with professors at the school who come from different backgrounds, national labs, industry or just academia," he said.

Dr. Shelby Pillai, an NC State faculty member involved with the project, said the makerspace is designed to support both education and innovation.

ALSO SEE | Future of flight displayed at NC aviation event

"I feel like it's a good mix," Pillai said. "There's pretty established fundamentals that we can learn and give our students a good footing, but then there's still a lot of space for the researchers to explore and try and innovate."

Unlike a traditional teaching laboratory, Pillai said the makerspace is designed to help students solve real-world problems and continue refining their work.

"We spent some time working on making her batteries, going through her process, and they're performing better now," Pillai said of one student project. "That's something that we can continue to support because this is a makerspace and not just a teaching lab."

For students like Bridges, the new facility represents an opportunity to be part of an industry that is rapidly evolving.

"Just looking at all the new equipment in here, I think it's going to be really cool," he said.

The Battery and Energy Storage Technology Makerspace officially opened last week.

name: North Carolina Environment
title: RTP 3.0: What the Research Triangle can teach us about building together - WRAL
authors: Steve Rao, WRAL TechWire contributor, Steve Rao, WRAL TechWire contributor
description:
When I moved to North Carolina nearly 20 years ago, I knew about Research Triangle Park.
Archie Davis believed Research Triangle Park had to be about more than private investment.
He helped transform the original concept into a nonprofit model, raising $1.425 million from more than 800 contributors to establish the Research Triangle Foundation and Research Triangle Institute.
From RTP to RTP 3.0 Scott Levitan inherited that remarkable legacy, but he understood that RTP had to evolve with a changing economy and workforce.
RTP 3.0 is more than a plan for the next 50 years of Research Triangle Park.
text:
When I moved to North Carolina nearly 20 years ago, I knew about Research Triangle Park. I knew it was home to IBM and some of the world's leading research and technology companies, and that Duke, UNC-Chapel Hill and NC State were central to the Triangle's growing reputation.

However, I saw RTP differently then than I do today. It was primarily a place where people went to work.

Today, it has become a destination — a place where people work, live, gather, innovate and build the future.

I have seen RTP's impact from several perspectives. Through my career in technology and startups, I saw how the Triangle's research, talent and business ecosystem helped companies grow. As a former Morrisville Town Council member, I saw how that success reached far beyond the Park's boundaries, attracting investment and talent, creating jobs and shaping the communities around it.

This evolution was the focus of a recent conversation I had with Scott Levitan, president and CEO of the Research Triangle Foundation, on my Leaders & Legends program on Radio Nyra.

Listen to my conversation with Scott Levitan

As Scott prepares to retire after nine years leading the foundation, our conversation gave me an opportunity to reflect not only on his tenure, but also on the much larger story of RTP and the leaders who made it possible.

The Visionaries Who Started It All

The story of RTP began with visionaries like Gov. Luther Hodges and Archie Davis, the legendary chairman of Wachovia Bank.

In the 1950s, North Carolina was looking toward a new economic future. Our traditional industries were the foundation of the state's economy, but leaders understood that education, research and technology would be critical to what came next.

Archie Davis believed Research Triangle Park had to be about more than private investment. He helped transform the original concept into a nonprofit model, raising $1.425 million from more than 800 contributors to establish the Research Triangle Foundation and Research Triangle Institute.

Then came Gov. Terry Sanford.

In 1965, Sanford helped secure a $70 million federal investment for the National Environmental Health Sciences Center in RTP. Soon after, IBM announced plans for a major research facility in the Park.

Those investments helped establish the foundation for the innovation economy we know today.

Sanford understood that economic development was not simply about recruiting companies. It was about creating an ecosystem in which universities, government, business, research and talent could reinforce one another.

That became the DNA of RTP.

Governor Jim Hunt and the Next Generation

Gov. Jim Hunt built on that foundation by making education, research, technology and economic development central to North Carolina's long-term strategy.

Hunt understood that our greatest economic asset was our people. Investing in universities, community colleges and research would allow North Carolina to compete for the industries of the future.

Under Hunt and the governors who followed, that strategy continued to evolve. North Carolina increasingly positioned itself as a destination for technology, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, advanced manufacturing and other high-growth industries.

The results can be seen across the Triangle and the state.

Companies such as Biogen, Novo Nordisk, Pfizer and FUJIFILM Diosynth Biotechnologies have helped make the region a major life sciences center. The next generation of technology investment is arriving as well, with Apple's planned North Carolina presence representing another significant chapter in the state's economic story.

Governors from Hunt through Gov. Josh Stein have continued to sell North Carolina to the best companies, entrepreneurs and talent in the world.

The names and industries change. The political parties change. The economy changes.

But the strategy endures: invest in people, strengthen our institutions, build infrastructure and create an environment where innovation can thrive. This is the winning playbook for North Carolina.

From RTP to RTP 3.0

Scott Levitan inherited that remarkable legacy, but he understood that RTP had to evolve with a changing economy and workforce.

His charge was to help transform RTP from primarily a place where people worked into a destination where people could live, work, gather and play.

He did exactly that.

Frontier RTP created a home for entrepreneurs and emerging companies. Boxyard RTP brought restaurants, retail, entrepreneurs and the community together in a new way. Hub RTP is creating a mixed-use environment where people can work, live, eat, gather and innovate.

And now RTP 3.0 is looking decades into the future.

What impressed me most during my conversation with Scott was his understanding that RTP's greatest asset has never simply been its land, buildings or companies.

It is the people — and the connections among them.

I have witnessed that firsthand. In technology, I saw companies come to the Triangle because of our talent and universities. As a Morrisville Town Council member, I saw the regional growth that followed — new businesses, new residents, new infrastructure and new opportunities.

RTP's influence does not stop at its property lines. It is part of the economic and civic fabric of the entire Triangle.

A Lesson for Divisive Times

Perhaps that is the most important lesson RTP offers us today.

We live in a time when our country can feel deeply divided. Politics divides us. Geography divides us. Institutions sometimes compete rather than collaborate.

But RTP's history shows what is possible when people choose to build together.

Archie Davis needed hundreds of North Carolinians to believe in his vision. Terry Sanford needed federal partners, universities and business leaders. Jim Hunt understood that education and economic development had to move together. Scott Levitan needed the community to embrace a new vision for RTP.

Each generation built on the work of the one before it.

None could have predicted exactly what RTP would become.

They simply believed that North Carolina could build something extraordinary — and they were willing to invest in that future.

This is the lesson we need today.

We don't have to agree on everything to accomplish great things together.

We can disagree politically and still invest in our communities. We can come from different regions, industries and backgrounds and still share a vision for a stronger North Carolina.

RTP reminds us that collaboration is not a weakness, but a competitive advantage.

The most important projects often take decades. They require leaders willing to build something that may ultimately be completed by someone else.

That means looking beyond the next election or the next political disagreement and asking a bigger question:

What are we building for the next generation?

Thank you, Scott, for your leadership, your vision and your commitment to North Carolina. Let's continue the great work you helped lead.

Your legacy will live on in Frontier, Boxyard, Hub RTP and RTP 3.0. But more importantly, it will live on in the entrepreneurs, researchers, students, workers and families who will build what comes next.

When I moved here nearly 20 years ago, I could not have imagined the RTP I see today. My career in technology and my years serving Morrisville have given me an even greater appreciation for what this region has become.

The leaders who created RTP could not have imagined it either.

They simply believed in the possibilities.

Now it is our turn.

RTP 3.0 is more than a plan for the next 50 years of Research Triangle Park. It is a reminder of what North Carolina can accomplish when we put aside our differences, find common ground and build together.

Different generations. Different leaders. Different perspectives. One shared vision.

That is the real legacy of RTP.

And perhaps its greatest lesson is the simplest:

We may not always agree on where we start or how we get there. But when we come together around a shared vision of a better future, there is almost no limit to what we can build.

That is the North Carolina I believe in.

And that is the North Carolina we should continue building — together.

name: American Energy
title: Turn Energy Efficiency Into Strategic Advantage - MIT Sloan Management Review
authors: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Ina M. Sebastian, Thomas Haskamp, Daniel Woerner, Lukas Falcke, Stephanie L. Woerner
description:
A predictable consequence of the conflict was a dramatic increase in the price of crude oil, the primary benchmark for global energy costs.
The pressure to reduce costs is likely to drive more corporate efforts to improve energy efficiency.
While that’s good for sustainability, our research suggests that energy efficiency can also deliver measurable cost savings, enhance resilience, and fuel growth.
Attention to energy efficiency can lower per-unit manufacturing costs, reduce exposure to energy-price volatility, and sustain margins during energy shocks.
Company executives made energy efficiency a clear priority, with defined accountability and performance targets.
text:
Businesses working to manage their spending on energy were dealt a blow in late February following military action by the U.S. and Israel against Iran. A predictable consequence of the conflict was a dramatic increase in the price of crude oil, the primary benchmark for global energy costs. The price of a barrel of crude oil shot up from $67 in early March to $112 in early April; by early June, it had come down to $80, still a roughly 25% year-over-year price increase.

Geopolitical conflict can bring exceptional volatility to energy costs, but steadily rising expenditures have been the underlying trend for companies since 2022, putting pressure on their profit margins. Energy is a central input in energy-intensive industries such as cement, chemicals, and metals, which account for roughly three-quarters of industrial energy demand. Companies that rely on global supply chains, and even companies that consume relatively less energy in their operations, like food processors, are feeling the effects of rising fuel and power costs.

The pressure to reduce costs is likely to drive more corporate efforts to improve energy efficiency. While that’s good for sustainability, our research suggests that energy efficiency can also deliver measurable cost savings, enhance resilience, and fuel growth. Attention to energy efficiency can lower per-unit manufacturing costs, reduce exposure to energy-price volatility, and sustain margins during energy shocks. The companies we studied have cut their energy use at some facilities by up to 50% and reported efficiency gains of 10% to 20% in their core industrial processes.

Upgrades to digital systems, manufacturing equipment, and facilities all played a role in those outcomes. The key to success, however, came not from any upgrade made in isolation but from having a comprehensive strategy that linked improvements together. Company executives made energy efficiency a clear priority, with defined accountability and performance targets.
